MIDDLE-CLASS ,REPIEF COM MI FrEES.
Help for, -the Lancashire co-operatives!
Help for the .Lancashire Trades Unionists !
Help for the.provident operatives of the cotton
districts I Help Y'or the victims Of Poor-law
'Help for the victims of the red-tapeism !
jealousies, favouritism, and prejudices, of the
Middle-Class Relief Committees.! These are
the cries now coming up, trumpet-tongued,
from the operatives of the distressed manufac-
turing districts to their ,brethren the working
men of London. The men of Lancashire make
no complaint of any backwardness in their fel-
low workmen ofLondon-and elsewhere to con-
tribute to the relief fund; on the contrary,
they acknowledge and honour the liberal ity they
are everywhere displaying, but they implore
them to send their liberal contributions through
a channel that will ensure their being dis-
tributed on the same terms as that on which
they are given., on that or 'distress alone,
irrespective of creed, politics, or class. While
acl:nowledging the workmen of London are
nobly performing one part of their duty, by
liberally subscribing, they say they are
neglecting the next important duty,—seeing
that the funds they thus contribute are dis-
tributed as they would themselves have
distributed them, were they acting as a relief
committee. The men of Lancashire complain,
and justly, that the local relief committees
now existing in the Lancashire towns and
villages are almost universally composed of
squires, manufacturers, clergymen, and the
well-to-do shopkeepers, working men being
systematically excluded. Sir JOHN KAY
SHIITTLEWORTH, on the first formation of these
relief committees, said:—" W orking men
_must not be allowed to send deputies to these
committees, because the squires and manu-
facturers would not sit at the same board with
them !" And this principle has been rigidly
enforced. Hence the dissatisfaction which
has arisen; hence the abuses which have crept
in; hence the refusal of relief to Co-operatives
and active Trades Unionists. Let it be remem-
bered, however, that while these committees
refuse to allow working men to sit with them,
they eagerly receive subscriptions from the
working classes; although unwilling to associate
personally with the working man in the holy
cause of Charity, they do not object to handle
the working man's subscriptions; and in the
same breath in which they insult the working
classes by declaring them unworthy to sit
with them on their committees, they praise
these working classes for the manly fortitude,
the Christian resignation, the patient endur-
.ance, and orderly manner in.which they bear
their unmerited privations. Out .upon such
hypocrites! The men :Of Lancashire do not
impeach the honesty of these relief committees,
but they, challenge the justice; policy,- and
humanity of their conduct. They'say that to
refuse relief, to a member .of a Co—operative
society until he has pauperised himself by
disposing of his shares, is neither just or ,
politic;' that it punishes provident habits,
and offers a premium to improvidence. They '
say to refuse relief to a starving man because
he formerly took an active part in a strike, or
trade, dispute, is inhuman, and displays a
spirit of vindictiveness unworthy of men
engaged in a charitable cause.
But it may be said, and indeed has been
said, what proof is there that these local relief
committees act as above described? Let me
state the indictment, and produce the evident
in its support.
The indictment-brought against the local
relief committees by the operatives of Lanca-
shire contains four counts, as follows That
they are exclusive in their composition. 2.
That they reftis'e relief to any operative who
may have connected himself with a working
man's committee to supplement the relief
given either by the poor-law guardians or the
middle class relief committees. 3. That they
refuse relief to co-operators holding shares in
any store or mill; as well as to active trades'
unionists. 4. That they refuse relief to any
operative Who may receive relief from the
poor-law guardians, although that relief is
notoriously insufficient.

To the first and last counts there is a tacit
plea of guilty, the fact is too patent for denial.
What is the evidence in support of the others?
Let me first notice that given by the Rev. Mr.
Verity, Chairman of the East Lancashire
Central Operatives Relief Committee. Space
will not permit me to notice more than one or
two of the eases he cites, but they are illustra-
tive of a large class.
,He says :

J. H., a man with eight children, was connected with
the Padiham Operatives' Committee. This man applied
to the middle class relief committee for a blanket, a bed,
and a petticoat for one of his family. As soon as he made
his appearance, a manufacturer said to him J. H. is your
name, is it not?' It is.' 'Don't you sit on the
working men's committee?' 'I do.' 'Well, as long as
you are connected with that committee, you get nothing
from us!'

B. K. was the brother of one of the members of the
middle-class committee. ' He went to the committee to
beg for food and clothing. The secretary, when he heard
the man's name said, 'there is your brother.' The
brother nodded his head. 'You had better fill up that form
and then get your brother to sign it, to corroborate the truth
of your statement, or you can have no rel,ef.' But the
brother refused to sign it, and the poor man was sent
away. The explanation of this was,_ that in a trade dis-
pute sometime previous the man, who was an operative,
refused to allow his three children to work as knobstica
for his brother, who was the manufacturer. -,
But now, when employment has ceased, the condition
of the co-operator is deplorable in the extreme. He finds
his little capital locked up. He cannot realise except at
such a disadvantage as will throw away, perhaps, the
savings of years. He cannot borrow money on the
security of his scrip on account of his inconvertibility.
The poor man goessto the middle class relief fund, and
asks for food or *raiment. The committee, composed of
manufacturers, turn round and say, 'We have you fast ;
YOU have sunk your capital, and need not expect relief till
you have sold your scrip.' Perhaps the man says, 'But
we cannot sell our scrip. Will you lend us something on
the security of the scrip?' The answer is, 'We are not
pawnbrokers. Go to the parish.' The naan goes to the
parish. The relieving officer says, 'Are you a co-operq.•
tor?' 'I am., 'Then we can't relieve you. 'You are
not a pauper, and we cannot give you relief.' So the
poor operative falls, to the ground. Many men have
thrown their scrip into the fire; others have sold £lO
worth for 10s. The case of one man which has come
before
destroye
my notice is extremely hard. This man actually
d his scrip ,in order that its possession might not
prevent him receiving relief. The relieving officer gave
the man relief to the amount of six or eight shillings.
The board, of gum diens heard of the particulars of the case.
They went to the secretary of the co-operative society,
and examined the books. The man had forgotten to have
his name eraßed.when he destroyed his scrip. His name
was, consequently, remaining on the books. Immediately
the man was taken op and imprisoned for receiving relief,
because his name was on the books of a co-operative
society at the time that he received the parochial relief.
The two delegates sent into Lancashire (and
every day further proves how important
it was they . were sent) by the Lon-
.
don Work.ing .Mens' Central Committee
,
to inquire into the truth of these statements
have ' returned, after one week's absence,
and made ' their report, entirely
cor-
roborative of all that has been. asserted by
the Rev. Mr. VERITY and the East Lancashire
Committee. The temptation that exists
amongst the Manufacturers on these relief
committees to revenge - themselves on their
workmen for old grievances, and trade dis-
putes, is very great, and is not often resisted.
i interviews ,

operatives. in Burnley, Bacup, Padiham, &c.;
who had been treated as Mr. VERITY describes,
and have embodied the "names; dates, and
circmnstances,, of their cases into a report
which will be laid before a special meeting of

articles.title: AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL.
articles.text:
AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL.

No. 63.

the London Trades' Delegates, to be called
together on the second Wednesday in January
next. The particulars of these cases will be
found to fully bear out all that has been stated
on this subject. In the meantime here are
a few of them. as a sample of the lot :
_

T. C. (Burpley) possessed three looms in a co-operative
mill. On applying for relief the, committee offered to ad-
vance him a small sum on a mortgage on these looms.
He objected to this mode of relief, and on his refusal the
committee turned his three children out of the school con-
nected with it!

H. T. had been a sa‘ing man. He held one £5O share
and eight £lO shares in a co-operative 'mill. Had been
out of work for twelve mor.ths, sustaining himself by
selling his shares, until he had but one £l.) share left.
Wishing to retain this, he was at last compelled to apply
to the relief committee; but although he pleaded hard,
they refused him any relief unless he would dispose of the
last £lO share. He declined to do this, and is now almost
starving! •
E. C., an operative, lived with his mother and sisters.
They each held one share in aco operative store. Appliel
for relief. Refused, unless he sold his share. Complied
with the request; and, having disposed of the share at a
sacrifice' applied again for relief. Was again refused,
until his mother and sister had also disposed of their
shares
A. 8., an operative, who had invested his savings of
£3O in the purchase of a pianoforte, and C. D., an opera-
-tive, who held a £3O share in a co-operative mill, both
applied for relief: C. D. was refused relief because he held
this £3O share, but A. B. was relieved without being re-
quired to dispose of his pianoforte I
In Bacup there are forty cotton mills, twelve of which,
employing when in work about 4,000 operatives, be-
long to co-operatives; only two of these are now working.
The operatives holding shares in these mills, although they
and idle' are producing no profit, refused relief!
And so on, ad infinitum.
If further proof were wanting in support of
these counts in the indictment, it may be found
in the last printed report of the Manchester
Central Committee, in which they acknowledge
the existence of the evil, but, considering it a
"delicate subject," refrain from issuing any
positive instructions to the local committees in
connection with them. The Rev. Mr. Verity
Oso, last week, accompanied by a deputation
from the London Working Men's Central Com-
mittee, waited upon the Lord Mayor's Com-
mittee at the Mansion House, leaving for its
use a written statement of the treatment of
Co-operatives by the local committees, and
praying for a special grant from that com-
mittee to the East Lancashire Operative's
Central committee. The Lord Mayor's Com-
mittee, however, met on Friday last, voted
several large sums of money to different towns,
and adjourned for a fortnight, without taking
any notice of the application made by the
deputation.
_ - - -

Working men of London! what is your
reply to the cry rising up from your co-opera-
the, unionist, and provident brethren in Lan-
cashire? Will you aid them, or still send your
subscriptions to those committees which
refuse them relief? Continue sending your
subscriptions to those channels which pour
them either into the Mansion House, or the
Manchester Central Committee, and your
brethren of the above classes will still go un-
relieved. Pay your subscriptions into the
London Working Men's Central Committee,
composed of delegates representing and having
the confidence of societies and . subscribing
bodies of working men, and they will go direct to
the treasurer of the East Lancashire Operatives
Committee, who relieve all classes, whether
co-operators or competitors; whether unionists
or non-unionists; whether paupers or non-
paupers; the only test being that of distress
from the prevailing cause, and unwilling idle.
ness. All monies sent into this committee are
acknowledged in the BEE-HIVE, and the ser-
vices of the committee and its officers are given
gratuitously. Continue sending your sub-
scriptions to the proprietors of journals,' be-
cause they have a reputed large circulation,
and they may serve to swell the pride of those
proprietors, but will not serve the cause of
your ill-used provident Lancashire brethren.
Pay them into the London Working Men's
Committee, and they will be ctevoted to these
men. By adopting the latter course, you will
be standing by your own order; by the former,
you will. be betraying its interests, at, cl well
deserve the SCOURGE.

ALLEORD MURDER 'ON BOARD SHIP.—A grave in-
quiry was conirnenced by Mr. 'Coroner Walthew, at
Limehouße, on Monday. The body of a young man
named Wm. Curtis was brought into the 'West India
Docks on board the ship Martha Pope. It was stated
that he bad died while the vessel was coming up the
river, and application was made to an undertaker to
bury him. The undertaker asked Doctor Giles to give
the necessary certificate of death, but that gentleman
after seeing the body declined to do so until an' inquest
had been held upon it. His description of the appear-
an6e. of the body is horrible. The unfortunate deceased,
according to the belief of Doctor Giles, had had no food
for a fortnight before his death, and when in a state of
tirostratisu had been brutally lashed with a thick cord.
Doctor Giles says the captain of the vessel offered Min
£7 to pass over the matter, which, as an honest man,
he indignantly refused. The captain, who was also
examined, denied this, and. stated that he had behaved
well to the man who is dead. The inquest was adjourned
for further evidence. The adjourned inquest was held
on Wednesday, and aiain adjourned, but Captain Stone
Was given into custody by the brother of the deceased
on the charge of murder.
FuEzuom TO THE SLAVE.—Daring the last fertnight
Mr. George Thompson in addition" to , attending
several meetings the metropolis, called for the
purpose of expressing sympathy with, the anti-
slavery policy of the United States Government and
Congress, has held similar meetings in Hanley,
Burslem, and. Newcastle, , Staffordshire; also at
Basingstoke, Hampshire; Stratford, Essex; and
Banbury, Oxfordshire. The audiences have been
large and enthusiastic, and without exception have
expressed warm approbation of the measures
adopted by the United Stites for promoting the
emancipation of the slave population. On the 31st
,inst., a great-meeting of the working classes will be
held in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, to adopt
resolutions and an address to President Lincoln;
and on the same day Mr. Thompson will address a
similar meeting in Sheffield.

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1862.

DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

LONDON WORKING MEN'S CENTRAL COM.

MITTEE.

The fourth weekly meeting of the trade delegates
forming this committee was held on Tuesday evening, at
the offices, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street. Present :
Messrs. Cremer (carpenter), Murray (boot •closer),
Jarvis (carpenter), Niettss (plasterer); Dormer (Car-
penter), Walker (bookbinder), Treinlett (carpenter);
Burns (brickmaker), Charlie (carpenter), with the
treasurer, Mr. Potter. The secretary being absent,
being at work on a country job, the treasurer acted
for him.

Letters were read from the Shipwrights' Union,
from the Plasterers' Society, and from the Rev. Mr.
Verity, the latter urging a meeting of the trades in
London at an early period, to which a deputation from
Lancashire should be sent if required.
After some discussion it was proposed and carried
That a special delegate meeting of the London trades
be held on the second Wednesday in January, on the
subject of the Lancashire distress, such meeting to be
convened by circular. _

Mr. Cramer brought up his written report of the
deputation to Lancashire, especially noticing the treat-
ment to which the co-operatives were subjected by the
middle-class relief committees. He had not had time
to notice all the cases that had come under the notice
of himself and his colleagues, but would complete them
by next weelc. .
It was resolved that the report of Mr. Cramer be
read at length' to the erisning meeting'd trades' dele-
gates, and that in the meantime its publication be
postponed.
- The treasurer reported that he had received up to
Monday, since the remittance to Padiham on Saturday,
£2O, but a considerable addition might and would be
received before Friday next; and he was instructed to
remit to the East Lancashire Central Committee at
Padiham on Friday next the whole of the monies he
might receive up to that date.
The expense of the deputation to the Mansion-
house, for loss of time, only its, was ordered to be
paid to Messrs. Burns and Cremer. '' •

- The committee adjourned until next Wednesday
exening at 8 o'clock.

EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL OPERATIVES'

RELIEF FUND.

The usual weekly meeting of the executive took
place on Monday evening last at the Committee
Rooms, Speak-buildings, Padiham. Present, the Rev.
E. A. Verity, 8.D., rector of Habergham (president);
deputies for Burnley: J. Pinder, L. Shackleton, and
James Crompton; for Habergham : G. Hargreaves,
James Heap, and Henry Whitehead; for Great Har-
wood: Enoch Mercer, Moses Redyherd, and W.
Fielden ; for Padiham: John Howarth, James Den-
bigh, Wm. Wilkinson, and Joseph Peacock (hon.
secretary.)
The minutes of the last meeting were read and con-
firmed.

The Secretary read several communications, an-
nouncing subscriptions as follows: From Mr. Stratton
Middleton-on-nes, Bs. 6d.; Mr. E. C. Denton, of
Leeds, 7s. 2d.; Mr. W. B. Dyson, Spennymoor, 125.;
Mr. Maitland, of London, £7 35.; and the London
Working Men's Central Committee, £4O. (Applause.)
The Treasurer read a letter from Mr. Charles
Williams, announcing a substantial gift about to arrive
from the Liverpool Working Men's Central Committee.
Last week, 280 families, consisting of 1,405 persons,
were relieved. Clothing was received from A. W.
Critchlie, Esq., of Anglesea, who has also offered his
services to collect.

The thanks of the meeting were tendered to each of
those gentlemen for their kind exertions.
The President then gave an account of his mission
to London. The best thanks of the meeting were
accorded him.

Mr. Denbigh was surprised to think that the Man-
sion House Committee bad, not long ago, sent a grant
to the poor co-operators, whose number must be about
28,000.

Mr. Shackleton gave much credit to the London
trades for drawing the attention of the Mansion House
Committee to this neglect, because if the neglect was
continued, it must be attributed to design.
Mr. Heap had no confidence that the Manchester
Central would ever assist co-operators in any shape;
they would be only too glad to bury it in a pauper's
grave.

The President thought the American subscriptions
might be secured to the co-operators, if proper repre-
sentations were made to the Ambassador in London.

Mr. Moses Redyherd suggested that the wO;lii-nc,
men of London should send a deputation to wait on the
American Ambassador in London. Cousins over the
water are sometimes more charitable than relations at
home. (Elear, hear.)
Mr. Fielden said, that in Great Harwood, so soon as
it was known that a Working Man's Committee was
formed in connection with the East Lancashire Central
the middle classes immediately formed one of their own.
(Cheers.)
All the deputies spoke of the intensity of the distress
and of the partiality and inadequacy of the middle
class committee.

The President announced his intention of forming a
relief committee in Blackburn at an early day.
Grants were given to the following places: Padi-
ham, £10; Bentley, £10; Habergham and Gannow,
£10; Great Harwood, a. The meeting then termi-
nated.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN OMNIBUS CONDUCTOR.-Mr.
W. Payne, held an inquest at Guy's Hospital, touching
the death of John Harvey, aged 38, an omnibus con-
ductor, who was killed on London Bridge, under the
following Melancholy circumstances. William Lambert
said that he was the driver of one of Wood's omni-
buses, plying between Hackney-road and Camberwell..
gate. On Friday evening last, as they were on the
crown of the bridge, coming towards Southwark, One
of the horses fell. The harness was taken off and the
horse was got up. Deceased stooped-down to get up
the harness, when some one struck the animal, which
kicked out and struck the deceased on the forehead
and under the ear. He was carried to the hospital,
but died before his admission. The coroner having
summed up, the jury returned a verdict of Accidental
death.'

DEATH FROM SWALLOWING FALSE TEETH.—An in-
quiry was held at the Prince • Regent Tavern, Globe.
road, Mile-end, by Mr. Walthew, respecting the death
of Mary Harrington, aged fifty-six, which occurred
from swallowing a plate of false teeth. James Stephens
said that last Tuesday deceased, while walking across
the room, she put both bands to her breast, and uttered
a piercing scream. He caught her and placed her on
the sofa. He thought she was in a fit, and ran for help.
She died almost immediately in great agony. Dr. J.
Reily said that he was called in, and found deceased
had just died. He took from the trachea a false tooth
and a portion of the metal plate. There was the cor-
responding portion of the metal plate fixed to the
palate. The metal was of the commonest material,
and was BO soft that the nail could be easily put through
it. It was highly dangerous to manufacture plates of
such porous, weak metal. There was a lump of ginger
in the mouth, and no doubt in biting it the plate broknv.
and deceased swallowed it suddenly, and died tiora
slow suffocation. The jury returned a verdict that
deceased lost her life through misfortune.

articles.title: CHRISTMAS ENTER TAINHENTS.
articles.text:
CHRISTMAS ENTER TAINHENTS.

THE PANTOMIMES AND BU RLESQUES.
- COVENT GARDEN.

The performances commenced with the opera of the
Bohemian Gin,' • after which was presented the new
pantomime of Mr. H. J. Byron. The story is very
familiar to all readers of nursery tales, and-is pretty
closely followed. The scenery is most magnificent, and
worthy the reputation of the house. The trandoima-
tion scene is by Mr. Calcott, and is one of considerable
beauty. The opening was well sustained by Mr. G.
H. Payne, the Prince of burlesque, and the pantomimic
portion of the piece by Mr. H. Payne and F. Payne
as clown and harlequin, Mr. Barnes as pantaloon, and
Mrs. S. Adams as columbine.

articles.title: DRURY-LANE.
articles.text:
DRURY-LANE.

Magnificently embellished, and thoroughly reno-
vated, this theatre opened under the sole management
of Mr. Edmund Falconer, the late successfullessee of
the Lyceum. The opening piece was the drama of
Next of Kin,' and followed by tha pantomime of
'Little Goody Two Shoes; or, Harlequin and Cock
Robin,' in which two familiar stories belonging to the
juvenile library hive been interwoven in a manner
that will doubtless satisfy the most scrupulous sticklers
for the dramatic unities, at the same time that the
impressions of childhood are strengthened rather than
disturted. The author is, as usual, Mr. E. L. Blan-
chard, who has invested the subject with an interest
that will commend it to children of a larger growth.
The principal parts in the opening are sustained by
that lively danseuse-subrette, Miss Lydia Thompson,
Miss Helen Howard, Miss Kate Saxon, Mr. Joe
Robins, Mr. Weston, and the indispersable Torn
Matthews. The scenery by Messrs. Grieve and Telbin,
the physiognoinical illustrations and artistic designs by
the renowned Dykwynkyn, the ballet arrangements of
Mr. Oscar Byrne, and the musical embellishments of
Mr. Barnard are unusually extensive, novel, and
effective. The double corps for the Harletuinade
consists of Messrs. Harry Boleno and C. Lauri for
Clowns, Cormack and St. Maine for Harlequins,
Tanner and .Deulin Johnson for Pantaloons and
Madadame Boleno and the Misses Gunnis for Colum-
bines. Numerous mechanical changes are intro-
duced, both in the opening and the Harlequinade.

HAYMARKET.

The first piece was the everlasting American
Cousin,' after which an extravaganza, by Mr. William
Brough, founded on Dr: Johnson's well-Known tale of
Ras- elas,' with its continuation in Dinarbes,'
followed. The opening scene discloses the 'Happy.
Valley,' and the story throughout follows With tole-
rable closeness the vicissitudes of fortune of the
philosophic prince. Rasselas ' is played by Miss
Louise Keeley, an.l Mr. Tilbury has been especially
engaged to represent Dr. Johnson; Mr. Compton is
Imlac,' Miss Lucy Rushton, ‘Dinarbes.' In the
course of the piece Mdlle. Idaho appears in A Diver-
tissement de Clochettes.'

articles.title: rEiNcEss's.
articles.text:
rEiNcEss's.

The performance here cdthinenced with the drama,
of 'Tim; Tries All,' and the pantomime was en-
titled 'Prince Itiquet with the 'tuft; or, Harlequin
Old Mother Shipton; and has been furtiisled by Mr.
E. L. Blanchard. The scenic illustrations, which are
from the renowned pencil of Mr. William Beverley,
are singularly fanciful and ingenious particulary the
Fairies Haunt in the Lake of the Water Lilies, when
the ballet takes place. Mr. Belmore plays the King,'
Mr. C. Seyton Prince Riquet,' Mr. Cockerill Mother
Shipton,' Miss Florence Gray Mother, Bunch,' Miss
Hudspeth the 'Princess Amouretta,' and'a troupe of
more than a hundred children and coryphees figure in
the ballet. • The Music is Mr. Charles Hall. Mr.
Milano is Harlequin, Mr, Power Clown, Mr. Halford
Pantaloon, end Mdlle. Marie Collinson Columbine.

articles.title: T. JAMES'S.
articles.text:
T. JAMES'S.

'Golden Hair the Good' is the title of the Christmas
piece here. It is a fairy drama by Mr. H. J. Byron,
and turns upon - the adventures of a certain wood
nymph (Miss Herbert) who disgraces her fairy friends
by falliniz in love with a demo-.. Mr. and Mrs. Frank
Matthews have both excellent characters in the piece,
which is put upon the stage in 'a first-rate style
of elegance and completeness.

articles.title: AbBLPHI.
articles.text:
AbBLPHI.

Mr. Byron has selected the drama of George Barn-
well' as the groundwork of his burlesque pantomime
at this theatre: While adhering to the moral of the
moral of the play, he has, however, contrived to divest
it of the objectionable feature, and entirely recast the
story. The pantomime characters are sustained as
follows : Clown, Mr. Walter Hilyard; Pantaloon, Mr.
Paulo; Harlequin, Mr. John Lauri; Columbine, Miss

THE PERMISSIVE BILL.—A deputation from the exe-
cutive council of the 'United Kingdom Alliance waited
upon Sir George Grey on Tuesday, in reference to the
licensing system. The object of the deputation was set
forth in a memorial which was presented to Sir George,
and which willed that the Government, in any measure
which might be brought in by them in reference to the
licensing system, would introduce a clause providing
'that any parish or township in which a majority of
two-thirds of the owners or occupiers so determine
shall be exempted from the operation of the provisions
for licensing the sale of intoxicating liquors.' The
prayer of the memorial was enforced by several
members of the deputation but Sir George Grey did
not hesitate to state his objection to what was asked.
While he believed the gentleman presenting the me-
morial deserved every credit for their efforts to check
drunkenness, he thought the mode in which they pro-
posed to do it as not practicable, and could not hold
out any promise of support. [Why should this power
be placed in the hands of the 'owners or occupiers '
only, who, in most cases, must be an actual minority
to the whole number of inhabitants?—ED. •
SERIOUS ACCIDENT IN A. LIVERPOOL , CIRCUS.—Mr.
Henry Delevanti, the trapeze performer in Bell's Hip-
podrome, Liverpool, had one of his ribs and thighs
broken during his aerial display. on Monday night.
Delevanti was going through the feats of Olmar when
the knot of one of the ropes slipped, and he dropped
heavily from the top of the circus to the bottom.. A
wire rope upon which Mrs. Delevanti performed broke
his fall, or he would have suffefed even more severely
than he did. No time was lost in conveying , the un-
fortunate fellow to the Northern Hospital, where he
now lies in as favourable a condition as might be ex-
pected. Delevanti, we believe, tied the rope himself,
and as he considered it sufficiently secure to risk his
life upon it, there is every probability that the knot
was good when he commenced his performance. Later
on, however, the strain, together, with the effect of the
atmosphere, must have caused it to slip, and hence the
accident. _ .

IThis society which employs several master book-
binders, has for the last three or four years adopted the
practice—in order to pay the least possible price for its
binding— of requiring fresh tenders for any job of mag-
nitude that it has to give out. The result of thus con-
tinually putting the work up to auction, it is superfluous
to say, is to set the employers to seek every means by
which the price of labour may be reduced, and cm have
no other end, finally, than that of the reduction of
wages. And however consistent this might be in the
firm of Shark, Graspall, and Grabbem,' it will be at
once seen that it does not harmonise with the objects
of such a society, which owes its support to the contri-
butions of the pious. Indeed this was seen by the
management of the society itself, who—upon the prac-
tice being commented upon in the publication The
Bookbinders' Trade Circular,' from which we make the
following extracts—disavowed it• altogether, and stated
that it was only under peculiar circumstances that such
was done, which circumstances having ceased to exist,
what appeared to be the , practice would cease also.
How this disavowal was acted upon the following ex-
tracts will show : .
We, however, are sorry to find that the same course
'is persisted in. There can be no doubt that on various
pretences fresh estimates are continually being re-
quired, not in the same way, but yet not the less
required and obtained, with the fullest intention of
getting the lowest .possible price, without the least
regard whether skilled and experienced workmen are
superseded, by boys, or whether, as the only possible
alternative, they are obliged to work for reduced
wages. There is always some reason given, but who
ever lacked a reason as an excuse for paying less? It
appears to be enough for the management of this
Society that the work can be done cheap, and the
cheaper the better, and such estimates will always
command the work of the Society. The intention can-
not be mistaken, for it is thus elucidated. Every one
connected with the trade knows that, in consequence of
the cotton famine, the price of the cloth used in bind-
in.' is much advanced; that which was before sold at
7d7 is now 91(1. per yard; the estimates for the books
covered with this material were made and accepted when
it was at its lowest price. In answer to representations
that the advanced price of this material in justice required
a corresponding advance in price, it was replied by the
management that there was no ajection to take into
consideration this rise, by putting the work up to
auction again. Those who do this work therefore must
either submit to this loss, make it up in the best way
they can, or run the risk of losing it altogether.
There is no doubt that the management of this Society
has a right to do this, but it does not comport with the
explanation given above. And we ask what could the
firm of Shark, Graspall, and Grabbem ' do more?
This question will require great force if we suppose
that among those from whom estimates have been
received there is a needy competitor who has lately
failed in business, and who largely employs boy
labour, that has repeatedly told the management that
be would take this kind of work at 10 per cent. leas
than it was paying to the other binders. And the
whole will receive further illustration from the follow-
ing fact. A new edition of the Psalms and Hymns
sold by this Society, comprising six different sorts of
books, from 24m0. up to ro3 al Bvo., has just been
printed, making together a large quantity of work.
For this fresh estimates were required from all the
binders, not that there was any necessity for this
course, as the difference in thickness, &e., could very
easily have been satisfactorily adjusted. This, how-
ever, we need not say, was not intended, and so
tenders were reqnired from each, and the lowest
tender accepted, which was stated by the management
to be 25 per cent, less than the highest. The accepted
tender was made by the individual above referred to,
who confessedly is only able to take it at this low
figure because be pays more than 33 per cent. less in
wages than the others. Of course he has a right to
pay what he pleases, but the fact remains that this low
price is only procured by the reduction of wages. Nor
is it difficult to get such a tender. It only requires a
needy man to whom ready money is an absolute neces-
sity to get almost any low price tendered. The Society
pays once a month. To get this return, to such an one
may be the difference between going on and stopping
altogether; he will, therefore, make any sacrifice, even
to the recoiling of scarcely any profit, or no profit at
all, to obtain it. And thus the prompt payment of
the Society may be used to great advantage, as the
above-menticined respectable firm would consider, to
obtain the •cheapetit possible price for the binding.
The only thing required is always To have at hand
such one from whom to obtain a tender.

The management very properly takes care that all
the binding executed for the Society shall be properly
done; to insure which a practical bookbinder has
lately been engaged to look over all the work sent in.
k low price, everybody knows, often insures an in-
ferior article; it, therefore, is in the highest degree
commendable to take every preizaution that the work
of this Society should not be executed in the inferior
way which is so often the result of paying a very low
price for it. But it also confesses the intention by the
care taken to guard against what is so frequently its
results. Should, however, the motive be denied, the
fact cannot be, nor its admirable adaptation to, and
perfect consistence with, the purpose mentioned.
We have nothing to do with the rivalry of different
employers, nor do we for a moment impugn the right
of the Society to call for what teAders it pleases; all
we insist upon is that such practice can only have in
the end one result, namely, the reduction of wages.
That such is also the opinion of the Society is clear
from the following extract from a tract on political
economy, published by it in 1857, called 'Lessons on
Political Economy,' taken from lesson the fourth, on
combinations and unions.'

The practice we have shown; here is the doc-
trine :

Wages are not dependent on the will of those who
pay them; nor is the master always able to pay his
workmen as large wages as he or they would desire. There
are various reasons for this. It may be that a master's
profit does not admit of his expending more than a given
sum in wages; and the capital he has invested in the
construction of '.his farm buildings, purchase of his
implements of husbandry, if he be a farmer; or of
his mill machinery if he be a manufacturer, oblige
him to require a remunerative interest for the money
he has laid out. In fact wages can only be altered by
changing the proportion between the number of labourers
and the funds set apart for their maintenance.' (The
italics are ours.)
Now we do not suppose the committee who super-
intended the publication of this work had
view the practice we have described above of calling
for fresh tenders until the price for binding was
so reduced that it, the master's profit, would not
admit of his paying higher' than a reduced rate of
wages, the 'given sum' which it would sure to be,
and indeed which it really is in the establishment of
the employer who obtained the last tender; but it
really fits it. The practice is just that of the cutting
firm we have alluded to, and this would be the defence,
supposing it to have employed as their solicitors Mr.
Samuel Warren's celebrated firm of 'Quirk, Gammon,
and Snap' to draw it up. We do not comment on the
rich bit of mystification about the funds set apart for
the maintenance Of labourers' so characteristic of this
firm and yet so transparent, for how at so low a tender
could more be 'set apart' for their maintenance?
Mr. 'Oiley Gammon,' of the above firm, would gloat
over enforcing a reason so indisputable that the men
must of necessity, receive less wages, as it was impossi.
ble for the employei out of his profit to pay more,
when he knew that the firm who employed .him had
cut under all others by a low price which created that
necessity! Nor would Quirk and Snap' be less
radiant with satisfaction at so successful a manoeuvre,
especially over those whom they believed could not
help themselves. •
But this is sad work. It grieves us to write thus
of such a 'Society; a Society which has for so long
worthily fulfilled the objects for which it was estab-
lished. Surely, if it has entered into coinpetition with
those whose only object is to realise money by any and
every means it has; for the time' mistaken its way, to
the injury Of the cause` and of the establishment it
represents. The.Establfshed Church, of which it is the
representative, has never taken this coarse. Emphati-
cally it has been the poor man's church, and has com-
manded respect accordingly. That there should be
proper economy no one 'will dispute, but it does not
become those who profess to promote Christian know-
ledge to resort to means which can only have the result
of reducing wages—the honest revenue of the poor. It
cannot be the wish of the supporters of this Society
that the poor should be made poorer that it may do a
greater amount of business as a trading firm. Surely
the contributions of the pious were never, given foithui
purpose.

MR. LANARD AHD HIS CONSTITUENTS—Mr. Layard,
M.P., addressed his constituents on. Monday night
at the London-bridge Hotel. After alluding to local
topics he went on. to deal with the foreign policy of
the Government. He defended what had been done
in China, and asked the approval of the meeting for
the course, pursued in regard to America. Referring
tG Greece he said the Government was prepared to
cede the lonian Islands to that country, if the
Greeks showed that they were able to maintain a
strong-constitutional government. A vote of thanks
to the hon. gentleman was passed. Nothing said
aibout, reform !

Nsw YORK, Dec 9, Evening.—The following is an
ibstract of dispatches published to-day, addressed by
Mr. Adams to Mr. Seward :
In June Mr. Adams writes that the darling desire of
the governing classes that America may be divided,
though subdued in expression by events, remains as
strong as ever. Mr. Adams writes, in October, th t he
has had an interview with Earl Russell, in which, refer-
ring to Mr. Gladstone's speech, Earl Russell said it was
not for him to disavow anything on the part of Mr.
Gladstone, but that Mr. G adstone had no idea, in say-
ing what he had, that there was serious intention to
justify any inferences of a disposition of the Govern-
ment to adopt a new policy. Earl Russell stated as
guardedly as possible that Lord Palmerston and the
other members of the Gibinet regretted Mr. Glad.tone's
speech, but it was still their intention to adhere to per-
fect neuL.L'ity, and let the struggle come to its natural
end without he smallest interference, direct or other-
wise. Earl Russell, however, could not say wh t cir-
cumstances might happen from month to month in the ,
future.'

Mr. Seward's recent communications to Mr. Adams
are summarisfd thus
'ln June Mr. seward writes that a list of purchases
made for the Confederates in England, which list had
fallen into the hands of the Federals, shows that the
complaints made to Earl Russell fell short of the re al
abuses of neutrality committed in England in the very
face of the British Government. 'The reb( Ilion,' says
Mr. Seward, is now approaching its end, and it is ju-t
at this moment proof becomes irresistible that if it had
succeeded its success would have been due to the
assistance derived from the English people.' Mr.
Seward says the President thinks it desirable that the
Enp.lish Government should consider before the war
closes what are likely to be the sentiments of England
and America towards each other after its termihation.
In August Mr. Seward writes that a war with England
could not fail to unite North and South. In November
Mr. Seward writes that while European parties are
more hostile than ever to America, America herself is
stronger to resist intervention than at aay former period.
Intervention would only afford an additional motive or
America to sustain her resolution to remain united.
Less than three years ago all England showed itself
desirous of friendship with America, and a similar desire
may before long recur. On the 3rd of the same month
Mr. Seward states that the President is compelled to
regard the destruction of ships by the Alabama as ,hav-
ing been made by British subjects in violation of the
law of nations. "It is presumed," says Mr. Seward,
"you have already brought the subject before the
British Government in that light. Legal proofs to
Support indemnity claims will be collected and trans-
mitted as soon as possible." A dispatch from Mr.
Seward to Mr. Dayton is also published, stating that
America has a right to insist that France shall not make
use of the war she is carrying on in Mexico to raise an
anti-Republican or anti American Government, or main-
tain such Government in power. France having dis-
claimed such designs, America is bound to wait, and
not to anticipate their exection. A dispatch from Mr.
Clay, in Russia, to Mr. Seward, dated January last,
urges him to offer to the Canadians union with America,
and to send men and money into Ireland to stir up
revolt. "V> ngeance will sooner or later overtake
England, the pel fidious aristocrat," says Mr. Clay.'
The cold is very severe in Virginia, and everything
is frozen.

Apprehensions of a battle in Tennessee have sub-
Bided.

n

articles.title: DISTRESS IN LANC.4SHIRE.
articles.text:
THE DISTRESS IN LANC.4SHIRE.

PRESTON-

Trade generally appears to he in a more hopeful con-
dition in Preston. The mills are running fuller time,
and the operatives are, as a natural consequenve, better
employed. The overseers have this week pleasatttlw
surprised all the ratepayers. It has been thought fkii
some time that the next rate they would levy would be
at the rate of ss. in the pound-2s. above the old one;
but they appear to think that the times are mending,
and they have fixed the rate at 2s. 6d. in the pound,
actually 6d. less than that for the post half year. The
number of paupers in Preston is decreasing; and the
chairman of the board of guardians thinks that we have
now seen the worst of these bad times. I hope he is a
true prophet. The fever is I regret to say, on the in-
crease. I cannot account for this. It was said thit it I
was caws d by the distress; but it is rather strange that,
whilst the alleged generator of it decreases, the malady
extends. The new fever ward, which was ordered several
weeks ago, has just been opened. The health of the town
generally seems to be satisfactory. The relief com-
mitt, e continue to prosecute tht ir duties in a most ener-
getic manner. This week they have expended upwards
of £3,000. For three or four weeks the Mansion
House and the Manchestfrr Central Committees have re-
fused to make any grant to Preston, in cousequence of
the large balance of money in the hands of the
treasurer. The result of this has been that the com-
mittee are found fault with for th ir niggardliness—
people say that they won't spend the money when, they
nave it. But another grant will soon be wanted if the
expenditure of this weak is any criterion. They have
distributed during the week 500 tons of coal, £1,50
wox th of bedding and clothing, 23.853 loaves of
bread, weighing, in the aggregate, 42 tons 12 cwt.;
35,741 quarts of soup, and 9,057 quarts of potato hash.
The number of cases they have on their books at
present is 10,571, comprising 40,627 persons. In com-
parison with last week these figures show an increase
of 272 cases and 296 persons. In regard to the general
expenditure there has been. an increase this week. of
£29 12s. 2d. The increase in each of the departments
named is nothing near so much as it generally has been.
The committee continue to receive immense quantities
of clothing, &c., from the charitable. The relief they
give is much more liberal than formerly,and its adminis-
tration produces far more satisfaction. In regard to the
guardians I may state that they are also working very
hard. They have now on their beaks, so far as regards
the township of Preston, 7,533 cases, including 17,611
persons. These figures show a decrease in comparison
with last week. in the union of Preston the percentage
of pauperism is 20k, and the rate of parish relief is
is. 6d. 4-10th; in the township of Preston the per-
centage is 21 1-rd, and the rate of relief is. 6d. 9-16th
per head. The number of able-bodied male and female
paupers in the service of the guardians is 5,011. In
reference to the cotton trade, there is not very much
alteration to report. If anything, there is a change
this week and last for the better. The number of
operatives working full time is 4,542; and the number
unemployed altogether is 13,020. The distressed over-
lookers and managers continue to receive most practical
assistance. This week 109 of them have been in
attendance at the school recently established for their
benefit. The relief committee, from some cause or
other, have refused to grant them any assistance as an
independent body. We have had a ' strike ' this week
amongst the stone breakers in the yard of the guardians.
Recently, in consequence of a scarcity of stones, the
men were ordered to be paid. by the day, instead of so
much per ton. But one day the order in question was
reversed, and they were told to resume work under the
old regime. This they refused to do, alleging as their
reason that the.days were now so short they could not
earn as much as could keep them, if put on the piece.
A strike followed; then an interview with the guar-
dians ; but I understand that they are yet dissatisfied;
and that they have refused to work, except on the day
principle. The matter will be brought before the guar-
dians next Tuesday, when a proper arrangement will,
no doubt, be effected.

WALTON-LE-DALE.
In this place, which, since the commencement of the
cotton famine,' has been one of the most distressed in
Lancashire, business appears to be improving—slowly,
certainly, but still on the right side. The relief com-
mittee have this week assisted 2,191 persons, 1,570 of
whom are in the receipt of relief from the guardians, at a
cost of £206 Bs. 100. These figures show a decrease
in the number of persons of 95, as compared with last
week, and an increase in expenditure of £7O is. 10d. I
cannot explain the increase in money and the decrease
in persons, except on the ground that the committee are
administering relief more liberally than hentofore. The
humber of girls at sewing schools this week is 140, last
week it was 136.

articles.title: GAR STANG.
articles.text:
GAR STANG.

It is not very many weeks since Mr. Farnall included
Garstang in his list of distressed unions.' He might
have added it sooner, for distress has long been manifest
amongst the operative portion of its population. In the
town itself there is not much distress, its staple trade
pertains more to agriculture than manufactures; but in
several of the adjoining townships of the union there is
considerable poverty, which has been specially caused
by the present depression of trade. The relief com-
mittee established at Catterall have now 250 poor per-
sons on their books. They have this week voted £7 for
educational purposes, £2O Bs. 2d. for bedding aud
clothing, .L 1 Bs. for fuel, and £4 6s. sd. for food.

articles.title: LANCASTER.
articles.text:
LANCASTER.

The distress appears to be at a stand-still in Lan-
caster, at any rate if there is any change for either
better or worse. The relief committee have relieved
this week about 500 persons. The soup kitchen has at
length been opened, and the committee have distributed
during the week about 2,500 quarts of soup and 'sconce.'
They have also given to the poor between 80 and 100
cwt. of fuel; 125 girls are in attendance at the indus-
trial school established by the committee. There is
also a sewing school in Bulk-street, and the articles
made by the females have been offered for sale in the
regular market way on a stall in the Market-place.
One or two night schools have likewise been opened for
the poor, and they are working most satisfactorily.
The relief committee, after a somewhat animated dis-
cussion, resolved at their last meeting that works on
secular subjects should be read in the sewing school
during the hours of labour.' Prepara';ions are being
made for giving several of the poor people of Lancaster
a gooi treat this Christmas; indeed, I may say, that
such is the case in the g,.ntrality of the distressed towns.

articles.title: CATON,
articles.text:
CATON,

Within the past few days 140 poor families have been
supplied with a ton of coals each, a truly welcome
present,' as a local paper says, at this season of the
year.'

articles.title: FYLDE.
articles.text:
THE FYLDE.

Kirkham is the only place iti-1.--t-he-Fylde of Lancashire
where any particular disress exists, and I am glad to
say that at this place it appears to be decreasing a little.
Poverty is still very keenly felt by many, and even if
the times should mend at once it will ba a long time
before some of the poor people re cover thtreselves.
The wealthy of the district have behaved very liberally
to those in distress, and throughout the Fylde, indeed,
there is a very praiseworthy disposition to assist these
in poverty, who have been thrown out of work by the
stoppage of the mills.

articles.title: TILVERSTON.
articles.text:
TILVERSTON.

I cannot ascertain anything of a very cheering nature
about Ulverston. In some of the townships of the
union the distress is increasing, whilst in others it seems
to have disappeared. During the past few weeks a.
committee of gentlemen have been canvassing Ulver-
ston, on behalf of subscriptions for the distressed opera-
tives, and they have now raised between £3.00 and £4OO.
In the mo•t unlikely place in ITlverston there appears to
be the greatest profusion and comfort; I allude to the
workhouse. The following has been made public in
regard to that establishment, which is one of a genus
which even the most inveterate paupers dislike :--` Dur-
ing the last few years, the • cost in beefsteaks for the
union workhouse of Ulverston has increased about 647
per cent.; the inmates have also consumed about 1,000
pint bottls of ale and 500 bottles of porter during the
same time.'

articles.title: CHORLEY.
articles.text:
CHORLEY.

At Chorley the distress lion the increase. In the
union there are nearly 4,000 in and out door paupers.
The relief committee have now in their care upwards of
300 poor persons, to whom they have distributed this
week 10,496 lbs. of bread, 3,840 lbs. of meal, 4,800 lbs.
of flour, 2,000 quarts of soup, 4 cwt. of soap, 4 cwt. of
sugar, 5 cwt, of bacon, 147 lbs. of coffee, 40 tons of coal,
and £lB 7s. in money; total expenditure, £220 2s. Bd.
Nearly 300 are in attendance at the industrial classes.
The committee have decided to give 25 per cent. of their
relief in money; they have also resolved to release neces-
sary articles pawned by the operatives. In regard to the
cotton trade in the town, I may state that four firms,
usually employing 1,472 operatives, are working their
mills full time; four, usually employing 965, three days
per week; and that five, employing on the average 1840
operatives, have closed their mills entirely. At the
bleach-works and the collieries in the neighbourhood,
several of the men engaged there are working short '
time. The weekly loss in wages in Chorley and the
neighbourhood through the present distress is estimated
at £1,400.

DARWEN.
There is not much difference this week in the state of
affairs at Darwen. For the past two or three weeks I
have had an improvement to report; but this week busi-
neas appears to be about stationary—neither better nor
worse—and I am sorry that I can't go on detailing good
news. The relief committee have now on their books
1,725 persons, of whom 1,010 are in receipt of relief
from the guardians. A number of men have been
drafted from the educational school to repair some of the
roads in the neighbourhood. At present there are not

articles.title: so many girls in attendance at the industrial school as formerly. In consequence of this decrease, the girments for distribution amongst the poor cannot be made fast enough. .

BLACKBURN:

Trade still. confines.* to look up' &littl in Blackburn.
The numborof operatives usually employed here in the
motton trade is 27,273—n.41y the same as in Preston.
keeording to the very latest return which I have been
able to obtain, I fine that of the number named 7,062
are working full time against 6,532 last week; 3,888 are
employed short time against 4 392 hurt week; and 16,323
are tetally unemployed Kg du,st 16,349 last week. In
every department, it will he observed, there is =niters
-
Eon for the better. 25 ot the asillsarerunning full time,
19 are working short time, and 43 ars entirel3r stopped.
In regard to the actual paupers, there also appears to be
an improvement; it is not much certainly, but still it is
an improvement, and that is what we all wish to see.
Aocordingto,the returns submitted to the board of guard-
ians at their meeting to-day, it seems that during the
week the number of cases relieved has been 5;982,
comprising 18,108 persons, of whom 8,967 were able-
bodied.

articles.title: ACCRINGTON.
articles.text:
ACCRINGTON.

No particular news this week relative to .Accrington.
The distrese is, if anything, on the increase The relief
committee have got into good working order, and their
labours give pretty general satisfaction. The educa,
tional and industrial classes are in full operation, and
are well attended.
• OSWALDTWISTLE.
Nearly 1,000 poor people are now in the charge of
the relief committee of Os.akliwistle. This is a large
number for a place so small. Their relief this week has
only cost .L 3 19m 6d. At Oswaldtwiaide,, seat Church,
preparations are being made to give a treat to the poor
on Christmas Day.
BURNLEY.

The charitable committee of Burnley have assisted
this week between, 6.1209. and 7,002 peewits, it a totat
cr,st of £491, 7s. 11d. Several handsome subscriptions
have just been received by the committee. At their
-
last meeting it was proposed to give a percentage on
the wages earned by those poor operatives in employ,
but the proposition did not meet with any favour, and.
it fell to the ground. It has been decided to employ
able-bodied youths and men in works connected with
the corporation. The committee have distributed a
good deal of clothing this week, and they have re-
solved to supply clothing to the amount of 3s. per
head to those persons in receipt of relief from the
guardians.
NEVir-CHURCH.

Here the distress slightly increases, but it is toler-
ably well met by the operKtions of the relief committee.
Schools for both males and females have been organised,
and they are working successfully.

BACITP.
A novel present has, within the past few days, been
made by Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., to the poor of Bacup,
'Hz., 500 copies of a small publication on economical
cooking. Whether this will suit or not I cannot tell;
probably some of the operatives will think that 'getting'
something to cook, and. not how to cook semething, is
the most important question,with them at the present.
In regard to the distress here, I am informed that it is
still very severe, and continues to increase.

articles.title: IRELAND AND THE LANCASHIRE
articles.text:
IRELAND AND THE LANCASHIRE

DIST_RESS.

We noticed briefly on F-iday the proceedings at this
meeting, called to devise means to aid in the relief of
the distress in the North, and presided over by the High
Sheriff of the county. Fuller reports of the proceedings
in the Irish papers show that the meeting was one of the
most riotous and disgraceful on record.
The Right Hon. Colonel Herbert, M.P., moved the
first resolution, but was interrupted during the whole of
his speech by storms of yells, groans, and hisses. To-
wards the close of his speech Colonel Herbert proceeded
to read a passage from a letter of the Rev. Mr. O'Sulli-
van bearing testimony to the ready manner in, which
subscriptions were given him in England for the relief
of the destitute poor of Kerry, and expressing his deep
gratitude to the English nation. It was difficult to
follow statements from the great confusion which pre-
vailed. The letter, he said, is my answer to the state-
ment made that this relief was given to Protestants.—
(Cries of Sit down.') (Here a determined effort was
was made to put Colonel Herbert down. The shouting
and groaning was so continued that it was almost im-
possible a word he said could be heard.)
A 'Voice: Do you eapect a peerage for this ?
Colonel Herbert: No; I would rather represent you,
.and I am sure you will vote with me at the next elec-
tion. [Colonel Herbert remained for about five minutes.
waiting for the subsidence of the hooting and groaning
which followed his last remark; but, as the vehemence
of the audience seemed to increase rather than diminish,
he was prevailed upon by his friends to conclude by
moving the resolution he had read.]
The resolution was seconded by the Right Rev. Dr.
Moriarty, Catholic Bishop of Kerry, whose speech was
received in a somewhat more orderly manner, but still
with some confusion.
The O'Donoghue, who was received with hurrahing
and cries of Bravo,' moved the amendment, That,
while we gladly avail ouselves of the opportunity
afforded us by this meeting to express our sympathy
with the distress which is said to exist in certain districts
in England, we are also fully sensible that the fearful
destitution prevailing under our own eyes amongst our
own friends, neighbours, and countrymen at home his
a first and irresistible claim on our charity.' (Great
cheering. He said—Some few might think that we
ought, first of all, to contribute our money to the relief
of the distress in Lancashire; while others might think,
with me, that we ought, first of all, to contribute our
money to the relief of distress at home. (Great cheer-
_

-A' Voice: More power to you. (Cheers.)
The O'Donoghue : I am aware, fellow countrymen,
that the motives which have induced me to move this
amendment may, possibly, be misrepresented. In that
case I must look to you to do me justice.
Mr. E. O'Sullivan: And we'll stand by you, never
feu-. (Cries of Hurrah, hurrah,' and cheering.)
The O'Donoghue: I am actuated solely by a motive
to do my duty to the poor of my native country. (Im-
mense applause.)
A Voice: 'Tis a murder we can't have you to our-
selves. (Laughter and cheering.)
The O'Donoghue : I am actuated solely by a motive
to supply what I consider to be a grievous omission—to
place on record, by a public vote of this great county
meeting, that we are not insensible to the appalling
poverty which stand shivering and famishing at the
corners of our streets, and which lies hid in our lanes
and alleys. (Cheers.) And in doing this I hope to set
an example which shall not be without its beneficial
effect on the people of Kerry and Ireland. (Applause.)
Although a very humble
A Voice; Humble! You're a prince.—(Deafening
chsrs.)
The O'Donoghue : Although a very humble indi-
vidnul, J feel I am justified indeed
Mr. O'Sullivan: Oh, you're the highest man in
Ireland, Sir—(cheering)—and the noblest, too.—(Con-
tinned cheering.)
A Voice: Three cheers for Edward O'Sullivan.—
_

(Iluzzaing.)
A Voice: Mr. O'Donoghue—(laughter)--you ought to
come to Kerry entirely, Sir, and unseat Herbert alto-
gether. (More huzzaing.)
At the close of The O'Donoghue's speech, which
was accompanied throughout by similar expressions of
approval,
The High Sheriff put the resolution of Colonel Her-
bert amidst a scene of indescribable disorder and tumult.
The ' noes ' were in a vast majority.
Mr. E. O'Sullivan: Now put The O'Donoghue's
amendment.

The High Sheriff.-----I will put it as a subsequent re-
srlution, though I do not see anything in it, as The
O'Donoghue says, contrary in spirit to the first.
The demand was renewed to put the amendment-; but
the High Shetiff continued his refusal amid continued
yelling. He said, I see nothing incompatible with one
resolution, why they both should not be carried.—(No,
No.) As well as I understood, you wish to put both
resolutioas?

Several Voices.—No. The amendment.
A Voice.—Subscribe money and give half to.—
(Shouting.)
Mr. O'Sullivan.—Oh, you, keep quite.
The High Sheriff again proceeded to put the original
resolution, and had gone as far as the words 'the work-
ing classes in the cotton manufacturing districts in
Lancashire have strong claims on our sympathy,' when
the crowd, who, up to that time did not know what
resolution he was reading, burst forth in a fearful roar,
and refused to hear any more of it.
On the demand being renewed to put the amendment,
amid dreadful screaming and shouting,
The High Sheriff said the meeting was called for a
special purpose, from which he could not wander.—
(Shouting.)
Mr. • O'Sullivan (standing up, waving his hat, and
swinging himself aroumi)—lf the High Sheriff does not
put The O'Donoghue's resolution first, I'll move that he
leave the chair.

The most deafening, frantic uproar followed these re-
marks. The High Sheriff, immediately on their being
uttered, rose and left the court-house, followed by all the
gentlemen who had been on the bench. The O'Donoghue
also withdrew. In the hurry of all to leave the court-
house men and boys tumuled over one another down the
gallery, and it is a marvel that broken heads and legs
were not the consequenze. An immense crowd, however,
remained, who resolved themselves into a second meeting,
at which the amendment was carried with acclamation,
but the proceedings continued of a. noisy and riotous
character.

articles.title: CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY.
articles.text:
CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY.

On the 20th, George Ruxtrn, a shipowner, residing at
Liverpool, an& james Birtie, the captain and part owner
of a merchant ship named the James Brown, were
placed at the bar of the Mansion-house justice-room,
before the Lord Mayor, charged with conspiring together
to cheat awl defraud the Universal Marine Insurance
Company, in Carnhill, of betweer. £BOO and £9OO.
The prisoner Balaton was recently tried and acquitted
on &similar charge at the Liverpo. d Assizes. On lea vir
the court he was arrested on a fresh accusation, under a
warrant emanating from the Mansion-house, and brought
to London. The prisoner Birtie was apprehen ,ed on
Monday last at Falmouth, just as he had arrived there
Oar a voyage.
-31 r. 11i'Cuiloch was counsel for the prosecution; the
prisoner Buxton was depended by Mr. sleigh ; and Birtie
by Mr Wentner, solicii or. ef Buckleshu-y.
Mr. William Nicholas de Mat as, of 27, Leadenhall-
street, merchant, was called. He said in November,
1860, he chart, red the ship Joseph Howe, belonging to
the prisoner Buxton, for a voyage from Car dill to St.
Paul de Loa, do, a. Portuguese port on the co ist of Africa,
with a full cargo of or als, through Smith, Simpson, and
Co., of Georg,-yard, Lombardestreez, shipbrokers, with
liberty to Knowles and Foster to ship 500 demi-johns (a
kind of bottle, so called), at a special rate of freight, for
his (witnee's) own agent at the port of destination. No
one besides himself, as the charterer, would be ent tled
to ship goods by the vessel as freight, stores exc,p. ed.
Mr. Todd, a shipbuilder at Cardiff, and son of the
Portuguese Vice-Consul there, deposed that he acted
as the deputy of his father during his ahsence in. De-
cember, 1860. St. Paul de Loando was what wee called
a Consular port, and it was requisite at such a pia, e
for the captain of a vessel arriving there to produce a
declaration showing the whole of his cargo. The
prisoner, Birti' e as the captain. of The Joseph Howe,
• signed, ttnmanife st produced; ag,lmll se a translation in
Portuguese, to which latter was appended a declaration
:by him that he had no other goo Is on board than those
mentioned in, the manifest, The two bills of lading
now produce i e ere shown to witness by the captain
before the vessel sailed, to enable him to make out the
manifest.
The two bills of lading referred to, and on which the
case of the prosecution mainly turned, were put in—
the sugsestion on their part being that they contained
entries of goods, including beer and flour in large
quantities, perfumery, pickles, preserved meats, pota-
toes, geese, cross-cut saws, buscuits, &c., slipped
by the prisoner Buxton, but of which it was alleged
little more than a tenth was actually put on board the
ves.,el, though the prisoner Buxton had effeettd an in-
surance for £l,OOO on the whole lot of the enumerated

articles.
Mr. Alfred Tozer, of 35, Cornhill, Secretary to the
Universal Marine Insurance Company, proved that on
the 29th of December, 1860, two policies of insurance
for £5OO each were issued by the company in respect of
certain goods purporting to have been shipped in the
Joseph Howe. A claim was arterwards made for the
insurance upon an alleged total loss of the ship and
cargo, and on the 25th of January, 1861, the amount
(X 1,000 was paid by the company to Messrs. Wardell,
Frazer, and Co., on the production by them of the bills
of lading and a protest that the goods mentioned in
them were entirely lost with the vessel. He added, in
reply to Mr. Sleigh, that when the insurance was effected
he knew nothing whatever about Wardell and Frazer's
principals in the transaction; but at the time it was
paid he knew for whom they were acting.
Evidence was given by people from Cardiff, employed
about the ship when she was preparing for sea, leading
to the inference that of the articles enumerated in the
two bills of lading not more than about 100 casks of
beer, a few barrels of flour, and about 70 mats of potatoes
were actually shipped. It was also proved that Buxton
was at Cardiff on the 24th of December, the day the
vessel sailed.
Mr. James Ranford Wardell (Wardell, Frazer, and
Co), ship insurance broker, Gresham-house, said the
policies produced on the ship Joseph Howe were effected
by him through Heathcock and Co. He had no com-
munication whatever with the prisoner Buxton with
respect to them' nor any conversation with him at any
time. He saw him in company with Mrs. Heathcock
when the insurance was paid to the latter. Heathcock
and Buxton came together, and the conversation be-
tween witness and the former might or might not have
been heard by Buxton. Witness received £l,OOO, the
full amount of the insurance, from the company, and
handed the money over to Heathcock by check. He
believed Buxton was not present when he did so. There
were other insurances on the ship effected by witness,
and he collected them all about the same time for Heath-
cock—viz. £1,500, £l5O, and £676, besides the £l,OOO
on the goods.
Two letters, written by the prisoner Buxton, from
London, to his son, at Liverpool, on the 13th and 23rd
of January, 1861, were put in and read. In the first
the prisoner said he had received information of the loss
of the Joseph Howe, that she had been struck by a heavy
sea on the 2nd of January and had sprung a leak, and
that the crew, who had abandoned her, with nine feet
of water in the hold, had been taken up by a passing
ship, and brought to London. He added that he was
well insured, there being £4,000 on the ship and freight,
and £l,OOO on goods, that Heathcock was getting his
papers ready as fast as he could, and that he expected to
receive £3,500 of the insurance on the following Wed-
nesday or Thursday. In the second letter Buxton said
he had received £1,500 of the money, that he expected
£2,000 en the next day or Thursday, Ad thatron receiv-
ing the balance he would be off home.
Thomas Smith, a detective police-officer at Liverpool,
said he aprehended the prisoner Birtie at Falmouth on
Monday, on board of his own ship. He told him as he
did so that he was a police-officer, and charged him with
conspiring with Buxton to defraud the underwriters by
losing the Joseph Howe. The prisoner said Yes, she
was lost,' adding shortly afterwards, I did a bad job
in signing those blank bills cf lading.' Witness asked
if he had any papers in the ship connected with the
Joseph Howe. He replied he thought not, that he had
de•troyed them, but witness could look for himself.
Witness brought the prisoner on shore to the office of
Messrs. Fox and Co., where the prisoner received a
letter addressed to him, and which he opened and read,
giving it afterwards to his wife to read. She returned
it to him, and he was going towards the fire with it,
when witness snatched it eut of his lifind. Witness then
read the letter, and asked him if Buxton owed him that
amount of money for back wages. Witness had pre-
viously asked him wh d the letter was about. The
reply was that it was for his wife.
By Mr. Wontner.—When he apprehended the prisoner
Birtie, witness did not tell him that he would either be
a prisoner or a witness, but he did afterwards, and showed
him a handbill relating to the charge.
The letter, which was anonymous, was not read, the
Lord Mayor ruling that a man was not to be answerable
for a letter that might be addressed to him, much lessi
an 'anonymous one, which might be designed as a trap I
for him.

On this evidence Mr. M'Culloch asked to have the pri-
soners committed for trial. He added in reply to the
Court, that the solicitors for the prosecution and him-
self had estimated that the value of the gocds actually
put on board was about £l4O, that £l,OOO had been
received for insurance, and that the company charged
the prisoners with defrauding them of the difference,
amounting to £B6O.
Mr. Sleigh and Mr. Wontner finding that it was the
intention of the Lord Mayor to send the prisoners for
forbore to address the Court in their behalf, con-
tenting themselves with asking that thcy should be
liberated on bail.

The prisoners were then committed to New-gate for trial,
the Lord Mayor deciding at the same time to hold them
to bail, themselves in £5OO each, and two sureties in £250
each, after giving the usual notice.

HIGHLAND BtRYING PLACES.—AII English artist
writing about the Highlands describes a lonely church-
yard in an island on Loch-Awe. The island, he says,
had been inhabited before, long ago, by a convent of
Cistercian nuns. They were turned out at the Reforma-
tion, and their poor little chapel has been left for the
winds to sing in ever since. Not many stones are left in
it now, and its foundations lie low amen° st the moss-
co cered tombs of the old chieftains. But the people
bring their dead here yet, and lay them under the shadow
of their broken walls, so that the island is a land of death,
of utter repose and peace. Was it not well in barbarous
mountaineers to bury their dead in lonely isles, where
the foot of the marauder trampled not the grass on the
grave, and where the living came not, save in sorrow,
and reverently? The mainland was for the living to
fight upon, to hunt upon, and to dwell upon; but this
green isle was the Silent Land, the Island of the Blest.
Hither the chieftams came, generation after generation,
borne solemnly across the waters from their castled isles;
hither they came to this defenceless one, where they still
sleep securely, when their strongholds are roofless ruins;
their claymores dissolved in rust; their broadlands that
they fought for all their lives, sold and resold; and their
descendants sent into exile to make a desert for English
grouse-shooters.

.has
reappeared in god health at his own home. If N'Neill
