articles.text:
Cii t .s T ER.

MareerrnsrEn, Dec. 21.—The express train from Lon-
don to Manchester last night was nearly annihilatt d
when within about four and a half miles of its destina-
tion. It left the Euston station as usual at five o'clock
p.m., and was due at Manch, ster at 10.10 p.m. It
was nearly twenty minutes behind time on pa-sing
Heaton Norris (Stockport), and had only proceeded a
short distance beyond that station when the engine and
carriages left the metals. From what cause the tete,
went off the rails is not known, but it wet off on
the out or westerly side It is believed that the
points were at fault at the junction of the line to
tiuide Bridge. Owing to the line being ballasted at this
part with sand, the train was brought to a stand without
much damage either to the carriages or passengers,
and the guard, who:e van was next to the engine,
ran towar,s the rear of the train with his red (danger)
lamp. Almost before he could get there, however, an
engine came up 0. hind and ran into the train with
great force, almost smashing the entire of it to atoms.
The train consisted of two first-class and a second-class
carriage, besides the van, and one of the first-class was
broken through- the middle, the wheels were knocked
off, and the body knocked almost into splinters. The
second-class cat riage was also a complete wreck, the
only portion of it left above the bed of the cat riage
being one single partition (the central one). All the
carriages were thrown into or across a deep trench by
the side of the line in ended to drain it. The engine
which completed this catastrophe was a pilot engine,
following the express, and. it is said that the driver
states, that, seeing the tail light of the express
train had suddenly disappeared in front of him,
he concluded that the express was further in
advance, than he had supposed, and had gone round
the curve at Levenshulme, a mile ahead. He then
put on steam, and consequently the collision was the
more severe. It was a dark and stormy night, and it is
supposed that when the express got off the line either
its lighta were extinguished by the juraping of the train,
or were hidden from, the driver of the following engine
by the abutments of a bridge. . Both engin s were
damaged, but that of the express not so badly as the
other one. The passengers, of whom there were fortu-
nately but few, escaped better than might have been
expected. So far as we can learn none were killed, but
several were badly injured. The railway officials lest
no time in obtaining assistance for the passengers
injured, or in getting conveyances to send them forward.
One of the pass ngers most injured is said to be a soldier.
A gentleman who escaped with his forehead slightly cut
said he got out through the roof of the carriage, which had
been ripped off, and through this he also dragged a lady
who was little injured. The whole of the night and
the greater part of to day have been taken up in
repairing the line and removing the debris of the
train

articles.title: HIUH TIDES AND _TIE4VT GALES.
articles.text:
HIUH TIDES AND _TIE4VT GALES.

DOVER, Sunday Evening.—Unusually high tides have
prevailed at Dover and Folkestone from Friday morning
to the present time (Sunday, 5 p.m.); strong gales have
prevailed from the N.N.W., and the storm 'signal drum'
is exposed at the pier-head; it is anticipated the gale
will be at its height this day (Monday).
Communication with the tpposite coast has been im-
peded. On Saturday the Belgian Government boats
were prevented leaving the ports of Ostend and Dover.
This morning the mails were shipped on board the
Samphire, and she lay in readiness from 9.10 until 4
o'clock, the ebbing tide preventing her departure until
to-morrow, if weather then permits.,. The Maid of
Kent not making her usual passage to Calais on Satur-
day, and the railways bringing an additional influx
of returns to the Continent, Lieut. Morgan (superin-
tendent of the London, Chatham, and Dover boats) ordered
the Queen to get up steam and proceed to sea at 9.30.
The Queen battled with the elements for some time,
until at, last she was compelled to return to harbour,
which she regained with difficulty. Several vessels are
in harbour windbound, and at twilight a barque entered
the roads with the flag half-mast high. Several tugs
have been busily engaged during the day, and many
minor casualties have occurred. The barque Ann
Patterson (Arundel), drawing 141 feet of water, went
aground within six feet of the pier-head at the mouth of
the harl)our, and was rolling hopelessly. From the crew
suddenly taking to the pumps, it is expected she is
riding on her anchors, which were let go over a most
uneven and dangerous bottom. 'Every precaution has
been made to keep her ofl' the pier-head. The Welsh
schooner Jane shortly afterwards grounded whilst being
tugged in by the Douro. She has been in collision, and has
lost nowsprit and figure- head; is also in a leaky condition.
A Dutch barque' painted entirely white and ascertained
to be laden. with sugar and rum, from Surinam, is wind-
bound, with about 200 other vessels in the roads and
harbour. On shore the damage from the tide has been
considerable; the cellars , those who reside near the
harbour and sea front ha A been inundated, and stores
of all kinds spoiled: the wa,hed-up shingle gives some
of our thoroughfares the appearance of a new-laid gravel
walk, and on Saturday some men engaged dischargirtg
ballast were washed from their carts, but fortunately
rescued from the waves. The planking of the Round
Pier is washed away, and a telegram informs us that the
Ostend pier and lighthouse have been demolished since
Saturd-ty moining. In Snargate-street (the principal
thoroughfare), two chimneys, of Mr. Foster, draper (No.
86), and that of Mr. W. E. Flashman, upholsterer
(No. 146), strew the road. Fortunately no person has
been injured e the fall. The north side of Mr. Foster's
residence, which was hung with weather tiles, has been
completely stripped, and asp lathing laid bare. On the
heights sentry boxes have been overthrown, and the
weather prognosticators declare the gale is not yet at its
height.

SHIELDS, Saturday Night.—This evening a telegram
was received from Admiral Fitzroy that dangerous
winds might be expected, and storm warnings have been
hoisted in the harbour. Coincident with the appear-
ance of the warnings, the wind veered round from the
W.N.W. to the N., and it is blowing a fierce gale, with
a heavy sea rolling across the bar. After dark to-night
a laden schooner was seen to make bad weather as she
was running for the harbour, ar.d eventually she drifted
on to the Herd Sand, inside the south pier, at the mouth
of the Tyne.
In a very few minutes after the vessel struck'the
South Shields pilots had their lifeboat out and manned.
They pulled her lustily through the surging billows,
and they have succeeded in rescuing all the crew and
have brought them into South Shields. The Tyne-
mouth new lifeboat put out, but she was too late. The
stranded vessel is the Isabella Grintey, from Sunderland
to Montrose, with coals. She has been knocking about
in the North Sea since Wednesday last. The weather
is extremely stormy.

TERRIFIC GALE ON THE SOUTH EAST COAST.

RAmsoA.ze,
pre-
vailed during Saturday night and this morning has been
the cause of a considerable destruction of property on
the coast in the vicinity of this town. The tide this
morning wa,s higher than it has been known to be for
the last twenty-tive years, and the waves, like mountains
of water, rolled in with terrific violence. The premises
of Messrs. Strong and Barnes, boatwrights, have been
greatly damaged. A large wooden marquee, used by
visitors in the season, has also been partly destroyed.
The coast guard station had a very narrow escape, and it
is feared the men and their families will have to turn
out before the next high tide. The waves washed com-
pletely over the station, and the water fell down the
chimneys, so as to prevent firesbeing kept by the occupants.
Even the Kent Coast Railway Company have not escaped
sustaining a loss. For some time past a tunnel has
been in course of construction through the cliff, the
chalk from which has been brought out to form an em-
bankment as a continuation of the line in the direction
of the town. This embankment was about 100 feet in
length, 50 in width, and from 15 to 20 Let high; but
now the whole has been washed away. At about half-
past four this morning the Ramsgate lifeboat went out to
a vessel (belonging to South Shields) which was ashore
on the Goodwin Sands. After much difficulty the boat
neared the vessel, and succeeded in saving the lives of
four out of five of the crew. The fifth man was lost,
having, we are. informed, jumped into the sea in en-
deavouring to Jump from the vessel to the lifeboat.
The damage done in the harbour is not extensive; there
are, however, several small craft sunk, and one or two
broken.

GALE ON THE EAST COAST.
YARMOUTH, Dec. 21.—Yesterday afternoon the crew
of the smack Excellent, of Hull, Captain Johnson, were
landed here and taken to the Sailors' Home. During
the gale, when distant from Spurn Head about eight
miles, a large brig, the name of which ha net transpired,
ran into and cut down the smack. Findmg that she
was fast sinking the crew hailed the stranger and im-
plored t4ose on board to rescue them. No attention was,
however, paid to their appeal, and
.the brig held on her
course. The smack's crew, consisting of four men and
two lads, then took to their small boat, and shortly after-
wards the smack foundered. The poor fellows had no
time to save their clothes or secure any provision what-
ever. After many hours fearful suffering the poor
people *ere Otserved. by the schooner Buchan, of Maldon,
which here down to their assistance and took them on
board in an almost stupefied condition. Yesterday the
sehooner put into our roadstead and landed the sufferers
during a lull in the storm.

articles.title: WILLS AND BEQUESTS.
articles.text:
WILLS AND BEQUESTS.

The will of Lieutenant-General Sir William George.
; Moore, K.C.8., late of Petersham, Surrey, formerly of
Chewles, and Berkeley-square, was proved in London
on the 22nd ult. The personalty was sworn under
' £30,000. The executors nominated are his cousin,
Captain John Moore, R.N., and John Carrick Moore,
Esq., of Corswall, Stranraer, N. B. This veteran general
officer has seen much military service, and ranks among
the heroes of WbJerloo, in which he participated, being
attached to the Quartermaster-General's Staff at that
memorable conflict. The late General Sir William G.
Moore was the nephew of that gallant and distinguished_
General Sir John Moore who fell at Corunna. The
testator, who executed his will iu,Febuary last, with a
codicil in August following, cited on the 23rd. of
October at the age of sixty seven. These docu-
ments, though but of moderate length, contain many
bequests to relatives, officers in the army anclnavy, their
wives and: widows, amounting to about £10,000; also.
legacies to his domestics, and an annuity of £lOO to his
servant, John Donald. The testator has also bequeathed
to the Natio r ail Gallery eleven pictures by the old masters.
His real estate, together with the residue of the person-
alty, he leaves to his cousin and executor Captain John
Moore, R.N.
The will of Brodie M`Ghie Willcox, Esq., late M.P.
for Southampton, of Portman-square, London, and.
Roydon Lodge, Ware, Herts, was proved in London on
the Ist instant, the executors appointed being his rAict,
together Allan,
iowseipthh his son,
m
n,13 Brodie Augustus Willcox; James
‘Leod, and Calvert Toulmin,
Esqrs. The personalty was sworn under £120,000..
The testator, who was an eminent shipowner, held
manyprominent appointments connected with mercantile
pursuits, was chairman of the Peninsular and Oriental
Steam Company, a director of the Southampton Docks,
and an East Indian proprietor. He also iepresnted
Southampton in Parliament fi om the pe,iod of 1847 to
the time of his death, which occurred on the Bth of
November last, at the age of 77. The will bears date
1857, with two codicils, 1861- 2; though of considerable
length, the dispositions are entirely of a family nature.
To his relict he leaves all his household furniture and
plate (except presentation plate), carriages, arid other
effects absolutely, and a life interest in his real and
personal estate, which upon her decease is to be
equally divided between his son and daughters, to each
of whom he has left an immediate legacy of £2,000.
There is one bequest which it may be interesting to.
notice; it is a silver centre ornament, richly embellished
with emlilematical devices, weighing 771 oz. This
costly piece of plate was presented to the testator 'by the
i
Peninsular and Oriental Steam Company, and s directed.
by the will to be held by his son for life, and upon his
decease to descend to the eldest son then living of his
(testator's) son-in-law, Pedro Jose de Zulueta, Count
Torre Diaz, the husband of the testator's e'dest daughter.
The will of the late Ichabod Wright, Esq., of Mapperly
Hall, near Nottingham, has juA been proved in the
London Court by the executors—namely, his son,
Ichabod Charles Wright, Esq.; hi a son -in - law,
George Le Blanc, Esq.; and his grandsons, George John
Shaw Lefevre and Charles Ichabod Wright, Esqs.—the
personalty in Great Britain and Ireland being sworn
under £lOO,OOO. The testator was the senior partner in
the old-established banking firm of j. and J. C. Wright
and Co., Nottinghamshire, and attained to the advanced
age of 95. He executed his will two years since. After
bequeathing legacies to his younger children, he has
given the residue of his personal estate to his eldest son,
Ichabod Charles Wright; Esq., M.A., and has devised to
him his estates in Nottinghamshire and Lincolnshire for
life, with remainder to his grandson, Charles Ichabod
Wright, who are the surviving partners in the bank.
The property in Glasgow he has devised in part to his
son, the Rev. Adolphus Wright, and the remainder to
his only unmarried daughter, Miss Lydia Sophia
Wright.

articles.text:
PRESIDENT LINCOLN.

We spent a few days recently in Washington city,.
and while there saw many things and heard many
things which to us seemed very suggestive evidence of
the extraordinary progress with which the nation is
rushing onward in its history. The presence of an
armed guard at the gates of the Executive mansion
every morning, and the care taken to keep strangers out-
side of the-approaches to the building, was to us some-
thing new. Upon inquiry we ascertained that this

guard was onli employed -to keep strangers out until
the President should arrive from the Soldiers' Home,
where he his resided for many months. His arrival
and departure from the executive mansion are, notwith-
standing the melancholy suggestions they render,
peculiarly remarkable. We saw hiraleave the building
Qn Sunday afternoon, and the manner was as follows:
Xbout half-past five a mounted guard, numbering some
thirty or more troopers, all armed with drawn sabres, ex-
tensive spears, dangling -Ind rattling scabbards fierce
beards, and revolvers stuck their holsters, dashed furi-
ously through the streets and entered the ground north of
the President's house. At the steps in front of the door,
end under the archway, was a carriage. The officer, or
one of the officers, of the mounted guard alighted and
entered the house. In about ten minutes he appeared
at the door, and, giving the signal, the carriage door
was opened, the guards put themselves in martial atti-
tudes, commands were given, and then the President,
bending under a weight of mental anxiety, which has
worked heavily upon his physical. frame, appeared with
a portfolio under his arm, and, with one or mole soldiers
at each side, walked rapidly to the carriage and entered
it. Two officers jumped in also, the door was slammed,
the guard galloped into position, and tile carriage con-
taining the President of the United States was driven
off, preceded by troops, followed by troopers, and
flanked on both sides by troopers. At a very rapid pace
the party left the ground, and upon reaching the avenue
proceeded at a hand gallop out of Fourteenth-street
towards the Soldiers' Home. All this, we confess,
appeared to us to be very ridiculous. Even Mr. Bu-
chanan whose conscience, "f it ever caused a President
a thought as to his personal safety, ought, perhaps, to
have been troubled as much as that of any one who.
ever held the office, never seemed, to fear assuesination
or personal violence, but habitually walked, unattended,
to all parts of the city. But justice to Mr. Lincoln
and to these who may have advised him to this proceed-
ing requires that the reaeons for the proceedine—we
mean the reasons furnish& by public gossip—should aloe
be given. One story runs that as the President was
returning to the city on horseback one morning some
months ago he was fired at just within the city limits;
that the President escaped, and that with whip, voice,
heels, and every other appliance used upon his horse,
that animal made such time to the President's house as
had never been equalled before. In the run the Presi-
dent lost his hat, and did not stop to recover it, but
reached his house in the city breathless and dust-
covered. The official report of the occurrence was that
the horse of the President had become frightened and
ran off with him. The next story is that as Mr. Lincoln
was riding toward the Soldiers' Home late in the after-
noon, and when he had entered the narrow and once
shady lane of that building, he was fired upon twice
by a man who stood behind the fenke on the side of the
road. The. President escaped unhurt, but his horse Was
slightly wounded. The alarm was given, the man was
overtaken, and is now confined in some one of the many
Government prisons where the order to commit is uot
required to name thi cause of the arrest. We repeat
that we give only the current stories of the metropolis as
to the alleged attempts to 'assassinate Mr. Lincoln. if
he has no fear of personal violence or insult, then this
mounted guard is in very bad taste. It is a step towards

over 80 years the Union has lasted without an army to
enforce its laws or to compel obedience to its Constitu-
tion. For the same period the Presidents of the

Their security has been in the honour and respect of the

fear by the President or any 'of his friends that he was

The following extracts from Mr. Russell's Diary will
be perused with interest :
•
VISIT TO THE PRESIDENT.

Soon afterwards there entered, with a shambling,
loose, irregular, almost unsteady g ,it, a ta 1, lank, lean
man, considerably over six feet in h ght, with stoopinf
shoulders, long peAulous arms, term nating in hands of
extraordinary dimens ons, which, however' were far ex-
ceeded in proportion by his feet. He was dressed in an
ill-fitting, wrinkled suit of blty-k, which put one in
mind of an undertaker's uniform at a funei al; round his
neck a rope of black silk was knotted in a large bu b, with
flying ends projecting beyond the collar of his coat;
his turned-d rwn shirt-collar disclosed a sinewy
muscular yellow neck, and above that, nestling in
a great black mass of hair, bristling and com-
pact like a ruff of mourning pins, ro.re the strange
quaint face and head, covered with its thatch of wild
Republican hair, of President Lincoln. The impres-ion
produced by the size of his extremities, and by his
flapping and wide projecting ears, may be removed by
the appearance of kindliness, sagacity, and the awk ward
bonhomnaie of his fate; the mouth is absolutely pro-
digious; the lips, straggling and extended almost from
one line of black heard to the other, are only kept in
order by two deep furrows-from the nostril to the chin;
the nose itself—a prominent organ- -stands out from the
face with an inquiring ansioui air, as though it were
sniffing for some good thing in the wind; the eyes dark,
and deeply set, are penetrating, but full of an ex-
pression which almost amounts to tenderne-s; and
above them projects the shaggy brow, runnin,g into the
small hard frontal space, the development of which can
scarcely be estimated accurately, owing to the irregular
flocks of thick hair carelessly brushed across it. One
would say that, although the mouth was made to enjoy
a joke, it could also utter the severest sentence which
the head could dictate, but that Mr. Lincoln would be
ever more willing to temper justice with mercy, and to
enjoy what he considers the amenities of life, than to
take a harsh view of men's nature and of the world, and
to estimate things in an ascetic or puritan spirit. A
person who met Mr. Lincoln in the street wou d not
take him to be what, according to the usages of Euro-
pean society, is called a " gentreman '-" and, indeed,
since I came to the United States I have heard more
disparaging allusions made by Americans to him on that
account than I could have expected among simple Re-
publicans, where all should be equals; but, at the same
time, it would not be possible for the most indifferent
observer to pass him in the street without notice.'
VISIT TO MOBILE AND PENSAOOLA.

At Mobile Mr. Russell was invited to take upon him
a responsibility which he declined with unqu, stituable
judgment and propriety Mr. Forsyth asked if I tad
any objection to take with me three gentlemen of
Mobile, who were anxious to be of the party, as they
wanted to see their friends at Pensacola, where it was
believed a "fight" was to come off immediately. Since
I came South I have seen the daily announcement that
"Braxton Bragg is ready," and his preseat state of pre-
paration must be beyond all conception. But here was a
difficulty. I told Mr. Forsyth that I could not possibly
assent to any persons coming with me who were not
neutrals, or prepared to adhere to the obligations of
neutrals. There was a suggestion that I should say these
gentlemen were my friends, but as I had only seen two
of them on board the steamer yesterday, I could not
accede to that idea. "Then if you are asked if Mr.
Ravesies is your friend you will say he is not." "Cer-
tainly.: "But surely you don't wish to have Mr.
Ravesies hanged ?" "No, Ido not, and I shall do
nothing to cause him to be hanged; but if he meets
that fate by his own act I can't help it. I will not
allow him to accompany me under false pretences."
At last it was agreed that Mr. Ravesies and his friends,
Mr. Bartre and Mr. Lynes, being in no way employed
by or connected with the Confederate Go iernment,
should have a place in the schooner which we had
picked out at the quayside and hired for the occasion,
and go on the voyage, with the plain understanding
that they were to accept all the consequences of being
citizens of Mobile.'
Mr. Russell next visited Pensacola, had an interview
with General Bragg, discovered an old Crimean ac-
quaintance, a relic of the Balaklava charge, inspected
Fort Pickens and the opposition camp, had an exciting
cruise and a narrow squeak' off Mobile, and then made
his way to New Orleans. Here, of course, he heard of
the ancient repulse of the Britishers, with the variation
that there were scarcely any cotton bales used in defence
of the American trenches. He also made here the
acquaintance of Mr. Slidell, with whose astuteness he
was much impressed, regarding Mr. Slidell as a superior
Therlo w Weed. New Orleans was even then in a
modified state of terrorism, on account of the suspected
presence of Abolitionist partisans. 'The moral mercies
of the lasso, of tarring and feathering, head shaving,
ducking and horseponds, deportation on rails, and
similar ethical processes, re highly in favour.' Fires
were also frequent there, and, though Mr. Russell
suggested bad flues a mysterious acquaintance whispered
in a low voice, Slaves.
When I was in the Consulate to-day, a tall and
well dress,Al but not prepossessing looking man, entered
to speak to Nor. Mere on business, and was introduced
to me at his own request. His name was mentioned
incidentally to-night, and I heard a passage in h's life
not of an agreeable character, to say the least of it. A
good many years ago there was a ball at New Orleans,
at which this gentleman was present; he paid particular
attention to a lady, who, however, preferred the society
of one of the company, and in the course of the evening
an altercation ensued respecting an engagement to dance,
in which violent language was exchanged, and a push or
blow given by the favoured prtner to his rival, who left
the room, and, as it is stated, proceeded to a cutler's
shop, where he procured a powerful dagger.linife. Armed
witn this, he returned, and sent in a mess age to the gen-
tleman with whom he had quarrelled. Suspecting
nothing, the latter came into the ante-chamber, the
assassin rushed upon him, stabbed him to the heart,
and. left him weltering in his blood. Another version
of the story was that he waited for his victim till
he came into the cloakroom, and struck him as he was
in the act of putting on his overcoat. After a long
delay the criminal was tried. The defence put fore ard
on his behalf was that he had seized a knife in the heat
of the moment when the quarrel took place, and had
slain his adversary in a moment of passion; but evi-
dence, as I understand, went strongly to prove that a
considerable interval elapsed between the time of the
dispute and the commission•of the murder. The prisoner
had the assistance of able and ingenious counsel; he was
acquitted. His acquittal wag mainly due to the judicious
disposition of a large sum of money; each juror, when
he retired to dinner previous to consulting over his ver-
dict, was enabled to find the sum of 1,000 dols. under
the Plato; nor was it clear that the judge and sheriff had
not pal ticipated in the bounty • in fact, I heard a dis-
pute as to the exact amount Which, it is supposed, the
murderer had to pay. He now occupies, under the Con-
federate Government, the post at New OrleAns which he
lately held as representative of the Government of the
United States.'

Axczszons OF NOBLEMEN. -It has long been the
just boast of our country, that the highest honours are
open to the humblest of her sons. In the roll of the
British Peerage will be found seventy names ennobled
by the successful practice of the law. Trade and.
commerce have been prolific sources of nobility. The
Dukes of Leeds trace back to a clothworker, the Earls
of Radnor to a Turkey merchant, the Earls of Craven
to a merchant tailor, and the Earls of Coventry to a
London mercer. The families of Dartmouth, Ducie,
Pomfret, Tankerville, Dormer, Romney, Dudley,
Fitzwilliam, Cowper, Leigh, Darnley, Hill, and Nor-
manby, were all founded by merchants or citizens of
London. In our own times commerce has added
Lords Ashburton Carrington, and Overstone to the
Upper House, and the Peerage is not less noble, but
more honoured and more useful, because it is occa•
sionally recruited from the ranks of honourable in
s Vicissitudes of _Families.

A SHILLING'S WORTH IN LONDON.-It has been said
—and I am inclined to believe it—that if any one were
to t tke an empty room and invite a pleasure-seeking
Public to the contemplation of its bare walls, the
Speculation would be a paying one, provided only
that the price of admission was fixed at One Shilling.
It would be a problem not without some interest to the
meta Physician to determine the causes which have led
to the adoption of this particular sum as the almost
universal equivalent for modern amusement of every
kind. Why should a poor, half' starved, half- stnpified,
barking seal command exactly the same price, for
instance, as the inclaculable treasures of the World's
Fancy Fair? On what mercantile principles does an
whose cost is reckoned by hundreds of
rely
for its sue,cess upon the identical
as ath f sum
which is calculated to pay for the weekly hire
enterprise,t thousands,
of a small back room? Why, in short, should neither
the quality nor the cost of the entertainment offered
affect in the slightest degree the price demanded or
i
the readiness with which it is paid? It is not so in
other matters. If I wish to buy my wife a
gown, I
am painfully sensible of the difference between cotton
and silk. If, after a hard day's work, I indulge my-
self in the brief Elysiura of nicotine, I at once realise
the pecuniary distinction between the aristocratic
regalia and the 'shag' or 'bird's-eye' of humble life.
But if for once in a way we sally forth together for a
day cr a night of 'popular amusement, I find that
quality is not any longer an element for consideration.
From comic songs to science; from Leotard to light
literature ; from Cornhill to Cremorne ; from the high
art of South Kensington or Trafalgar Square to the
high rope of the Crystal Palace or Ilighbury Barn, the
price is still the same, and when once we have made
up our mind to expend each our shilling, the world
seems all before us where to choose.—Once a Week.

articles.title: OPINING OF A PROTESTANT CHURCH IN NAPLES.
articles.text:
OPINING OF A PROTESTANT
CHURCH IN NAPLES.

A correspondent at Naples, writing on the 16th,
records an event of high interest to the British commu-
ni y there—the laying the first stone of an English
protestant church. Two ye rs or so have passed since
Garibaldi presented a piece of land for the site of the
building, a gift which, after the lapse of some time and
after various vicissitudes was, through the po aerf u 1
influence cf Baron Ricasoli, confirmed by the govern-
ment of Victor Emmanuel. It lies in the Stra.da San
Pasquale, at the back of the Riviera di Chiaja, a quiet
yet central spot It was a bright cold morning on the
leth, and there was a strong muster of English visitors
and residents on the spot, with whom were inter-
mingled a few Italians. On the north-west side
of the futw e Christian church '—the first, by the by,
that will ever have been erected for protestant wor-
ship in Southein Italy—a small temporary building
had been thrown up, covered over, as the fashion
is, with tricoloured hangings, and surmounted hy the
British and Italian flags. in the ihterur of the build-
ing, too, there was the cross of Savoy worked in the
tapestry. The proceedings opened with a pray, rby
the chaplain, the Rev. Pelham Maitland, and some little
wonder was created by the fact :hat the n• xt great act
of the day was not performed by her M ijesey's consul,
who represents the British Government in Napes, and
n whom devolved that duty, more especially as the
government guarantees a certa n sum annually for the
support of the chaplain. Mr. Bonham was in Turin;
but whatever might have been th 6 reasons for the non-
observance of so ob7ious a compliment to our ,e-overn-
ment, an admirable substitute was found in the Duchess
01 St. Arpino. An English lady by birth she has, though
married to a Neapolitan nobl man, clung tceher church
and religion even when the times were evil; and it was
deemed a suitable acknowledgment to ask her to lay the
first stone of this English Protestant church. A mem-
ber of the committee addressed the Duchess to the fellow
ing effect:—' She had been requested by the committee
to act on that occasion, not in censequence of her high
social position, but of her adherence to the faith of her
fathers in times when firmness was a greater v;rtue.
Another motive, too, had influenced them, and that was
a de ire to acknowledge through her husband—an Ita-
lian and a liberal-minded nobleman—the sympathy
which they had received from the Italian nat:on, more
especially from that great and good man who conquered
the liberties of this southern province, and from the
Sovereign who so honestly maintains the civil and
religious liberties of his people.' The Duchess very
briefly and gracefully replied:—' It is difficult for
me to find words to express the pleasure it has
given me in having bee selected by the commit-
tee to lay the foundation stone of the first Pro-
testant church in Southern Italy. I must also thank
the committee and express to them the gratification I feel
at this flattering proof of their regard. lam sure that
it is a day that trill be long remembered in every heart
to which the protestant religion is dear, and with thank-
fulness to the Almighty that He has permitted us to
belong to so pufe a church.' The architect, Mr. Smith,
who is well knewn as the builder of several protestant
churches on the Continent, and very recently of one at
Nice, which was opened at the beginning of the month,
then presented tie trowel to the duchess. Among those
present were his Serene Highness Captain the Prince
Leinin gen, the Duchess of Sutherlaud, Lady Strachan,
the Hon. Mrs. 16wley and her daughter, the Hon. Mr.
and Mrs. de Grey, Lady Sarah Maitland and Colonel
Maitland, besides a host of others more or less distin-
guished, who toe]; a lively interest in the ceremony.
Already £3,400 has been collected for this building,
but probably £1,(00 more will be wanted—a sum which
the friends of religious liberty will undoubtedly soon
make up.

FEDERAL FINANCE.—If the slaveholders' rebellion
shall be suppressed berore the Ist of July next—as we
believe it can and will be if the principles of the pro-
clamation of freedott shall be thoroughly enforced and
lived up to—the entire national debt will be less than
one thousand millions of dollars, and its annual intei est
less than fifty millions, while we shall have a tariff and
internal tax law yielling together an aggregate of not
less than two hundred millions per annum. We can
then proceed to take off the most onerous taxes to the
extent of fifty =dams per annum, and still have
seventy-five millions for the support of government,
fifty millions for the payment of interest as aforesaid,
and twenty-five milliots for the annual reduction of the
principal of the debt; an income which would suffice to
pay off the eniire debt within the ensuing thirty years.
—New York Tribune, Bee. 8.

of Burns the poet have just been disposed of in a sale
by auction at Messrs. Pettick and Simpson's, Leicester-
square. They consisted of upwards of twenty auto-
graph letters, with sone( poetry and a common-place

SHOCKING OCCURRENCE.—Loss OF THREE LIVES.—
In the midst of the storm which swept over the country,
a fatal accident took place on Friday night or Saturday
morning in Shropshire. This was at the Tibberton
Paper Mills, rear Newport, which are the property of
Mr. Martin Billing, of Bingham, and are worked by him.
There are two chimney stacks, one of which has been
recently built, and is square' 120 feet in height; there
are several cottages close by it, within some fifteen
yards. In the midst of the storm, and in the dead of
the night, some sixty feet of this climney was snapped
off, and descended with a frightf al crash on to the
cottages. A man veld his wife were killed in their beds
upon the instant. There were five children and their
parents sleeping in an adjoining cotage ; one of the
children was killed; that the others should have
escaped is almost a miracle. The eottaees were destroyed
at a blow, the inmates forced from their beds, and in
other respects the damage was very great. Mr. Billing
himself was sleeping in a cottoge close by, but the mass
ot buil ding which fell did not reach it. The occurrence
has created much excitement in the diktriet, and being
I within a short distance of the famous Lelleshall Iron-
works, a great number of persons have -visited the scene
of the disaster.

The prospeutus of the Cape of Good Hope Copper
Minning Company (Limited) is issued. The managers
are Messrs. John Taylor and Sons, and the undertaking,
as a whole is very respectably Constituted. The object
is to purchase from Messrs. Phillips, Bing, and Co., the
present proprietors, some large tracts of land in Nama-
qualand, comprising valuable copper mines, and held at
an almost nominal rent. I appears that the properties
in question extend over no less than 202,940 acres, and
that since the year 1855, when the sales of ore at
Swansea became considerable, mining operations have
been attended with' considerable profit. Since 1853,
18,999 tons of copper ore realising £515,752, and
yielding a profit of upwards of £115,000, have been
sold in this country. The average price cbtained has
been no less £27 3s. per ton. The concern is now in
full working order, but a tramway 'of about 15 miles in
length is contemplated. The purchase money of the
estates, buildings, machinery, plant, stores, mineral
rights, and the present accumulations of inferior ores, is
so arranged that of the capital of £150,000, nearly
£77,000 is to be left for the working and development of
the undertaking.
The Constitutionnel contains a paragraph signed by

The Moniteur announces that M. Drouyn de Lhuys

andria, with the Lyons and Marseilles Chambers of Com-
merce, in order to obtain practical information respecting
the increasing interest with which the employment of
silk exported from China is regarded by French
industry.

A FRENCH ATROCITY.—That unf rtunate expedition
which has been regarde as 'a justifiable necessity'
has done the French cause in Attica much harm. The
French troops pursued the Oulaad Ri h, who had 1), en
guilty of numerous outriges, a d, being hard pressed,
the AT abs took refuge in the cave of Khartani. Some
seven hundred persons, in men, women and children,
thronged th windings of this subterranean stronghold,
where a few armed men suffic d to oppose even a much
stronger force than was then under the command of
Colon ,1 Pelissir, the pt esent Duke of Malakhoff. The
Arabs w re repeatedly summoned to surren ter, but they
remained obstinately ,ilent. It was impossible to force
a way ,nto it. 'I he Arabs might have been starv, d. to
submission, for the cave had no other outlet than the
one euarde I by the French troops; but, I believe, the
apprehens:on of the expected arrival of fresh hostile
forces decided the commander upon precipitate action.
An immense fire was kind ed at the mouth of the cave,
and sedulously fed during the whole of that night with
every kind of combustible which was calculated to in-
crease the intense smoke, volumes of which the wind
drovi into the cave At dawn of the following day,
and after sufficient time had elap,ed to rehder the air
of the ilent cave breathable, some soldiers were ordered
to ascertain the state of things within. They were gone
but a few minutes, and they came back, we are told,
pale, trem ling, and terrified; and no wonder, for they
had found all the Arabs dead—men, women, and chil-
dren—all dead! As death had left th -m, so they found
them the old man grasp ng his grey beard —the
young,r one grim, rigid, stern as iron, with frantic
h tred and despair depicted on his countenance—the
dead mother clasping her dead child ! De th rtigned
throughout the vast cave of Khartrni.—.Ruined Cities
in Africa. By N. _Davis.
PROFESSOR WILSON'S LAST CHRISTMAS.—On Christ-
mas Day, 1853, he assembled around him his entire
family, sons and daughters, with their children, to
spend the day in his house. It was almost merry.
His servants decorated the rooms with evergreens, and
one little garland with touching love he ordered to be
laid on his wife's picture, which hung over the
chimneypiece in his bedroom. He was unable to dine
down stairs, but we visited him after dinner, and re-
joiced in the cheerfulness that lighted up his counte-
nance. It seemed a harbinger of coming peace, and
we felt no strangeness in wishing him a happy Christ-
mas, nor thought, as we gazed upon that beautiful
face, that the snows of another such season would fall
upon his grave. My brother John, with his wife and
some of his infant family spent this New Year with
him. This was a great happiness; and for some time
the old fervour and animation seemed to return. They
remained with him to the end. There were two sub-
jects he had been wont to dwell on with affecting ten-
derness—the memory of his wife and his beautiful
home on Windermere. Had they faded from his
vision now, or were they only more sacred as sights
now connected with the glories of another world, puri-
fied in his thoughts from all earthly contact, renewed
in spirit and in beauty, just as his sight was about to
close, and his heart to cease from participation in
things here below? I cannot say, but the name of
'Jane' and of Ellary ' never more escaped his lips.—
Mrs. Gordon's Biography.

IMMUNITY TO RUFFIANS.-Why should one single
known bad character be allowed at large? What is
the use of a police force if it does not keep a sharp look
out after the once convicted felon. The system of
surveillance should be very much closer than it is over
these men, and they should certainly be liable at any
moment to be called upon to show what are their means
of living. What is your trade? Are you actively
engaged in it? Whom do you work for? What do
you receive? These are questions which ought con-
tinually to be put to all those persons who have once
come under the professional care of the police, and the
correctness of the answer made to those questions
should by no means be taken for granted, but should,
on the contrary, be rigorously inquired into. If a man
have no obvious means of living, and yet does manage
to live, it is high time that so extraordinary a mystery
as his mode of subsistence should be looked to.—
.Dickens' s All the Year Bound.

EIDER Dow:sr.—This down, the eider-duck plucks
from its breast to line its nest; it and the eggs are
taken away. Again the nest is lined, and again
robbed. The third time the drake repairs it, supply-
ing the down; and if this be also taken away, the nest
is altogether deserted by the ill-used pair. One nest
yields about two and a-half ounces of the finest clean
down, or about half a pound in all if removed three
times. What is plucked from the dead bird, it is said,
possesses none of that wonderful elasticity which
constitutes the value of the other. We should think,
however, that this would depend on the state of the
plumage at the time. Many thousand pounds weight
of it are annually exported for quilts' pillows, cushions,
&c. It sells in Iceland at from 10s. 6d. to 17s. 6d. per
lb. From three to four pounds are sufficient for a
coverlet, which, to be enjoyed in perfection, ought to
be used unquilted and loose like a feather bed. Quilt-
ing is only useful where a small quantity of down is
required to go a long way; but, with three or four
pounds at command, there is no comparison in point of
comfort between loose and quilted—we have tried
both. The eider coverlet combines lightness and
warmth in a degree which cannot be otherwise ob-
tained. With a single sheet and blanket, it is sufficient
for the coldest wintry night. Its elasticity is pro-
verbial; hence the Icelandic conundrum we had pro-
pounded to us by our good friend Mr. Jacobson, ' What
is it that is higher when the head is taken off it?'
Answer—' An eider-down pillow!' Pen and _Pencil
Sketches of Faroe and Iceland.
AN ANCESTOR OF GENERAL APOLELLAN.—On the
death of William, fourth lord, under age and without
issue, the Maclellans lost their land, and the Lords of
Kirkcudbright of their own free will kept away for a
time from the assemblies of their order But the
right of the collateral heir male was so universally
known and acknowledged, that at the Union this peer-
age was considered as a subsisting one, and as such
preserved on the roll. On several occasions the votes
of the Lords Kirkcubright were subsequently ad-
mitted at the election of Scotch representative peers,
and in 1741, William Maclellan, Lord Kirkcudbright,
recorded his, at the general election. Despite, how-
ever, of his lordly character, the poor peer followed the
humble occupation of a glover, and for many years
used to stand in the lobby of the Assembly-rooms in
the Old Town, selling gloves to the gay frequenters of
the ball; for, according to the fashion of the time, a
new pair was required for every fresh dance. The only
occasion on which he absented himself from his post
was at the ball following the election of a representa-
tive peer; then, and then only, did he doff his apron,
and assuming the garb of a gentleman, associate with
the company, the most of whom he had usually served
with gloves during the rest of the year. The glover.
lord's son, mindful of the pristine glories of his race,
entered on a more ambitious career than his father,
attained the rank of colonel in the army, and, not
satisfied with anything short of legal recognition, sub-
mitted his peerage claim to the House of Lords by
whose decision he was declared seventh Lord K'irk-
cudbright on the 3rd of May, 1773.'—Burke's Vicissi-
tudes of Families.
LORD ANGLESEA'S DRESS.—Quoth I, 'Lord Anglesea!
some admire you as lord-lieutenant, some for your hero-
ism, but I admire you for ' Lord A. What, Lady
Morgan? pray shock us!' Lady M., For the cut of
your coat; who is your tailor? or is all this your own
order ? ' Lord A. (laughing:) 'Oh, I never give an
order, I have an old model coat, the great great grand-
father of this; I always say "make it like this coat, that
is all my order.' Lady M. The fact is, you dress better
than any one, et je ney connais bien ! ' Lord A, 'Well!
I did dress well when I was young, so well, that my
early and kindest friend, the late king, did me the honour
to enter the lists with me; I remember his saying, at a
hall at Devonshire-house, There is that d—d Paget,
better dressed than ever. He went further than this.
One day I went to Carlton-house, by appointment; we
were to go together, the Prince and I, to some morning
fete, I forget where. I had waited some time in the
drawing-room, when a groom of the chambers put in his
head, looked earnestly at me, and retired. Presently
the valet of his Royal Highness put in his head, stared,
and retired. I began to get a little impatient, when a
page entered, walked round, and followed the other two.
The Prince then made his appearance, dressed exactly
like myself! I heard afterwards that he was dressed
when I arrived, and had sent to see how I was dressed,
successively changing every article, till be was told he
was my double! All this now appears ridiculous, but then
it was tout de bon.—Lady Morgan's Memoirs.
SELLING 'WITHOUT ABATEMENT.—II is 110 easy task
to introduce an improvement in any trade. A certain
linendrapery establishment on an extensive scale
in a large city having been opened on the prin-
ciple of having a fixed price from which no
abatement whatever would be given, had, nearly
proved ti failure from its novelty. The custom
was a new one, and the people, among whom it was in-
troduced for the first time, could not be reconciled to
it. Like the young lady who consented to be married
on a summary notice, but who still insisted on having
her proper allowance of courtship, many ladies insist
that they shall be allowed the privilege, which is theirs
prescriptively, of higgling over every purchase they
make at the linendraper's. But when at length the
price of goods purchased at the no-second price
establishment was compared with that of others in the
same trade, in the same city, and found to be lower—
which* it could afford to be, because the whole was
based on a sound calculation—business flowed upon the
concern, and it became ultimately the most flourishing
in the city. Yet, before the public found out that they
could be well and cheaply served, the proprietors,
despairing of the success of their plan, had had part of
their stock packed up in bales with the intention of
abandoning the enterprise.—elfctemillan's Magazine.

NURSERY RHYMES.
There was a young lady of Pinner,
She said, How I wish I was tanner;'
Said Mamma, A good way
To do that, I sh,uld s
Was to go for a week w thout dinner.'
There was a young lady of Harrow,
Who would go to church in a barrow,
It stuck in the aisle
And she sad, with a smile,
'They build these here churches too narrow.'
There was a young lady of Bicester,
One day that her lover hnd kissed her,
She seemed quite erplexed,
And to show she was vexed
She gave such a slap to her sister.
There was a young lady of Stroud,
Whose voice was so a fuily loud,
When she went for a walk,
They forbad h-r to sulk,
For fear of attracting a crowd.
There was a young lady:of Oldha.m,
And when she got presents, she sold 'em,
When folks said, How mean ! '
She replied, All's se i ene,'
And that was the whole that she told 'em.
There was a young lady of Leeds,
Her eyes were the bigness of beads,
When they said, Do you squint?'
he replied, I've got lint,

A QUESTION FOR LORD DITNDWEARY.
If a woman mawwy a man, and her husband dies,
what do people call her ?—A widow.
If she then mawwy again, and the second husbano

THE POPLAR UNION.
The Approaching Marriage of the Prince of Wales
with the Princess Alexandra of Denmark!
Three cheers, boys!

articles.text:
A SONG FOR SUMMER.

With sunshine now the Summer's come,
The bee from flower to flower cloth hum:
Poor insect! ah, I know too well
That wax-work oft turns out a cell.

SLAWILENBERGIUS ON NOSES.—The large aquiline
nose of Mr. Punch is an indication of the ardour of his
Judyism.

LivrNG LIKE A PRINCE.—A certain rich nobleman,
who keeps a French cook, is accustomed to call his chef
`.Minister of the Interior.'

CUTTING OBSRRYATIONS.—Why is a biting jest like
a stale proverb! Because an old saw must have teeth.

AN ANTITHESIS OF Evms.—Mity cheese and weak
ale.
A FLING FOR A HORSE-LATJGII.-4 timid rider is
generally a good-natured fellow, because he is slow at
taking a fence.
BATHS AND WAsnnousEs.—The beneficent exertions
of sanitary reformers for the good of the working-
classes in densely crowded districts are never more suc-
cessful than when they make a clean sweep.
DOMESTIC ECONOMY AND MEDICINE.—` Stuff a cold,'
says the proverb, and starve a cough.' Accordingly a
cough is the cheaper complaint for a family, because in
starving it you save your butcher's and baker's as well
as doctor's bills.

OBSERVATIONS ON GROUND BAlT.—Boys are often
taught, though they never learn, to regard fishing as a
cruel amusement, when nevertheless angling, at least as
most commonly practised in the Thames, is universally
admitted to be particularly and pre-eminently the gentle
craft.

CON BY A CONVERSATIONALIST.—Why is a negative
like frozen rain? Because it's no.

Love AND CALonic.—.A.coording to one of the songs
of the day, Love will Thaw the Ice. It had long been
known that love, like many a skater about Christmas,
would break the ice; but its effect in the liquefaction of
that substance is a discovery. Will love thaw the ice
at 32°? In that case, what a comfort it would be, if,
during a hard frost, Love would get up 'betimes of a
morning, and impart fluidity to the contents of the wash-
hand-jlig

A MODERN OBACLE.—‘ As regards diet, how about
malt liquor ? ' was the question put to a mesmeric som-
nambulist practising medicine in the state of clairvoyance.
The reply of the Seer was No beer but All-sop.'
AN OBTUSE ANGLE.—An Old Maid fishing for a com-
pliment.
SEw-SAw.—Devote your leisure to needle-work. The
richest lady in the land is the Old Lady of Threadneedle-
street.

A COMMON FORM OF SHORT-SIGHTEDNESS DURING THE
HUNTING SnASON.—Not being able to see the end of a
run.

CONUNDRUM FOR THE COUNTRY.—Which wind does
the Pig see plainest ? The Sou-West.
'OH! HORRIBLE, MOST EIoRRIBLv, ! ' Of what General
are you reminded by seeing a stable full of horses eating
hay? Why of General Bay-gnaw, to be sure !
How does a fellow's marrying a wife influence his
choice of Counsel? When he gets She(a) he generally
gives up his Chambers.
NEW NAME FOR SIR CRESSWELL CREsswELL.—The
Judicious Un-Hooker.

A FACT IN NATURAL HISTORY.—If you are anxious
to know what marvellous things the tongue of the
Adder can do, and what extraordinary lengths it will
sometimes go to, listen attentively to a Richmond
waiter, in the height of the season, when he is reckoning
up our score. _ _ _ _

-Tan RACECOURSE AND THE RING.—She who takes a
flporting man for better or for worse, may find him both
better and worse than she expected.
CON BY •A POOR CROSSING SWEEPER.—Why is a
tirch-broom like a weeping willow? Because it 's a
thing as (s) weeps.
AN OLD BEAU.—Stubbs, at eighty, stained his hair
and whiskers. lle died at a good old age—didn't he?
THE QUESTION OF THE DAL—Have you been
garotted?
RIDDLE FOR A BEGINNER.—When is a cherry bigger
than a pumpkin? When it's a bigaroon.

To ANY ON FOND OF GOOD gUITERS. - Become a
Policeman.

Garibaldi has been invited to pay a visit to Naples
when his wound is healed, and 53 Neapolitan ladies have
undertaken to pay all the expenses of the General and
his suite as long as they stay.
THE KING or SAXONY.—On the anniversary of the
King of Saxony's birthday last week a solemn Te Deum
was sung in the Catholic Cathedral at Dresden. His
Majesty has now entered his 62nd year. After the
religious ceremony the King reviewed the garrison as
well as the corps of cadets and artillery pupils. The
troops appeared in their new uniforms. In consequence
of resolutions adopted at Wurtzburg, it was decided that
the greatest possible uniformity should be established
in the equipment and arming of the Federal troops;
Saxony has conformed to that resolution by modifyina
the dress of almost every corps in her army.
A RUSSIAN PRINCE.—We had just returned from a
long, dreary drive, tired, cold, covered with dust, when
a thundering knock came to the door—J. Thomas flew
to open it; enter a creature fine and foppish—a sort of
tartar turned dandy—who asked in a foreign accent,
for Lady Morgan. Thomas, sulky as a pig, because he
hates my lady having them furriners,' cried I don't
think my lady is at hdrne ; but I'll thry, sir. Who shall I
say, sir?' The Prince Pucklau Muskau '! ! ! Away
-went Thomas, tumbling down the kitchen stairs—
Jack fell down and broke his crown,
And Jill (Morgan, with a bottle in his hand)
—came tumbling after.
I, like Miss Polly, tumbled up stairs to the drawing-
room and stood in all mv dust and dowdiness to
receive l'Altezza, whom is cher J., announced as Prince
Pickling Mustard,' (Jut as last summer he persisted in
calling Prince Cimatelli, Vermacelli.') Well, I put
on the best face (a dirty one) I could on it, and endea-
voured to excuse things. The Prince put me at once
at my ease. He is a most finished fop.—Lady Morgan's
Memoirs.

The Prussian Minister at Rome, w recently becalm
insane, is said to be in such a dangerous state that there
is little hope he will recover his reason.
AN INTERNATIONAL PURC/lASE.—‘ We have reason to
know,' says the Patric, 'that the negotiations opened
between the Italian Government and that of Portugal,
for the cession by the latte: of an island intended to serve
as a place for transportation. are on the point of being;
concluded. Portugal is to cede for a pecuniary compen-
sation one of the small islands she possesses on the coast
of Mozambique.

Lord Raynham is leading an appeal on 'behalf of the
destitute wives and chiltiren of the miners who lost their
lives by the B trrsley colliery explosion.
Balfe has nearly completed a grand opera, which, it is
said, will be the next novelty (after the pantomime) at
the Royal English Opera.
The widow of Sir William Don has made her first
bow, since her berea, ement, before a Liverpool audlence,
as Captain Macheath
It is undel stood that the Confederate Government are
endeavouring to issue in this county, privately or other-
wise, bonds bearing interest at the rate of elght per cent.
per annum.
During her Majesty's absence, great prepal a.‘ ions
will be made for the forthcoming wedding, particu any
in Ed n ard the Fouttn's Tower, which will be occu2ied
by the P. incess.
The ifoniteur announces that five flags captured by
the French in M,xico have been brought to Paris and
presented to the Emperor. They are to be placed in the
Invalides.

The B rmingham arms trade are said to be busy in
the execution of urgent orders for small revolvers, a
demand which seems to have risen from the frequency
of st eet robberies in the mAropolis and its environs.

The other day, in a Scotch kirk, a minister, of not
over-brilliant talents, in order to illustrate his subject,
said—' If any of the planets were losing their attraction
to each other, they would immediately fall to the
earth.'

A society has been formed in London for the pur-
pose of exploring the mines in Greenland, and to trade
in the furs of that count.y. The society has obtained
this sole privilege for thirty years from the Danish
Government.

It is rumoured that the Bake of Devonshire has
offered £l,OOO for the 'bullet extracted from Garibaldi's
foot. Had it been a lady who had made the offer we
might have given credence to it, but as it is, we suppose
it is only a conard.

The new railway-bridge across the Rhine at Mayence
was tried last week by a luggage-train bound from
Mayence to Frankfort. There were thirty-six luggage-
vans, and drawn by three engines. It was opened
for passengers on the 20th of this month, hen the
directors gave a large entertainment to celebrate the day.
Four hundred invitations were issued.

A German doctor, who has seen Garibaldi at Pisa,
says that notwithstanding all the reports that are circu-
lated as to the General's rapid recovery, so far from that
being the case he is suffering from a fever that is rapidly
consuming him, and what with that and repeated attacks
of gout, which threaten to seize on vital parts, there is
little hope of his living till the spring.
It has been remarked that the three first subjects in
the realm have been fellows and tutors at Oxford. The
Archbishop of Canterbury was student and tutor of
Christ Church; the Lord Chancellor, fellow and tutor
of Wadham College; the Archbishop of York, fellow
and tutor, and afterwards Provost, of Queen's College.
A monster casting, weighing 52 tons, and intended as
a bed or anvil for the powerful Nasmyth steam hammer
in use at the gun factories department of the Royal
Arsenal, was on Thursday removed from the mould. In
consequence of the immense body of metal, the casting
was upwards of three weeks before it became perfectly
cool.
_ _ _

Trafalgar-square seems, in short, destined to become,
as was lately observed by a contemporary, a sort of
out-door Chamber of Horrors.' The statue of Napier
vulgarises, in a very painful manner, the well-remem-
bered aspect of one of the greatest of our modem
heroes; and that of Havelock, with its large heavy
head, is scarcely less objectionable; while the statue of
Nelson, placed almost out of sight on the top of a column
(disfigured by a very ugly lightning conductor), justifies
the simple remark of the old Greenwich pensioner, who
exclaimed, when first taken to see it, Why, they've
mast-headed the Admiral.'

The spirit mediums have a new power (trick ?) de-
veloped in them. They say they can photograph the appa-
ritions that become visible to their eyes. The operation
requires to be performed by a medium, who can combine
a spiritual nature with a proper knowledge of photo-
graphy. We conclude to produce these portraits they
require to be alone, for fear the spirit about to be
photographed should be as visible to anyone else ns to
th( mselves.
Two ships loaded at Liverpool with warlike stores for
New York. The Ncrthern spies inquired into the
matter and found it all right, especially as the
Southerners were doing all they could to stop the load-
ing. The steamers filled and sdiled ; after they had been
oft' two or three days, it came out that they were really
bound for some other port—that is, for the South—and
the Yankee was done!

It is rather amusing to read that a prisoner, who was
brought before Mr. Justice Byles, at Exeter Zssizes last
Monday, on a charge of horse-stealing, had been con-
victed of an offence at Jersey, and there had been sen-
tenced to three months' imprisonment, and five years'
banishment to England ! ' We suppose it is true, as it
is reported in all the daily papers; but it makes us a
little curious to see the Judge who passed the sentence.
A letter from Rome says, The pami.hlet of the secre-
tary of Prince Napoleon reached this city with great
difficulty. Copies of it were seized from al f9rtigners
who had them in their possession. A Jesuit, who has a
great taste for examining into old archives, is, it is said,
making a collection of documents in a quite contrary
sense.' _ _ _

Whilst the German band was playing on the Espla-
nade at Brighton on Monday last, a lady was suddenly
seized with madness; she became violent, and it was
with great difficulty she was removed. It is said that
the particular air the band was playing at the time was
the immediate cause, it being one that was mingled in
some way with a sad episode of her life.
The mysterious book of Mr. Kinglake's, about the
Crimean -War, which has for such a long time been fit-
fully announced in lists of books about to appear, has
once more dis,ppeared therefrom. What sort of a book
it is, and why it can't get out are questions which can-
not be answered.

The Mon iteur meets the reproaches arising out of the
case of Rosalie Boise by pointed reference to the late
exhibition in the British courts, disclosing what befell
11-111, locked up in virtue oc Dr. Semple's certificate,
and cells it an exemplification of habeas corpus, a pro-
cess the very meaning of which is unknown to most
Frenchmen.

Another instance of the remarkable manner in which
the firms connected with the Greek trade who were
compelled to suspend during the crisis at the beginning
of 1861 have surmounted their difficulties and honour-
ably discharged every liability has transpired, Messrs.
Ede, and Co., Levant merchants, of George-street,
Mansion-house, whose engagements amounted to
£161,800, having settled all claims in full, with interest
at 5 per cent.
' Retrenchment ' is expected to turn out the great card
of the Government during the coming session. A semi.
official organ in London says, that the process of lopp-
off ' in the Army Estimates will be confined to useful
administrative reforms, such as reductions in the dis-
trict staffs and at the recruiting stations. lathe present
state of Europe, and with the Northern States of
Ammica all but threatening war against us, it would
scarcely be prudent to make any great reductions in the
Army or Navy.
The deep black, says an American paper, which our
ships have been painted, has proved to be a very promi-
nent mark to shoot at, in consequence of which a change
has been made to a greyish drab. The steamers R. R.
Caylor and Ossipee, now at the Portsmouth Navy Yard,
have been painted this shade, which makes them much
more 'invisible,' so that one standing on one side of the
river can hardly distinguish the vessels from the wharf
or the water, whereas a small black boat and a schooner
stand out in bold relief. _ _

_
At a meeting, held at Tralee lately for the purpose of
raising funds in aid of the Lancashire operatives, an
amendment was moved by the O'Donoughue that no-
thing should be done for Lancashire, as the wants of
their own people had a prior claim to their consideration,
and the amendment was carried. This is a beautiful
return for the charity lavished on Ireland and Irishmen
by the people of Great Britain in former times of
destitution and distress. Other parts of Ireland, how-
ever, have nobly done their duty towards Lancashire.
We are happy to perceive that the great co-operative
association of Rochdale, the Equitable Pioneers' Society,
has as yet ridden out the storm. This society has a
store, or rather series of stores, a corn-mill, and a cotton
mill, all built, owned, and worked wholly by operatives.
The stores last year earned a profit of £lB,OOO, and last
quarter the profits amounted to 2s. 6d. in the pound.
The principle is that members shall be paid profits on
their amount of consumption, so that the more they buy
the more they get. One man, for example, who, in
1854, had £7 10s. in the concern, has dealt with it
steadily for eight years. He has had all his goods
better and ch, aper than he could get them elsewhere,
and the amount to his credit is £132 10s. ! The corn-
mill made, in 1861, £lO,OOO, and is, of course, little
affected by the distress, and the cotton mill is at work
three days in the week. There are thirty such societies
in the county, and these are all weathering the storm,
though, in some cases, with exceeding difficulty. There
is the true protection for the working man.—Spectator.
The New Society of Painters in Water Colours has
put forth a scheme for obtaining aid towards relieving
the Lancashire distress. Each memher has been invited
to contribute a painting or sketch in water-colourss, and
every member ot the profession known to paint in water-
colours, is solicited to carry out the object. The whole
collection is to be e,xhibited in London, Manchester, and
Liverpool, and afterwards allotted to subscribers as
prizes. The whole of the receipts of the exhibition and
subscriptions received, less working expenses alone, will
be devoted to the end named.

effected Monday's rates were maintained. There was a

articles.title: METROPOLITIAN CATTLE MARKET.
articles.text:
METROPOLITIAN CATTLE MARKET.

There was a moderate supply of foreign stock here to.
day, in middling condition. Amongst it were 128 oxen
from Corunna and 122 ditto from Oporto. The Portu-
guese beasts were very small. Sales progressed steadily
at full quotations. Considering that the great market was
held on Monday last, the show of beasts this morning was
rather extensive, and most breeds came to hand in good
condition. On the whole the beef trade was firm, and
last week's quotations were well supported. A few superior
Scots realised ss. 2d. per filbs. ; but the general top figure
for beef was ss. per 81bs., and a good clearance was
effected. From Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, and North-
amptonshire we received 1.200 shorthorns, &c.; from
other parts of England, 540 various breeds; from Scot-
land, 120 Scots and crosses; and from Ireland, 400 oxen
and heifers. Although we were well supplit d with sheep,
the time of year considered, the mutton trade was some-
what active. Downs and half-breds advanced 2d, per
Sibs., the top figure being 58. 10:1„ and the value of all
other breeds was firmly maintained. The supply of
calves was limited, and the veal trade was brisk, at an ad-
vance in the quotations of 4d. per 81bs. The best veal
was worth ss. per Sibs. Pigs were rather dearer, with a
steady inquiry. A market will be held here on Friday
next, instead of Thurshay as usual.

PATitioTs.—‘ General,' said Major Jack Downing, I
al ways observed that those people who have a great
deal to say about being ready to shed their last drop of
blood are amazin' partic'ler about the first drop.' We
have too many of that style of patriots now-a-days.
ATTACK UPON A WARDER BY A CONTICT.—As a
gang of convicts, under the supervision of a warder
named Deane, were employed on Friday in the junk
store of Portsmouth dockyard, one of the fellows,
named Frazer, made a ferocious attack upon the
warder, felling him to the ground with the oaken rung
of a 'Jacob's ladder,' and kicking him severely while
on the ground. He was speedily secured and removed
to the convict prison adjoining the dockyard. Deane
was removed to the hospital for medical treatment.
AN AURORA BOREALIS SEEN FRO3d MAZSRILLBS.--A
magnificent aurora borealis was observed at Marseilles
on Sunday evening last. It first appeared at twenty-
four minutes past six. Its white crown was visible due
north, and its most brilliant rays were seen is the west.
Its various movements lasted until twenty-five minutes
past seven, and during all that time it waseasy to follow the
innumerable changes in the shade of the colours presented
by the phenomenon. It reappeared from twenty minutes
past nine to thirty-nine minutes past nine more briefly,
but much brighter, than the first time. According to
the observations of M. Tempel, an astronomer residing at
Marseilles, the breadth of the aurora borealis Was more
than 100 degs.

day night a chimney stalk in the premises of Mr. Waiter
Donald, cut nail and rivet manufacturer, 55, St. James's-
road, Glasgow, was blown down, doing considerable
chmage in its fall to property, but 11,14'4 unattended
by any fatal results to human life. The stalk was built
rather more than a year ago, and was 120 feet in height.
It was surrounded somewhat closely on nearly every side
with workshops and dwelling-houses, and it was but a
few yards from the street. Fortunately it fell in an
easterly direction, as there was scarcely another way it
could have fallen without almost certain destruction ta
human life.—North British Mail.
