SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1862.

SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

The Greeks have unanimously chosen Prince
Alfred as their future King; and Prince Fer-
dinand of Portugal, to whom the three Powers
Britain, France, and Russia, offered the Gre-
cians, declines to receive them. Mr. Layard,
of Southwark, the Under-Secretary for Foreign
Affairs says, that the British Government is
willing to make over the lonian Islands to the
Greeks when they can give evidence of their
capability to maintain a Constitntional Govern-
ment. The Greeks may not, however, be able
to satisfy the British Government on that
matter, until the Greek Kalends.

Prince Alfred may be yet advised to accept
the election to the Athenian Throne; and if
he really possesses the energy ascribed to him,
in process of time he may convert it into a
Byzantine throne. He might prove a thorn on
the flank of Russia, and in a quarter where the
political relations are in a volcanic state, he
might gain by one or more wrecks.
The idea of aggrandising Greece at the cost
of Turkey, can scarcely be entertained during
the reign of the present reforming and resolute
Sultan. Empires occasionally fall as they
sometimes rise with a great man. But the

character of the Turkish Sultan leads us to
expect that he Will keep a firm, yet a just hand
over his mixed multitude of subjects.
Dost Mohammed was besieging Herat atthe
date of the latest accounts from that quarter,
and the Sultan thereof was making a resolute
defence of the stronghold. The Russian
forces have again been defeated in the Cau-
casus, but the contest there is a hidden struggle,
of which we have few particulars.
The Emperor of Austria in parting with his
Parliament desired its members to spread
among their neighbours a knowledge of sound
constitutional principles.
Some of our journals assert that the Em-
peror has to learn them, and that may be true;
but Austria has made great progress since
Solferino, and its banishment from Rome may
turn out to be the safety of the State.
Napoleon has paid a seven hour's visit to Ba-
ron Rothschild, the French Baron, at his coun-
try seat, and the interview between these men of
metals was magnificently expensive; quite as
much so as the celebrated meeting of the
English and French Sovereigns for seven days
on the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

An Italian minister, has been in Paris for
the purpose of soliciting permission from Na-
poleon to have the new Italian loan quoted on
the Paris Bourse. The Italian financier was
also charged with some negotiation between
his Government and the Rothschild's, regarding
Italian railways. The expenditure and income
of the Italian nation must be brought into
accord before it can be deemed established
and safe.

The French are now advancing in Mexico
and towards the capital, but their bulletins are
unpublished. The Federal Government allow
the merchants of New York to earn a little
money by supplying the French with military
stores for the Mexican war. The Federal
Government cannot forbid the transaction,
although we believe that they desire for the
stores a rapid passage to the bottom of the
sea. Their powerlessness should be a justifi-
cation of other transactions.

A subscription in behalf of the Lancashire
Operatives at New York amounts to £20,000:
but many complaints appear of distress, both
in the eastern and the western States. Gold
continues at a premium of 32. Notes of the
Confederate Government had sold at half-price.
An expedition under General Banks had
sailed from New York. It consisted chiefly of
Northern regiments, and was expected to land
at some point from which the army, numbering
from 20,000 to 30,000 men, could act against
Richmond from the South, but the stearners
conveying the forces have been met so far to
the South, that some other locality must be
their destination—probably Charleston.
A. private teiegraphic message received on
I Wednesday, per the Hibernia; states that the
Federal . General Reynolds attaCked the Con-
federate entrenchment's behind Fredericksburg,
at half-past nine a.m. of the 13th, and that the
Confederates replied with artillery. The con-
test was proceeding at eleven o'clock. The
Confederate generals will probably not risk
a great battle near the Rappahannock, but draw
their opponents farther from their supplies;
unless it was true, as formerly reported, that
General Stuart with their cavalry had crossed ,
the Rappahannock to the north.
If the latter report be true, the Confede-
rates had determined probably to fight on that
spot. Further intelligence will almost cer-
tainly be received before the publication of all
our editions.

COLONIAL.

The intelligence from the colonies is ex-
tremely meagre. The Dutch settlers who mi-
grated to the north from the Cape Colony pome
years ago, are at war among themselves.
Business in that colony had materially im-
proved. The Lancashire distress had caused a
considerable subscription in the eastern pro-
vince. Of the colonies we • have at home
abundant intelligence. The public companies
formed to operate within them during the last
six months, have a capital of not less than
twelve millions. The New Zealand Trust
Society, with a capital of half a million, is the
last of these projects. A copper mining
company for the Cape, with a capital of
£70,000, has been recently proposed. And
even the oil wells of Canada have already and
profitably absorbed a considerable capital.
With the close of the year, and the eve
of Christmas, better news came up from
Lancashire, where a marked reduction has
occurred in the number of the unemployed.

teries. This idea, however, although assiduously
inculcated by the concederacy, is - a great mis-
take; within the lowest depth, there is a lower,
and that of course is not Strictly grammatical,
and is strictly sensational. A man who has
once become a Templar is liable to be made a
Bencher. "They that are down need fear no
fall," wrote good honest John Bunyan, in an
erroneous line of a work that has few erroneous
lines; but although the Pilgrim had seen in
vision, many stoutly contested quarrels, yet he
had not seen the gritii fight between Bye and
Hudson for a book and the • championship
of the Bencher's den; and he did not know
that liability of a human being, as before said,
to be down at a Templar's doom, and yet be
liable to fall farther to a Bencher's fate. The
Benchers, or Committee of the Templars, are
an irresponsible and self-elected body,who hold
in their hands and management the accumula-
ted funds of centuries, and may hire fighting
men and myrmidons, if they be so inclined, to
do their will. These Benchers assemble in a
hall "hidden from public view ;" within this
secret recess they dine, they drink, they discuss
I the Templars, they summon their slaves into
their presence, they investigate their most
personal transactions; andthus they become ac-
quainted, or they may.. become acquainted if
they please', with the most cherished secrets of
families: the half of England may be considered
theirs: in that den post prandium, post vinum
—they charge, they examine, they cross exa-
mine, they garrotte or grapplewith; and towards
the mirk midnight, when scarcely a shadow can
be seen on the gloomy Thames, they subdue
by throttling their victims, or even their victim's
witnesses.. What imaginative orator in the
great debating clubs of Fleet Street, of which
Napoleon the little was afraid, and wherein
Train the mad taught, ever imagined the
horrors of horrors," that may be going on
between their last pot of beer and the black
river, as they arise to depart and to leave the
place rendered famous by eloquence, gehius,
and political sagacity, to become a bar room or
parlour deserted. The omnibus drivers, ac-
quainted as they are intimately with the tradi-
tions of their route, never even dreamed that
the respectable houses of Fleet Street on the
right, going towards the rising sun, concealed
the secrets of an oppressive system that des-
troys all the energies of free action; and of free
trade; secrets which might be wrought into no
end of interesting tissues.
There was a Templar named SEYMOUR—Mr.
DIGBY SEYMOUR,—who was elected to repre-
sent Sunderland in Parliament, and having
displeased the electors of that place was re-
turned for Southampton. In the course of
his professional career, Mr. SEvuoun. wore a
coarse stuff gown, and next was authorised to
appear in silk, and to place Q.C. on his card.
Mr. SEYMOUR also attained unto the Recorder-
ship of Newcastle, and was altogether a fortu-
nate man for his years. During his youth he
had hastened to be rich by taking part in joint
stock companies, for the use of which the M.P.
_ _ _

and Q.C. are valuable helps; even barrister-
at-law not being altogether worthless. In the
course of his experiences, Mr. SEYMOUR went
into gold mining, not personally, but as
director, or chairman of directors, or something
else. A prosperous man makes foes some-
times. Mr, SEYMOUR excited- envy among
the Benchers. Jealousy is not over nice,
but haunts the precincts of the Thames
at all states of the tide, and all hours of time.
Accordingly-, some of the Benchers pounced
upon Mr. SEYMOUR. They wanted to know if
he was no better than he should be, and insti-
tuted a committee of inquiry. Let us correct
our statement. They—the Benchers—are a
standing committee of inquiry upon the cha-
racter and conduct of Templars, and their fit-
ness for employment. They decide who among
them shall be permitted to earn their daily
bread in the profession to which they have
been educated. In some circumstances • the
Times would describe this power as a detestable
imperium in imperio, the reprehensible dicta-
tion of an irresponsible society; an interference
between the employed and the employers that
must be suppressed by law as unendurable.
Fortunately for themselves, so far as the Times
is concerned, the persons implicated in these
proceedings are only Benchers, and not
builders.

Mr. SEYMOUR was charged with being a
black-sheep. According to the Benchers, he
had committed an unprofessional act: Being
indebted to an attorney, he requested that
gentleman to take the debt out in work. We
do not know whether the Benchers applied
the term "unprofessional," to Mr. SEYMOUR'S
resolution to meet his liabilities on the prin-
ciple "base is the wretch who pays ; " but we
think the word is rather connected with the
practice of canvassing for briefs from a creditor.
It is a very delicate task to act ai.a touter for a
barrister, and requires great tact.
During the inquiry, Mr. HUDSON, not the
identical railway k ing, 'but another of the name,
was examined. Mr. HUDSON and Mr. SEY-

MOUR both belonged to the same gold com-
pany. As Sergeant SirEE, the counsel for the
secret society said, somebgdy rigged the market,
quoad the gold 'company's shares 'spoken to.
/This somebody, as the sergeant informed the
jury, was connected with ROBERTSON, who was
familiar with LA.ICEMA.N, who Was friendly with
HUDSON, who was intimate with SEYMOUR.
By this chain of assumptions or facts, Sergeant
%LEE endeavoured to connect the unhappy
SEYMOUR with somebody who rigged the gold
company's shares. According eo Sergeant
STIES, the legal maxim was amplified into
SEYMOUR. facit per HUDSON, qui facit per
LAXEMAN, qui facit per ROBERTSON, qui facie
per "Somebody," sic SEYMOUR facit per
"Somebody." We remark, as a cariosity,
that our laughing Lord Chief justice omitted
to smile at the chain employed to pull down
SiYmoun, by the weight of Somebody at "the
other end."

In order to examine this matter, the
Benchers requested Mr. HUDSON to enter their
den.

"Will you walk into my parlour,
Said the spider to the fly."
"Fly HUDSON" believing in the honour of the
Benchers, and probably also in their wine,
complied, with the invitation. After he had
been examined in every possible way, he
inquired whether the inquisitors were finished
with his.
..own private letter or memorandum
book, which appears to have been put astray,
and then to have been first seen by its owner
among the Benchers, who replied that they
had finished with the little book, arid one of
them made it over to Mr. HuDsoN, and he
placing it in his pocket intimated his resolu-
tion to part no more with his old favourite.
Then arose a hurricane, not to be matched in
our records, saving always on that occasion
when ROBERT BURN'S friend, a respectable
farmer, dared to speak among the witches at
" Allowa's auld haunted kirk." Pity for poor
HUDSON that he spoke before his foot was in
the stirrup. Why could he not have imitated
the policy of Marmion, and been half-way over
the drawbridge before he dared the anger of
the chiefs of Tantallan ? HuDsor,i's memoran-
dum book became immediately valuable in

these benehers cues as the Sybill's books in
the eyes of the Roman senate. • Pap rose the
Benchers, like furies to the charge an their soli-
tary witness; led by three stalwart knights, the
bold Sir Wiviirmat ALEXANDER, the good Sir
RICHARD PnrummouE, and the strong Sir
FREDERICK •SLA.DE for ,never Juan was more
respectably auobbed than Mr. ItunsoN. They
hustled him, .and jostled him, and called finally
for the offiiials of the inquisition, as the chiefs
could not irecapture the book. Two of the
latter appeared—one of them by name" Bye,"
of great strength, clad in the armour of an
old Templar; or so we gather from the circum-
stance that he swore his inability to know
when a man punched him on the ribs—a cha-
racteristic which Bye in armour would share
with a large tortoise; but it may be possible
that to the present date Mr. BYE has not met
the right 'man. BYE is the chief porter to the
Benchers; but that is mekely, we suppose, a
title by courtesy. BYE'S duties towards
HUDSON—his engagement, as he termed it,
with HupsoN—consisted in first holding this
man's head uppermost, according to nature;
next, his heels against nature; then placing
him on his back upon two chairs; ultimately
putting him on the ground with his back against
two chairs; while searching, as he says, the
upper part of the man's person for that man's
own book; while all the time the HUDSON
kicked outrageously, except when the under-
porter held his heels in a sort of vice.
It must have been a delightful skrimmage
for all the imps to witness, and we have no
doubt of their presence among the Benchers on
that occasion; but the Peelers put in an ap-
pearance and commanded Mr. BYE to unloose
the Benchers' victim. After all in these
regions of law if we are not strictly under civil
liberty a man has at least the defence of the
police.
At the trial Mr. BA.GSHAWE, Mr. RODWELL,
and other Benchers, maintained that they em-
ployed no personal violence; they only em-
ployed Bye; but if BAGSHAIVE pzujnat per ROD-
WELL—we beg pardon per BYE, we suppose he
should take the results.
The police persuaded all the parties to go to
the station, where HUDSON begged to be
charged for stealing his own book, and BAG-
SHAWE declined to charge him for more than
taking the book, and the inspector refused to
entertain the matter.
Thereupon, Mr. HUDSON raised an action of
damages against the Benchers for false im-
prisonment. This was the action that was
tried on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday
last, before the Lord CHIEF JUSTICE, and the
Jury in the Guildhall, and the Jury were dis-
charged on Wednesday because they could not
agree: but if the actors and the scene had

be-en changed, we think that the Jury could,
and we also think that they should, have
-agreed, on the supposition that the Benchers
had been brickmakers for example, who had
been rough with a "black sheep," and used
personal violence by their door keepers or
porters to any man who came to speak with
them for a neighbour's right.
, We should have heard in that case eloquent
arguments against the tyranny of combinations;
against their assaults on the freedom of labour,
against their " contemptible " efforts to sup- ,
press a man's right to sell his labour to the
cheapest or the lowest bidder, against their
cruelty towards his innocent wife and children,
in endeavouring to drive him from employ-
ment in one of their yards.
The eloquence of Sergeant SHEE on this sub.-
ject would have been grand as a torrent from the
mountains of Connemara; that of the Lord
Chief Justice would have been cold and severe
as the ice of the North Pole; and the jury
would have agreed, and the sentence would
have been penal servitude; for the police
inspector would have taken the charge
on the other side—the magistrate would
have committed, and the whole case would not
have been civil, but criminal.
We ask equal consideration for the open and
published proceedings of trades' societies with
that given to the orgies of this great secret
society, having men "of great strength" hired
to do assault and battery on the Queen's sub-
jects ; but we neither ask for the legal guild,
nor for any other guild or society, power to
break law or order, or to employ violence.

~1.M..-.. --....-•-•...

DEA.TH IN THE PIT.

Death in the pit! Unfortunate Barnsley!
Another fifty or sixty lives lost; and, as usual,
no one in fault. We beg pardon; the Times,
as usual, by both letter and leader, on Thurs-
day week, throws the whole blame upon the
men. And so, with a great deal of
pity, but no real help, the risks and dangers.
of the British miner will probably continue
for some years longer to increase and be fatal;
will in fact continue, until the idea be formed

that the British miner is a man, and has both
a body and a soul to be cared for, or that
life and limb are of equal value as wealth and
works.

It is little mere than eighty years ago that
actual and legal slavery of the miners was
abolished; and even yet these men; whose
labour is so necessary, and so arduous, are still
treated as either serfs or overgrown children.
They are worked by their employers solely for
gain, and in many Instances with much less
attention paid to their safety than to their
horses; simply because they cost less to obtain
[in one instance of bye-laws now before us,
eight relate to the care of the men, and fifteen
to the care and comfort of the horses]; while
the public, or rather, perhaps, the Legislature,
;look upon miners as useful instruments for the
development of wealth, who have neither
knowledge nor discretion to guide themselves,
either towards safety in working, or propriety
in life. And thus, betwixt the condition of
chattels in serfdom, and children in probation,
the miner is suspended; as betwixt two stools;
and; as we know by the old proverb, how
frequeptly they thus fall to the ground. Deny-
ing distinctly and positively, as this case of
the Edmund's Main catastrophe definitely
proves, that the men are the chief faulters, it
cannot be denied that, as a class, they are
proverbially careless. True, the lives of the
miners is all to them, and that their Wives and
families have for and redeive as much love from
them as do others; but then the daily work ot.
these men is constantly surrounded by and in
the very midst of danger, and thus, like poverty,
met constantly in the face, it loses its terrors;
aud men grow even careless of risk, when
there is the least uncertainty of results. In
this, as the creatures of habit, miners ire no
more in fault than others are Who daily risk
their lives, and in whom it is thought to be
rather a duty than otherwise.

Another chief evil miners are uncler is igno-
rance. That they are born ignorant is scarcely
a fault; and that the very life of colliers has
hitherto kept both their fathers, them,selves,
and their children ignorant of their ignorance,
igncrant of the, disadvantages they labour
under, ignorant of the evils they might remove,
and ignorant of the benefits they might derive
from knowledge, is 'not only their misfortune,
but it is more—a positive fault in their capital-
ist employers. The master 'miners have -been.

constant and uniform in opposing all and every
means of education that the State would have
applied, proVided, and-. enforced, Mr' the educa-
tion of this class of their fellowmen. It is not
often that ignorant men ask for education; but
both in 1853, and especially in 1860, the
miners importuned Parliament for it, and in
both cases they were successfully opposed by
their employers. And if thus ignorant, and thus
habituated to danger, the men are instructed,
stimulated, and ordered to work, and if, having
no other means of obtaining a living, they
follow in the track thus directed to,, an explo-
sion follows, and hundreds are killed, how is
it their fault? In the case of this
.Edmund's
Main, it is well known, in order to complete
certain works desirable for their. employers,
that the men were pushed on to work by extra-
ordinary shifts, and even by the stimulation of
extra pay. It was known that the workings
were dangerous. Ventilation. was alluded to;
and the use of safety lamps. enforced. And
this would have met the ordinary risks of the
general and gradual flow of inflarnable gas
from the work. But in order to facilitate the
works in progress, powder was used to blast;
and a fall of coal thus made is liable to liberate
a flood of gas, which the blasting is as liable
to set on fire. In this
.case ventilation, that is
the supply of atmospheric air, only gives
greater scope for the explosion. To shut out
the air when fire has once got hold, i§ to put
it out; and this was attempted, and, alas, in
vain. Now, so far, how were the men in fault?
Tempted by the ordinary stimulus of pay,
and by the extraordinary pay of bounty for
extra work, the use of powder was common.
For the men to have refused either to work, or
to blast, would have been certain loss of work
and living also; for it should not be forgotten
that in Barnsley the employers, who are in
strict union, have a system of requiring notes
from their last employer" before a master will
take a man on to work; and in this way, any
collier who at all shows himself particular of
safety, can be, and is, effectually kept out
of work. The men, of Barnsley have
thus to , subscribe • hundreds ,a year to
maintain a victim fund the victims
being men marked by the employers as
" troublemme." Well, in ,this way, by extra-
ordinary working and .blasting in dangerous
works, we have an explosion, or rather, gas
fired, say at nine o'clock in the morning: but
not until near two hours, or say at eleven, did
the explosion occur that brought death to some
fifty-seven men. Now, what was doing in the
interim? For nearly two hours there were
ineffectual attempts to put out the fire.
Ventilation was stopped for. that purpose,
which made it only so much the -worse for other
parts of the pit. Half an hour's warning
would have cleared all the men out; and that
warning was not given. Now, I,vo's was the
fault? The Times attempts to throw blame
upon the men, for which, by the way, there is
not the slightest title of evidence.
Juries, chiefly shopkeepers, or gentry living
in the neighbourhood, are all under or in-
fluenced by the pit owners. The evil is done,
and cannot now be helped; the cause, i.e., the
last link in the chain of causes, is often ob-
_

,
scure : and so what wonder, as easiest and as

most pleasant to themselves who have not
suffered, these juries say, by their judiciously
chosen foreman, Verdict—" Accidental death.'
Under ordinary circumstances, no doubt, the
verdict of a jury is the best means of obtaining
the substantial truth. We believe also, as a
rule, that justice and judgment are fairly and
even remarkably administered in England, with-
out prejudice to class or station. But even
the impartial rule of justice, and the general
right of a verdict, may become a danger; if we
assume the rule under circumstances where
the rule does not obtain. Now, in the mining
districts, the appointment of coroner, and the
selection of juries is well known to be effected
and even tampered with by the mining capL-
talists. To expect, therefore, an impartial
examination, or even a just judgment, in min-
ing localities, is therefore, a fallacy. Matiy a
verdict that ought to be wilful murder is toned
down to "faulty carelessness ; " and many a
verdict of " manslaughter" is cooled down to
"accidental," with a recommendation of—more
care—by a selected jury, and by a sympathis-
ing coroner, both of whom know, how the land
lies relative to their own pecutiiary- affairs.
There is more injustice passing current under
the still waters of society, than society is at ap
aware of. Well, but is there not an Inspector's
Act? Have we not mining inspectors, able
and skilled men, and well paid, having six
hundred pounds yearly, whose duty it is to go
constantly round to see tint the safety of the
men as provided for by law, is duly observed?
And have they not ample powers to do all
that is required, and to punish the guilty?
And are not these all honourable men? True!
Oh, reader! all this is correct: but these said

inspectors were themselves appointed by the
mining capitalists ! ! The inferenee is clear;
the whole tone of their reports shew that their
general• sympathy is with the employers;—by
whom, by the way, it was made a condition,
that the inspectors should have been one. So

that while in all other departments of legisla-
tion it is laid down as a rule that the employers,
who receive the benefits of wealth, are respon-
sible for the conditions enforced by law, in
mining works it appears the rule to throw all
blame and results uport the employed. Rail-
way accidents, cab accidents, and in fact, all

other accidents involving responsibility, fall
upon the capitalist, because it is they who em-
ploy, rule, and can discharge. But they
manage these things better in pits; and hence
we are not likely soon to have "death in the
pits " less frequent, or less fatal—the most
dangerous of all.
We will return to this subject in our next
number.

A YOUNG LADY BURNT TO DEATH.—Yesterday an a.cci-
dent occurred, terminating fatally, to Miss Augustaßous-
field, aged 24 years, who resided in Upper Eaton-street,
Belgrave-square. It appeared that the young lady was
passing the fireplace, when her dress of light muslin,
which was distended by her crinoline, took fire, and
she was enveloped in flames. Her screams drew the
attontion of the servants. The flames were extin-
guished, and she was removed to St. George's Hospital,
where every assistance that surgical skill could 'Suggest
was given, but she expired shortly after her admission.

MANSLAUGHTER. BY A CABMAN.—Froderick Woom-
ton, a cabdrivir, was charged yesterday at La
ie
Police-court, with causing the death,of Harry 0 1Y)
by driving over him. From the evidence it appeared
that the prisoner on Monday evening last, while
intoxicated, drove along the Kennington-road at a rapid
pace and on turning the corner,' at the norns Tavern
knoled down the deceased arid drove over him. He
was going on as if nothing had happened, but was
stopped by a constable, when he made use of the most
blasphemous language, and refused the use of his cab
to remove the unfortunate man to the hospital. The
poor man was taken to St. Thomas's Hospital, where
he lingered until Wednesday, and he died of the
injuries he had received. The prisoner was remanded
and bail was refused.

opium. The jury returned it verdict that deceased died
from poison, tut that there was no evidence to show

articles.title: DOMESTIC.
articles.text:
DOMESTIC.

The Mansion House Committee transmitted
money on last Saturday to provide a Christmas
dinner for all the families out of work. It was
a considerate and kindly act, well calculated to
excite sympathy and be remembered.
A violent storm passed round our islands on
Saturday and the following day, causing many
shipwrecks; but in proportion to the loss of
property the destruction of life was compara-
tively limited.

We shall have passed into another year
before the publication of our next number.
From the period of suffering and trial society
will pass into another with hope and without
regret. May the future compensate for the sor-
row of the past in restoring employment and
prosperity, and bringing back wages and work
to all the homes within the land.

ASTOUNDING REVELATIONS OF THE
SECRET SOCIETY AT TEMPLE BAR.
WE live the greater part of every day, and
some portions of many nights, near the domains
of the Benchers, almost within arm's length
of the imperturbable Bye, nearly under the
controul of the Templars, and their secret and
terrible tribunal. We live in terror, if men
can be said to live who pass their time in
trembling for the officers of the Inquisition.
Respectable people exist in this quarter; quiet
bankers, with snow-white neckcloths; long-
established tradesmen and their families, with
a balance at the'r bankers that might buy an
estate; elderly ladies, of ample means, occa-
sionally frequent the Temple Gardens, along
with knots of innocent nursery maids, and
groups of still more innocent children,
insensible to the jeopardies that beset them on
all sides. No doubt "where ignorance is bliss,
'tis folly to be wise ;" but the proceedings in
the Court of Queen's Bench, before the Lord
Chief Justice and a jury; have opened, or may
open, people's eyes to a danger incomparably
greater than that of garrotting. The Templars
are a secret,society, whose principal rule is to
have no table Of fees for their services, and to
live upon what you please. It is a bad rule
to begin with, but forms no part Of their
secret machinations.
This association, or conspiracy, as it may be '
aptly termed, admits to its membership new
companions of the order, by evening processes ,
extending through many years. The ordeal
is extremely severe on the gastronomic powers
of the body, and by disordering them, the
Templars entirely change the mind of their.
coming man. When he is, body and mind,
thoroughly subdued to their designs,
they call him to the bar. From that day they
proclaim him to be acquainted with the mys-

AMERICA.

GBEAT'BATTLE AT FRKDERICKSBITAG..

TERRIBLE SLAUGHTER. TWO GENERALS
KILLED.
(Per 'City of Manchester, vie Cape Race) -
New York, Dec. 15 (Morning).
Early on the morning of the 13th inst., in the midst
of a dense fog, General Reynolds, commanding the
I left of the Federal army at Fredericksburg, advanced
and engaged the Confederate infantry.. The Con-
federates immediately opened fire from batteries of
heavy artillery. Two hours later the fog disappeared,
and two divisions of infantry charged the Con-
federate position in the rear of the city. The
Federals experienced a check. Having been rein-
forced they again charged the enemy, but were again
repulsed. From that time heavy firing continued on
both aides till dark. The Federal General Franklin,
who commanded on the left, succeeded in driving the
Confederates about one mile. The latter then attacked
him, but were repulsed with loss of 400 prisoners. On
the night of the 13th the Federals slept on the ground
where the ibattle had been fought. The Federal
Generals Jackson and Bayard were killed. Five
Federal Generals were wOunded.

The Confederates continued to throw shells into.
Fredericksburg until eight P. General Longstreet
commanded the Confederates' left wing,
.and held the
main works. Generals Hill and Edmonds were in
front of General Franklin, with Edmonds's right
wing resting on the Rappahannock.

I No battle occurred on the 14th. The Confederates
were occupied in extending their works and strength-
ening their position. The. Federal dead in front of
the Confederate works remained where they fell. It
is Supposed that 40,000 Federale were engaged in the
battle on the 13th. The whole of General Lee's army
is; believed to be at Fredericksburg. The egmfede—
rates are supposed to have six lines of works behind
the city. It is expected that General Burnside will
renew the engagement to-day. A large number of
Federal officers were killed, and the loss of life on
both sides is believed to be very heavy.

LATER FROM AMERICA.

DEFEAT AND RETREAT OF THE FEDERALS.

NEW YORK, Dec. 17.
The battle before Fredericksburg, on S9.turdav, was.
one of the fiercest and most calamitous to the Federal
The troops fought with the greatest courage, but the
positions of the Confederate General Lee gave hire the
advantage.

The Federal attack was. repulsed with great
slaughter, amounting to 10,000 men.

On Monday General Burnside gave orders to the.
Federal army to recross the Rappahannock.
Great excitement and dissatisfaction exists at New
York.

CRRISTMAS AND BOXING DAY.

The weather on Christmas-day was extremely fine,,
conducing much to the comfort of these parties visit—
ing
_their friends. " .

the usual hospitalities were given to the inmates
of the metropolitan workhouses, who were regaled with
roast beef, plum pudding, and beer; the older inmates
also having tea and cake in the evening. The average
number of inmates is about the same as last year.
The prisoners for debt in Whitecross-street and
Horsemonger-lane, of whorl there are in the former
78, and in the latter 21, were also recipients of the
bounty of the city, and of benevolent. individuals. A.
plentiful supply of Christmas cheer was provided. for
them.

The in-pensioners of Greenwich Hospital, about
2,400, were mustered and inspected by the governor,
after which each man was supplied with 11b. of roast
beef, vegetables, plum pudding, and a quart of ale.
This was in addition to the usual mess of mutton, beef,
and potatoes, and the ordinary allowance of beer.
Tobacco and snuff were also supplied to all the mts.
who were consumers of the weed.

BoXING DAY opened rather gloomy as regards the
weather, but this did not seem to interfere with the
determination of the holiday people to enjoy theM-
selves. From an early hour the streets were thronged;
business in all the public offices and wholeslle estab-
lishments, and in about one half of the retail shqpg
being suspended. Several of the Music Halls gave morn-
ing entertainments, which were well patronised. Large
numbers visited the Crystal Palace, the British
Museum, the Polytechnic, Colosseum, and other simi-
lar institutions. Towards evening the neighbourhood
of the theatres gave evidence that Phntornime was
about holding high festival, from the 21.owdli of
devotees that were making their pilgrimagb toWilas
their respective favourite shrines-s. The jolly god,
Bacchus had also many votaries during thm day, and
plentiful libations were poured out in his honour.

articles.title: LOSS OF THE LIFEGUARD STEAMER AND FIFTY-TITTO PERSONS.
articles.text:
LOSS OF THE LIFEGUARD STEAMER
AND FIFTY-TITTO PERSONS.

SHIELDS, Friday.—The Lifeguard sailed from the
Tyne on Saturday afternoon, deeply laden, for Lon-
don, and two hours after she siiled she was over-
taken, by a terrible gale of wind from the north. She
was passed, off Scarborough, on Saturday night by the
Pioneer, one of the General Steam Navigation Com-
pany's vessels, which also left Newcastle on Saturday
afternoon. The weather was then extremely squally,
and the sea running at a tremendous height. It re-
quired all Captain Harty's skill and attention to keep
the Pioneer afloat, the sea breaking over her fearfully.
He took her to London, however, in safety; but no
tidings have been since heard of the ill-fated Life-
guard; and the owners have long since abandonded
all hope of her. Her engines were placed Very far
aft; and it is generally supposed that the waves had
overlapped the vessel astern, filled her engine-loom,
and extinguished her fires; and that she then broached.
to, and foundered, carrying all on board down with her.
Even if there were time to get out the boats, they
would not have been able to'live a minute in the seas
that were running. Her commander was Capt. John.
Barry, and the ship and cargo (there was no deck cargo)
was valued at about £lB,OOO. Since the vessel has
been overdue, the scene at the London wharf has been
most painful, there being an incessant crowd of anxious
inquirers.after friends and relatives among both pas-
sengers and . crew. The Golden Crown, a new and
very large 'iron vessel,left the Tyne about ten days
ago, and has 'not since been heard of. It is feared
that she went • down, with all hands, in the Downs
during the recent gales. A large East Indiaman
which sailed fioni here on Saturday is also missing.i

articles.title: IRON AND WOODEN SHIPBUILDERS AND THE TIMES.'
articles.text:
THE IRON AND WOODEN SHIPBUILDERS
AND THE TIMES.'

Last week we noticed some extraordinary admissions
made by the Times with respect to the dispute existing
in these trades. We then showed that this menda-
cious journal had unblushingly contradicted all its
previous assertions, and entirely corroborated the
statements made by the iron men as to the respective
Capabilities of the workmen in the two branches. This
week, knowing whom we had to deal with, we looked
for a contradiction to the statement of last week; but,
to our great surprise, find that the Times continues to
advocate the same views as last week; in other words,
that it holds the same opinions for at least six consecu-
tive days. Its confirmation of the statements made by
the iron men is even more emphatic than before. After
alluding to the proceedings connected with the repairs
to the pinion of the tubular travelling crane in the
armour-Plate workshops. at Portsmouth Dockyard, it
goes on to say To drive the iron wedges a line of
rail had been set up on each side of the plate bed with
three small iron viheels on each rail, each wheel having
a metal suspending link. Of course all worked sepa-
rately from each other. To these links were suspended
by lines driving " tups " of about I cwt. each. Twenty
men were labouring at the Setups yeste;rday, under two
working and four " directing " foremen, besides an oc-
casional order from a superior officer. It was not a
great triumph. The thought would obtrude itself upon
the mind that these men 'would have been far more
profitably employed on board the Royal Sovereign; at
the same time their places at the plate bending press would
,filled by a lesser number of men habitually accustomed
to handle large masses of iron.'
To what can we attribute this entire change of
opinion to that held about two months since by the
Times? Surely it has not become open to the sense of
truth and justice. Let us hope so, for its own sake.

the committee say :—Fellow-workmen, in presenting

amongst the women employed in his establishment;
but another disaster, which threatens to be fatal, has
drawn forth an absolute prohibition.

. DREADFUL CASE OF BURNING.-011 Monday a fire
broke out on the premises belonging to Mr. G.
Elnis, 27,' Hampden .street, Somers-town, which will
no doubt be attended with fatal consequences. It
appears that a loud cry of Fire!' was heard to pro-
ceed from the house in question, and on the police
entering they found the ground floor in flames, and
in the midst of one of the rooms was seen Mrs. E.
Elnis completely
enveloped in flames, and the bed
and furniture also on fire. The parish-engine and
three of the London Brigade quickly attended, and
the flames were extinguished, but not until nearly
everything in he room was destroyed, and the
unfortunate female burned in such a frightful
manner that she was obliged to be removed to the
hospital, where she remains Without hope or
recovery.
THE SUICIDE OF A Soucrrou.—At the inquest on
the body of Mr. Fleming Stuart Nicholson, a solicitor,
aged 30 years, who committed self-destruction by
shooting himself, with a. pistol, at his residence, 12,
York-buildings, Adelphi, on Friday morning last, his
brother stated that for somc time past deceased had
been the subject of curious religious feelings. He
thought that God required a sacfifice, and said that
.God demanded his life, as be had not attended to him
in his youth as he ought to have done. He never said
anything about committing self-destruction. He was
constantly reading the Bible and praying. Verdict—
temporary insanity.'

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1862.

CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
GENCE.

KEIGALEY.—CO-OPERA.TIVE SOCIETV.—The members
of this society held a special meeting in the Albion
Hall, on Wednesday night, for the purpose of receiving
tenders for the agency, their present agent having
given notice to leave. The two gentlemen who ob-
tained the highest number of votes were both in the
employ of co-operative societies, one at Saltaire and
the other at Halifax. The person at Saltaire was at
the head, and the committee are trying to arrange
with him.

NORTHOWRAM.—A* tea party was held on Saturday-
evening, in the Church school, New-road, of the mem-
bers of No 1 Branch Store of the Industrial Society of
Halifax, when 150 persona'sat down to well supplied
tables. After tea Mr. B. Whiteley took the chair, and
the secretary, Mr. J. Thornton, read the half-yearly
report. Short addresses were delivered by Mr. Isaac
Kellett, of Northowram, and Mr. Job Whiteley, of
Kings-cross, who gave some very useful information
on co-operation. The meeting terminated by passing
a vote of thanks to the ladies for providing the tea, and
to the speakers and singers, also to the Rev. Mr.
Wawn for his kindness in the gratuitous use of the
room.

Co-orEna.TrvE FARMS.-Mr. John Gurdon, of As-
sington Hali,.Suffolk, writes to the Times About
thirty years ago, upon a small farm in Suffolk becom-
ing vacant, I called together about twenty labourers,
and offered to lend them capital without interest if
they would undertake to farm it, subject to my rules
and regulations. They gladly availed themselves of
my offer. In the course of ten years they paid me
back my capital, so that I was induced to let another
farm of 150 acres to thirty men upon the same terms.
These have also nearly paid back the capital lent to
them, and, instead of eating dry bread, as I regret to
say many of the agricultural labourers are now doing,
each man has his bacon, and numberless comforts that
he never possessed before; thus the rates are reduced,
as these 59 families are no longer burdensome. The
farmers are sure to meet with honest men, as convic-
tion of crime would debar them of their share, and
the men themselves have become much more intelli-
gent, and present happy, cheerful countenances. If
every country gentleman would follow my example,
distress among the agricultural poor would not be
known. I merely add that I have no land so well
farmed. I shall be happy to send you my plan, rules,
and regulations, if required.'

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FREEMASONS.

GOOLE.—On Tuesday last, the 12th inst., the mem-
bers of the Aire and Calder Lodge held their annual
festivity in their lodge-room, at the Sidney Hotel.
After dinner the chair was occupied by Mr. William
Wake, supported by Mr. Lee, of Leeds, and J. John-
stone, Esq., M.D., Goole; the vice was filled by H. D.
Patten, Esq., of Goole, supported by Mr. H. Russell
and Mr. Brown. The members of the St. Cuthbert
Lodge, Ho wden, honoured them with their presence.

ODDFELLOWS (MANCHESTER UNITY.)
CARDIFF.—On Monday evening the Widows' and
Orphans' Committee, M. 11.0., gave a concert in the
Assembly Rooms, for the benefit of their funds. The
room, though not crowded, was well filled, and was
decorated by a number of flags belonging to various
lodges.

articles.title: FORESTERS.
articles.text:
FORESTERS.

NEWCASTLF,.—On the 11th Nov., 1861, Forestry
was revived in Newcastle, when the first court, called
'Pride of the Tyne,' was opened, and since that time
it has made wonderful progress, there being at the
present time no fewer than five courts open: On
Friday night, a new court was opened, at the house of
Mrs. Nichol, Ridley Arms, Hewgill-terrace, Shielfield,
under the name of Sir Matthew White Ridley.' The
following gentlemen were elected as officers :—Chief
Ranger, Robert Simpson; S. C. R., John Ridsdale ;
secretary, William Ayres.

articles.title: DRUIDS.
articles.text:
DRUIDS.

PATRINGTON. —At a -rn-e-e-ti-n-fgr-o- the members of the
Sherwood Lodge, No. 467, held at the Three Tuns
Inn, Patrington, on Monday last, it was resolved that
a subscription be opened to relieve the distress at
present exiting in that town. The sum of £4 7s. 6d.
was raised, and a committee appointed to collect
further subscriptions, and to distribute the amount at
Christmas, in coals, flour, and other necessaries,

BENEFIT SOCIETIES IN FRANCE.—From a report just
presented to the Emperor it appears that on the 31st
of December, 1861, there existed in France 4,410
mutual benefit societies, comprising 605.346 members,
of whom 68,991 wore honorary, and 536,355 partici-
pating ones. The latter were divided into 455,489
men and 80,866 women. In Algeria there were 15
societies, having 3,961 participating members, and 804
honorary. The total assets of the societies, includine:
the pension funds, amounted to 27,905,358 f. The
receipts of the year reached the sum of 9,64,217 E, and
the expenditure 7,562,626 f., showing a surplus on the
former of 213,459 f. Compared with the returns of the
preceding year, 1861, it shows an increase of 83
societies end of 45,526 members, and in the total of
the assets of 2,-501,320f. The number of sick in the
year 1861 was 113,921 men and 22,363 women, being
in the proportion of 25 per cent. of the male members
and of 18 per cent, of the female. There have been
paid '2,743,274 days of sickness-2,336,452 for men and
406,822 for women; 20 68-100th days have been paid
for each man's sickness, and 18 19 100th for each
woman's. The average number of days' sickness for
each participating member was 5.23-5.25 for men and
5-18 for women, being half-a-day less than in Bel-
gium, and a day and a half less than in England.
The number of deaths was 6,446. The number of
societies approved on the 31st December, 1861, was
2,653, having 60,220 honorary and 324,860 participating
members, the latter consisting of 271,004 men and
53,856 women. The assets amounted to 15,685,606 f.
There has, therefore, been an increase of 139 in the
number of approved societies, and of 2,092,843 f. in
assets.

articles.title: DESTRUOTIVE PIR.E AT DAVIS'S
articles.text:
DESTRUOTIVE PIR.E AT DAVIS'S

WHARF.

On Tuesday afternoon the outbreak of another fire
at the extensive water-side premises known as Davis's
Wharf, Horselydown, in a line with Tooley-street,
and opposite the Tower of London, created much ex-
citement among the shipping in the upper part of the
pool and on both sides of the river. The disaster
appears to have originated from some unaccountable
cause in the jute or D warehouse situated at the rear
of the main buildings and separated from them by a
narrow roadway. In this building were stored some
thousand bales of jute stacked up to the roof, there being
no floors. The men had just returned from dinner, and
were instantly set to work in extinguishing the flames,
but the fire travelled so quickly from stack to stack, and
the smoke was so overpowering, that they had to retire.
The steam, land, and other engincs quickly arrived,
as also the two floating engines, but as is usually the
case at large fires on this side of the water, there was a
laxity of water to work the land engines. It was
feared the fire might extend to the other warehouses,
causing their total destructicn, as in a conflagration
which took place 20 years ago, but the exertions of the
firemen sufficed to confine it to the warehouse in
which it began. During the height of the lire, Capt.
Shaw received a serious injury to his hand by a slate
falling from the roof. The .official report states that ,
Upwards of 2,000 bales of jute auu hemp were destroyed,
and the roof of the warehouse. The owners of the
wharf, Messrs. Curling and Co., are insured in several
offices. A somewhat similar fire took place in an
adjacent warehouse in the autumn of last year, in con-
sequence of which there was a meeting of insurance
companies, where a resolution was come to that no in-
surances would be taken of such warehouses unless
certain alterations in the construction were made.
The warehouse now burnt was built in accordance with
these alterations.

MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A. GENTLEMAN.—An inquest
was held yesterday at the Spread Eagle, Homerton,
before Mr. J. Humphreys, on the body of a gentleman
who was found last Wednesday morning in the river
Lea. The jury returned a verdict of 'Found drowned
in the river Lea, but how he became immersed there
was no evidence.'

PROTECTION OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN IN BLEACH
FIELDS.—On Thursday next, the new Act to prevent
women and children in working in blench fields will
come into force. It is declared that, for the health and
morals of the parties, they should not work between
(ight o'clock in the evening and six in the morning in
Bleach Fields.

RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.—IIereford, Friday Morning.
—Yesterday morning a fearful accident occurred on
the Merthyr and Brecon Railway, by which one life
was lost, and several persons seriously injured, some
of whom are not expected to recover.-1 collision,
involving serious injury to several passengers, and a
great loss of property, happened on Wednesday after-
noon at the Barnet station of the Great Northern
Railway. Four passengers were severely hurt. Yes-
terday the directors were engaged in instituting an
inpliry into the collision. It is stated that the aux-
iliary signal was put on, but too late, or rather after
the train had passed.

articles.title: EXPLOSION AT EaVON.I,B 3I4LY COLLIERY.
articles.text:
THE EXPLOSION AT EaVON.I,B
3I4LY COLLIERY.

THE ADJOURNED INQUEST.

The adjourned inquest upon George Pickering and
William Davey, the two men whose deaths were
caused by the explosion at the Edmond's Main Colliery,
near Barnsley, on the Bth inst., was resumed on Mon-
day, at the Masons' Arms, Worsbro', by Mr. Taylor.
By the catastrophe at the pit the lives of about fifty-six
persons were sacrificed, and, with the exception of those
of Pickering and Davey, none of the bodies have been
recovered. An attempt would probably have been made
at the latter end of last week to enter the pit, but the
explosion which occurred on Wednesday last proved
that the fire was still raging, and the only safe plan to
be adopted then was to close the pit, and so to seal up
the shafts as to render them air tight. In the mean-
time, the subscription for the widows and orphans of
the unhappy men now lying entombed in the mine is
increasing, and at the present amounts to upwards of
£BOO.

The evidence discloses a great amount of carelessness
on the part of those who were superintending the opera-
tions going on in the mine at the time of the explosion.
John Guest, of Welsbro' Common, fire trier at Ed-
mond's Main, who deposed: I have been at Edmond's
Main eighteen months. I was last in the dip board
gates on the 6th of December, the Saturday before the
explosion. I examined the dip boards a little after
twelve at noon, and at that time they were as bud, as
regards gas, as I had ever seen them. The gas tired
in the lamps when I held them up, and exploded. It
was the worst at the top. I did not take the men
away; they were working with locked safety lamps.
Did not consider the board gates dangerous at that
time.

Mr. Morton: When you found the gas in the lamp,
do I understand you to say you did not recommend
the men to leave work? Witness: No. I thought
the men safe because they were using safety lamps.
Mr. Morton: Do you think that it was safe to blast
with powder when the gas was firing in the lamps ?
No.

The Coroner: Did you tell anybody so P—Witness :
Yes, I told both Henry and George Lawton on
Saturday, in the pit bottom. George Pickering heard
me.

Mr. Morton: Did Lawton give orders for the blast-
ing to be stopped ?—Witness: No. He gave no orders
any way. 1 told Lawton that the drivers ought to
have safety lamps.

_
Mr. Morton : Was it proper to have naked lights
within eight or nine yards of the face when gas was
firing in the lamps ?—Witness : No.
William Fisher, miner, said he was employed at the
mine. Having described the mode of working the
pit, he said: Formerly we used wedges instead of
firing to get the coal.
Mr. Morton: Why did you not stick to wedging?
—Witness : We could not make wages at the
price ! ! ! !

Mr. Morton: You had no difficulty in wedging tht
coal ?—Witness: No; if we had had the price!!!
Mr. Morton: What was the difference in price.
Witness : Six shillings for wedgivg and five shillings
for blasting. We told Lawton we could not make
wages at the price. Lawton two months ago said,
we're going to begin wedging again. I don't
like the thoughts of blasting.' He said he would give
us 68. if we would go on wedging. After trying for a
time I gave up wedginc, as it would not pay at that
price. We commenced blasting two months ago. A
fair price for wedging would be nine shillings.
After a refusal of the Coroner to go into the causes
of the accident which he contended had nothing to do
with the death of the men before the court, the jury
retired, and after two and a half hours' deliberation re-
turned the following verdict

" We find that William Davy and George Pickering
came to their deaths by an explosion of gas in
Edmund's Main it on Monday, th,- Bth of December,
1862. For their immediate death we are unable to
attach blame to any individual. The jury at the same
time desire to express their unanimous opinion that
the cause of the explosion was owing to the incautious
and unsafe working of the dip board of this colliery.
The mode of blasting with powder they (the jury) con-
sider to have teen highly injudicious, and feel sure
that it ought not to have been allowed by the under-
viewer or prosecuted by the workmen."
Mr. E. Parker protested against the verdict.

THE CITY WAHDMOTES. —The annual wardmotes of
the city of London were held on Monday. They
passed off upon the whole very quietly. The general
metropolitian improvements, the lighting of the public
streets, the Lancashire distress, and the traffic bill
about to be introduced into Parliament, appear to have
been the principal topics of discussion We notice
that in Bisuopsgate Ward, where there was a contest,
Mr. Richardson, the secretary of the City Garibaldi's
Meeting, and a staunch radical, was returned at the
head of the poll.

TERRIFIC EXPLOSION AT A FIREWORK MANUFACTORY.
—On Wednesday morning, between eight and nine
o'clock, a terrific explosion took place at Mr. Clitlieroe's,
an artist in fireworks. The premises are surrounded
by dwellings of poor persons, in Spicer-street, Bethnal
Green. The house itself was nearly blown into ruins,
and distressing cries for help were heard. With
assistance were extricated Miss Ellen Clitheroe, aged
20; Mr. John Clitheroe, aged 60; Samuel Pelham,
aged 23, all most frightfully burnt. They were con-
veyed to the London Hospital. Mrs. Clitheroe was
also rescued, but not severely burnt. The fire was
extinguished, but not until very considerable damage
was done.

THE MURDER IN EDGWARE ROAD.—It Will be re
membered that about two months since a woman's
throat was cut in a coffee-house in New Church-street,
Edgware road. She and her husband had gone there to
sleep, when the landlord, hearing cries of murder, went
to the robm in which they were and found her with a
tearful wound in her throat. 'The husband said she
had done it herself, but she shook her head in denial.
Under careful medical treatment she had so far re-
covered as to be able to artkulate indistinctly, ai,d on
Al empty she appeared as a witness against her husband,
Jan.es Wadden. He was committed, for trial for at
tempting to murder her, and he was also committed
fo•• trial for bigamy.
SUICIDE WITH OXALIC ACID.—Mr. Walthew held
an inquest at the London Hospital respecting the
death of Robert Lisk, aged 57.. The deceased, a
labourer in the north quay of the London Docks,
had been in great distress throneh pecuniary
. On Saturday last he went into the taproom
of a public house, and had not been' there long
before the potman saw him open a paper, and mix
something in a pint-pot, the contents of which he
drank off. hurriedly. The potman seeing a paper
labelled: Oxalic acid, poison,' procured assistance,
and deceased was taken to the above hospital, where
he died in great agony shortly after his admission.
Verdict, Temporary insanity.'
, Two BOYS RUN OVER AND KILLED.—The first ease
was that of H'emy Watley, aged fourteen years, whose
parents reside at No. 32, Quaker-street, Spitalfields.
The deceased was crossing High-street, Sboreditch,
when he was knocked down by a cab, numbered
10,247, and one of the wheels passed over the deceased's
left leg, whieh sustained a compound fracture. He
was removed to the London Hospital, where he ex-
pired from gangrene of the limb. The driver was
not to blame. The second case was that of Richard
Henry Anderson, aged eight. years, of No. 29, Alpha-
place, Three Colt-lane, Cambridge-road, Bethnal-
green. The deceased a few days since was knocked
down by a cart in Whitechapel-road, whereby he re-
ceived an internal injury, through the horse trampling
upon him. He was carried to the above-named insti-
tution, where he died yesterday.
EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF SELF-MUTILATION —A re-
markable case of self-mutilation has taken place by
the wife of a barman, named Jane Brickland, aged 38,
living in York-street, Camden Town. The woman
had given way to drinking habits, and while intoxicated
she deliberately chopped off her left hand and wrist.
She then wrapped up her arm, and in proceeding to the
University College Hospital she called in at the Lord
Wellington, and, having taken some brandy, she
walked into the hospital, and told the porter she had
cut herself. Unwrapping her arm, she said she had
left her hand at home; it was a beautiful hand, and she
was sorry she had not brought it, as they might have
put it on again. During the exhibition of the limb she
maintained a remarkable degree of coolness. The arm
was operated on, and it is believed that the woman will
recover.

SUDDEN DEATH IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. -- The
sudden death of a respectable young woman named
'Ellen Clark, occurred on Wednesday, while travelling
on the line with the intention of proceeding to
Swinton Junction. It appears that in consequence of
indisposition, she had lett a situation she filled at a
drapery establishment in Poplar, and was proceeding
to her home at Cricklade, in Wilts, where her father,
a hay dealer, resides. As the train approached the
Reading station she was observed to turn very pale,
and appeared to be fainting, she was at once removed
to the waiting room, but on the arrival of Mr. F.
Bulley, surgeon, in a few minutes, life was pronounced
to be extinct. An inquest was held in the evening
before Mr. Blandy, the coroner for Reading, and
evidence was given that the immediate cause of death
was inflammation of the intestines and congestion of
the lungs, and a verdict in accordance with the medical
testimony was returned. The deccaecd was 29 years
of age.

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENCE,
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENCE,

COURT OF QUEEN'S BENOIT.
(Before the Llrd Chief Justice Cockburn.)

HUDSON V. SIR F. SLADE, AND TICE BENCHEM OF TILL

TEMPLE.

This important case arising out. of the inquiry
entered into by the Benchers of the Temple some
months since, as to the alleged improper conduct of
Mr. D. Seymour, M.P., has occapied the court for the
last six days, and has excited considerable public at-
tention. The facts are simply these Seymour,
amongst other things, was accused of unfair conduct
with respect to some transactions with the Waller
Mining Company, in which he was a large shareholder.
To justify his conduct, Mr. Seymour induced a
Mr. Hudson, also a shareholder and director in
this mining company to attend before the Benchers,
and give evidence. Mr. Hudson seems to have excul•
pated his friend, Mr. Seymour, in the eyes of the
Benchers, but in the course of a searching examination,
which Mr. Hudson contended was conducted in a most
ungentlemanly way, a book was produced, belonging
to the Walter Mining Company, which by some un-
accountable manner, had come into the possession of
the Benchers, and from which Mr. Hudson was
examined by Messrs. Rodwell and others. In the
course of the inquiry, this book was handed to Mr.
Hudson, who, having obtained possession of it, refused
to part with it again • telling—in no measured terms—
the benchers, what fie thought of their conduct. A
scene of great confusion and violence ensued; and two
of the porters of the inn were called in, and ordered to
take the book from Mr. Hudson by force. He resisted the
attempt, and, in the struggle, was thrown on the floor,
and, as he alleges, assaulted by Sir F. Slade and others
of the Benchers. A policeman was then called in, and
Mr. Hudson, and several of the Benchers, went down
to the Fleet-street Police Station, when Mr. Rodwell
gave Mr. Hudson in charge for 'taking' the book,
refusing to charge him with stealing.' After some
considerable disputing, the inspector on duty declined
to entertain the charge as one of 'taking,' and Mr.
Hudson was allowed to depart on his promise to appear
again if wanted. Mr. Hudson at once commenced an
action for assault and false imprisonment against Sir
F. Slade and his colleagues, and hence the present
trial, which has taken place before a special jury, the
leading counsel for the plaintiff being Mr. Montague
Chatnl7ers, and for the defendants, Serjeant Shc..e. The
Chief Justice having summed up at a great length on
Wednesday, the jury retired, and, after an absence of
three hours and a half, came into court and stated
there was no chance of their agreement. The Chief
Justice urged upon the jury again to retire, and con-
sider whether they could agree upon a verdict, but
they said it would be of no use, and the jury were
accordingly discharged. The case will, no doubt, be
tried over again.

SECOND COURT.

(Before Mr. JuBtice Crompton and a Common Jury).

A ItEFRACTORY JURYMAN.

A strange occurrence took place in connexion with
the case of 'Thewlis v. Mumford'—an action for seduc-
tion. The jury retired and were locked up from 1
o'clock till 10 at night through the obstinacy of one
juryman, who would not yield his opinion to the other
eleven. During their deliberation several angry alterca-
tions took place between them, in the course of which
the obstinate man struck a brother juryman, and after-
wards hurled a chair at him. At last the other i, feel-
ing so much annoyed and disgusted at his conduct, set
on him, and in the course Of the scrimmage got him
against the &or. The usher in charge, thinking they
were knocking for him, opened the door, and he tell on
his hack vith his head out on the passage. At 10
o'clock they were called into court, and it being found
they were not likely to agree they were discharged
without giving a verdict.
On the following morning one of the gentlemen who
was locked up addressed his lordship. He applied to
have steps taken to prevent the gentleman complained
of from sitting on the jury any more. Upon his enter-
ing the room he positively refused to listen to the other
jurymen, who endeavoured to convince him that his
opinion of the case was wrong, and later in the even-
ing be hurled a chair at another gentleman's head.
His lordship said that no doubt from what he had
been told the gentleman complained of had acted in a
manner that would meet with the disapprobation ofi
his brother jurymen. He, however, did not think the
court could interfere in a case where the judge had
left before the disturbance took place. Had the count
been sitting at the time, probably a juryman acting in
such a manner would have been liable to be charged
with contempt of court. As the matter stood he re-
fused to interfere. The juryman then withdrew.

COURT OF COMMON PLEAS.
(Before Air. Justice Wales.)

SINGULAR TERMINATION OF A CASE.-PROWSE V. LOXDALE.

This action for libel, by a volunteer against the pro-
prietor of the West Middlesex Advertiser, was brought
to a close by the plaintiff's counsel electing to be non-
suited. This result was arrived at in a somewhat ex.
traordinary manner. In the course of his reply Mr.
Ribton conceiving that one or more of the jurymen
were not attending to him, said he would sit down. 'The
foreman observed that it was hard if he might not
I smile, but that his laughter had not been excited by
Mr. Ribton, but by a fellow juryman who sat in the
upper part of the court. Mr. Justice Willes said that
counsel had no right to make remarks on the
conduct or demeanour of . the jury, who, in the
present instance, were trying the case most carefully.
Mr. Ribton then expressed his sorrow for having hurt
the feelings of thejury, and proceeded with his speech. In
the course of about an hour the learned counsel sud-
denly paused, and after looking steadfastly at the jury
for a few moments said : If you have made up your
minds against me Pll sit down. The Foreman (rising) :
Really, sir,
,we have not made up our minds against
you, but-Mr. Justice Willes . Gentlemen, I have
endeavoured to induce the learned counsel to conduct
himself decently towards you, but I have failed. Let
me advise you (he has ,now been speaking for an,hour
and twenty.five minuted) to hear him out patiently,
and,when the right times arrives, to deliberate on your
verdict. Mr. Ribton: After that expression of your
lordship's opinion, which I feel I do not deserve, and
as the jury are against me, I elect to be nonsuited.
This decision on the part of the learned counsel
took every one in court by surprise, and the plaintiff
was called in the usual way.

articles.title: COURT OF BANKRUPTCY. (Before Mr. Commissioner. ETolioyd.) IN RE SHEPPARD.
articles.text:
COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
(Before Mr. Commissioner. ETolioyd.)
IN RE SHEPPARD.

The bankrupt was a baker, of R9therhithe, and ho
now applied for his release from custody.
Mr. DennSr opposed for a creditor named Harding.
It appeared that the bankrupt had been in business
for two years as a baker, and that some two months ago
he sold his business for £lOO. He received the money
on the 2nd December, and paid £4B which he had
borrowed on his lease, and the remainder went for
rent and sustenance. He denied that he told Mr.
Harding that it was his intention to leave the
country. _ _ _

Mr. 'Harding deposed that on the 10th inst., he was
at the Windmill public-house, in the Lower-road,
Rotherhithe. He saw the bankrupt there, and he
(witness's) spoke to him: The bankrupt replied, Ido
not wish to have any conversation with you,' and
subsequently he said to a third person, in his (wit-
ness's) hearing, that he was going to Australia or per-
haps to some other place, or perhaps to the North
Pole (laughter).
Cross-examined.—The bankrupt might have been
drunk at the time.
The Cornmissioner.--I do not think I can refuse the
bankrupt's release on the ground of some vague
assertion in a public-house that he was about to leave
the country.
Release irom prison ordered accordingly.

SHERIFF'S COURT, RED LION-SQUARE.
(Before Mr. Commissioner Kerr.)

RUMBLER V. DBMS-THE ALLEGED MURDER IN FEN-

CHVRCH-gTREET.

This was an action to reeover damages for the alleged
wrongful detention of certain female wearing apparel,
plaintiffbeing a married woman, named Humbler, who
was living in Gardner's (the sweep's) house at the time
of the murder of his wife, and who was admitted as
evidence for the Crown, and it was then stated that she
had left her husband to go to Gardner. After the con-
viction a sale took place at the premises in Northum-
berland-alley, and the place was cleared. Defendant
was a large purchaser, and indeed laid out £3O. Mrs.
Hambler now laid claim to some of the goods, and said
that Gardner had no claim whatever to hem.

John Humbler, the husband of the plaintiff, said the
present action was authorised by him.
Mrs. Humbler was called and said—l have written
down all that belongs to me. There was a bed, bolster,
and pillow' a washstand, a two flounced silk dress, some
plates and dishes, and a mug. They were mine before
I was married. I was married fourteen months ago. I
did not go to Gardner'shouse till eight or nine months
after I left my. husband. Mr. Gardner fetched the
things about three months before Mrs. Gardner met
her death. Part of the time Mrs. Gardner had my bed
under her feather bed. I left the house the mornino.
that Mrs. Gaither was found dead. My mother haa
some goods. I told Sergeant Mobbs what goods were
there. I told him about a ring. I earned all these
things by shoe-binding. Nothing else. My husband
might have bought some.
_

befendant said that the very day that Gardner was
condemned the landlord put in an execution, and he
(defendant) condemned the things. The very day the

man was to have been hung a disturbance was male
about the goods. Defendant bought the goods fairly.
gave Gardncr £3O for the things, because I respected
the man, and I believe he was innocent. He married
my mother in 1842, and she died in 1850. The things
were little or nothing.
_ . _ _ _

His Honour—l must hold that the plaintiff has made
out a good claim, and I find for the plaintiff, with costs.

articles.text:
ASSIZE INTELLIGENCE.

NORTHERN CIRCUIT.—YouK.
(Before Mr. Justice Keating.)

EMBEZZLEMENT BY A FRIENDLY SOCIETY SECRETARY.

John Ha.stie was indicted for embezzling a slim of
426 Bs. 6d. from his masters, the trustees of the Don-
caster Benefit Building Society.
It appeared that a benefit building society had been
established about 14 years ago at Doncaster, the
members of which in respect of the shares they held
were called on to pay a monthly subscription of 10s. a
share, and were entitled in respect of this accumulating
capital to obtain loans at 5 per cent. interest from the
society on mortgage of houses or land they might pur-
chase, and to redeem the mortgage by the continued
payment of their subscriptions on the shares they might
hold, or, it more convenient, by paying up the amount
of their shares at once, the amount of the shares being
calculated at 14 years' subscription. The society was
established under the Friendly Society's Acts, the
prisoner being the paid secretary. There were trustees,
directors, stewards, and an auditor appointed, and the
rules of the society, enrolled and certified under the
Friendly Society's Acts, denoted the duties of each of these
officers. On the 13th of Feb., 1860, a Mr.' Townend, a
member of the society, who had a mortgage on some
property to the society, wished to redeem his mortgage
and took the proper steps to do so. The solicitor to the
society, Mr. Marratt, obtained the receipts of the trus-
tees endorsed on the deed for the repayment of the
mortgage money, and Ur. Palmer (Mr. Townend's
solicitor) paid the sum of £426 Bs. 6d. to the prisoner,
as the secretary of the society, in discharge of the
mortgage, and received from him the title deeds. This
sum the prisoner it appeared had not paid to the bank,
or to the trustees, or the treasurer, but, on the con-
trary, had entered subscriptions, as continued to be
paid by Mr. Townend, in the stewards' books, as though
the mortgage was still subsisting. On a general balance
of the books it was discovered that this and other sums
had not been accounted for by the prisoner, and he then
made an assignment of all his real and personal estate,
amounting to about £2,000, to the society to meet his
deficiencies, which were said to amount to £3,000, and
the present proceedings were instituted against him.
On being taken into custody a private memorandum-
book was found, containing an entry of the receipt of
Townend's money by him.
Mr. Foster addressed the jury, contending that the
prisoner's conduct fairly viewed showed no intention
to defraud. He had given up all his property to meet
the deficiencies in his accounts. His conduct had been
reprehensible and lax, but so had been the conduct of
every officer in the society, not one of whom had ful-
filled the duties cast upon him.
His Lordship having summed up, the jury found
the prisoner Guilty. His Lordship then ordered the
prisoner to be detained until the opinion of the Court
of Criminal Appeal can be ascertained on certain
points of law raised on his behalf, and postponed pass-
ing sentence.

articles.title: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

BOW-STREET.

THE END OF A LOTTERY.—John Shaw and William
Colleen, the two men who got up a lottery at the
Whittington Club, professedly to raise funds in aid of
the Lancashire distress, were brought up for re-exami-
nation. It will be remembered that on the first hear-
ing of their case they pleaded guilty to having acted
illegally in setting up the lottery, but said they were
honestly intent upon handing over the proceeds to the
relief fund without making any profit for themselves.
The Treasury had instituted the prosecution, and its
representative consented to a remand to enable the
defendants to prove their good faith. They now put
in accounts, and called witnesses; but Mr. Corrie said
it appeared to him that they had intended to make
profit out of the affair. He therefore sentenced them
to fourteen days'.imprisonment with hard labour.
THE LOST PARCEL—. A gentleman whose voice and
features gave conclusive testimony to his Hibernian
origin, applied to Mr. Corrie under the following cir-
cumstances Sir,' said the fipplicant, I went on
Saturday to the post-office, 338, Strand, kept by a
most respectable tradesman, Mr. Jones, a jeweller, to
buy some postage stamps, and to put one on a letter
and post it. I had with me a brown paper parcel con-
taining some valuable deeds. Well, sir, I left the
parcel there. I laid the parcel on the chair while I
put the stamp on the letter, and when I was going
away I forgot all about the parcel. Now, the deed is
of great value to me, and being registered it is not
worth a brass farthing to any other person. I offered
£2 reward to any one who would send it to my
address. But, sure, they would see the advertisement,
and without knowing about the reward they won't
take the trouble to send it. I thought, Mr. Jones,
being a respectable tradesman, a jeweller, besides
being postmaster—circumstances which tend to.create
confidence on the part of the public—that any one
leaving property there would be enabled to make him
responsible. Mr. Corrie: Responsible! nearly twenty
persons may have been in and out. If you had left it
in his care he would be responsible, but it would be
very hard on a tradesman if he were to be called to
account for property which parties leave in his shop by
their own negligence. I hope whoever found it
may return it for the sake of the reward, but I am
sorry to say 1 can give you no assistance.

WORSHIP STREET,

DETERMINEED ATTEMPT AT SELF DESTRUCTION.-

Maria Pearson, 30 years of age, was charged before
Mr. Cooke with attempting to commit suicide by
poison. The prisoner, a fine young woman, but whose
countenance , was strongly marked with the traces of
much and recent suffering, was assisted into the dock,
and with difficulty supported herself through the fol-
lowing examination ot witnesses: Dr. Granger Tandy:
About two o'clock yesterday I was called to 23, Gun-
street, 4italtields, where, in an upper back room, I
found the prisoner in a most exhausted state, and
retching violently; a bottle that had contained laud-
anum and a small box of oxalic acid in it were near her. I
instantly perceived that she had, taken a portion of each,
and proceeded to further the expulsion of the poison by
emetics; the acid, doubtle4s unintended by her, acted to
a certain extent as an antidote to the laudanum, of
which she must have taken a considerable quantity.
The exhaustion, which at intervals tended to insensi-
bility, continued until eight o'clock in the evening, and
she is yet very weak. I have been given to understand
that she is in great distress, and that her husband is an
inmate of the hospital.—Magistrate (to prisoner) : Do •
you wish to say anything now ?—Prisoner: Only that
I took the poison in consequence of not having any
food. My ,husband has been in the hospital a con-
siderable time, and during it I have been compelled to
part with, everything for food. He was to have come
out this day, but I afterwards heard that it was im-
possible and I could bear my position no longer.—
Mr. Cooke: I shall remand you that some inquiries be
made, and also to ascertain what can be done to assist
you.—The prisoner was removed in a cab to the House I
of Detention.

articles.title: CLERKENWELL,
articles.text:
CLERKENWELL,

EXTRAORDLNARY ELOPEMENT.—.. NICE Wipz.—John
Eaton, aged 34, a dirty-looking fellow, described as a
brick maker was charged with stealing a coat and a
large quantity of other articles, the property of
Jonathan Rowland, a pig feeder, of Hornsey-road.
The complainant said—Thi prisoner is a scoundrel,
and eloped with my wife on Saturday night. She
was a very kind wife, but she went away with him
and took all my things, and I have since got back a
cart-load. The prisoner has lodged with me since last
Whitsuntide. Although my wife went away with him
on Saturday Aight, he forced her away, saying he
would kill her if She did not go. My dear wife has
told me all about it, and :it is a bad job, for she would
not have gone had he not been a bad fellow and forced
her. Prisoner—Why, she would have gone away with
me three months ago if I would have taken her. You
have used her badly, and not behaved as a man towards
her, and that's why she liked me. She loves my little
finger better than your whole body, and you know it.
You never gave her half enough to eat, and all you are
fit for is to feed the pigs. (A laugh.) Prosecutor—
My wife is now in court, and loves me. (A. laugh.)
She was always a good wife to me until three months
ago. She has always stuck to me until that follow
there (pointing to the prisoner) came to my house, and
was very kind and good. The police here stated that
the prisoner slept in the same room with the prosecutor
and his wife, and that the prisoner did not go out of a
morning until some hours after the prosecutor went to
work. The prosecutor—My room is a large room, and
I did not think it was any harm for us all to sleep
there. •. The coat .produced is my property. Other
evidence having been given, the prisoner said he was
not guilty. He was cohabiting with the prosecutor's
Wife, and she had 'given them to him to pawn. The
prisoner was fully • committed for trial, and bail
refused. •
