articles.title: WA NDSWORTH.
articles.text:
WA NDSWORTH.

MAbTEItS AND MEN: OF DAY.--Mr. Geo.
Bean, of South-villa, Wandsworth-road, was sum-
moned before Mr. Ingham for refusing to pay Richard
Rowls certain wages as a journeyman painter. An
important point arose in the case. The question in
dispute was whether the complainant was hired at
4s. 6d. per day of ten hours, or at short days. The
complainant swore that it was usual in his trade to
work short days for three months in the year, and his
engagement with the defendant was for 4s. 6d. per
short day. He also said that the question of ten hours
per day was never mentioned. The defendant on his
part declared that the engagement was at the rate of
4s. 6d. per day of ten hours, and he had offered the
complainant his wages, computed upon that scale. The
defendant called a witness, a master carpenter, to prove
that the custom of the building trade was to calculate
a day at ten hours, and that he had never heard of
short days. Mr. Ingham wished to know how the
complainant defined a short day. The complainant
said: Half-past seven to eight o'clock in the morning,
with half an hour at dinner, and to work until dusk.
He called a decorator, who stated that it was custom-
ary in their trade to work short days; but he admitted
that there was no fixed time. He mentioned the shops
of Mr. Freake and Mr. Kelk, where the men worked
short days, but their times were different. Mr. Ingham
said, with a day of ten hours there was something de-
finite; and all his experience went to prove that a day
of ten hours was the acknowledged custom of the build-
ing trade. There were some days at this time of the year
when a workman could not see outside a building more
than two or three hours in a day; and again, there was
the wet weather, when the work would be valueless to
the master. He asked, in those cases, whether the
master was bound to pay his men wages for short days.
The complainant and his witness stated that on the
days they were unable to work they went home, and
charged the masters FO much an hour for the time they
had worked. The witness stated, however, that there
was some kind of work they could do in bad weather.
Mr. Ingham said it was preposterous to suppose that a
master would allow his men to fiddle their time
away in bad weather, and to pay them at the rate of
short days. He again asked the complainant for his
definition of a short day. The complainant said eight
hours and a half, and when they did not work to be
paid at the rate of 6d. an hour. Mr. Ingham said there
did not appear to be any definite time with respect to
short days, for the complainant had first stated that it
consisted of nine hours the day, and afterwards eight
and a half hours. They then came round to 6d. an
hour for the time they worked, and that was calculated
upon a scale of 58. for ten hours, which was proof to his
mind that a day meant ten hours.. He would, how-
ever, give the complainant an opportunity of having
the case decided by a jury in the County Court. The
complainant preferred having the magistrate's deci-
sion. Mr. Ingham then said he decided that a day
consisted of ten hours; and he made an order accord-
ingly.

articles.title: LAMBETH.
articles.text:
LAMBETH.

TICKET-OF-LEAVE MEN AND THE POLICE. —Mr.
Dry, a medical practitioner at AValworth, applied to
Mr. Elliot for his advice and assistance, under cir-
cumstances, as he considered them, of peculiar
hardship. Mr. Dry Haid he brought with him a
person who had the misfortune of committing a crime
for which he had been transported, but, owing to his
good conduct obtained a ticket of leave, and ieturned
home three years ago. Soon after he obtained a situa-
tion at a silk-mercer's, where he conducted himself
with the strictest propriety and honesty', but in con-
sequence of information having reached his employer
from the police, he was discharged. He obtained a
second situation on the South-Eastern Railway,
where his conduct was unexceptionable; but from
similar information from the police he was again
discharged. Aware of the perfect determina-
tion of the young man to redeem his former
character, and thinking it extremely hard that
he should be prevented from doing so, he (Mr. Dry)
called on the railway authorities, and, in reply
to his inquiries, they admitted that while employed
there they had not the slightest fault to find with
him, and that the only cause for their discharging
the man was the information that had been given of
his being a ticket-of-leave man. He asked them the
name of the person or parties who had given the infor-
mation, but they refused to give it, and thus, it appeared,
he was to be hunted down with perfect impunity. In-
spector Dann said it was quite contrary to the express
direction of the commissioners that any officer of
police should take notice of ticket-of-leave men in
employment, and he should very much doubt whether
any officer did. He (Mr. Dry) could speak with con-
fidence as to this fact, as he was a member of a society
of which he was the chairman, and could assert that
no one was more anxious to wipe out the stain; but
this would be useless, if he was to be hunted down by
the police. The natural consequence of such a course
would be to drive such persons so unfortunately
situated back to their old associates and former crime.
There was one thing more which he wished to mention,
and that was that the man had married a respectable
young woman, and that the first time she was made
acquainted with her being the wife of a ticket-of-leave
man was on his discharge from the railway, her
husband feeling bound to tell her to account for the
loss of his situation. Mr. Elliott said the matter was
one in which he could not interfere, but recommended
an application to Sir Richard Mayne.
An inspector from Scotland-yard subsequently waited
on Mr. Elliott, and said he was directed by Sir
Richard Mayne to inform his worship that, in reference
to the above statement, it was not true that the dis-
charge of the ticket-of-leave man was owing to any
interference on the part of the police; and Sir Richard
Mayne therefore requested that the statement might be
contradicted.

articles.title: EXECUTION AT DURIIAIi:
articles.text:
EXECUTION AT DURIIAIi:

The execution of John Cox for 'the murder of Ann
Halliday took place at Durham on the 22nd. Th.
prisoner and his wife, who are Irish people, lived in a
cottage at Hobble-trot, near Durham; and Mrs. Halli-
day, who was 83 years of age, occupied apartments
separated from theirs by a thin partition only. On the
night of the 10th of August Mrs. Halliday was
brutally murdered; but the Coxes were the first to
give the alarm. Suspicion attached to them from the
tact that any noise in Mrs. Halliday's room must have
been heard by them: and at the trial at Durham assizes
both man and wife were convicted and sentenced to-
death. The woman, being enceinte, was respited ; the
man has suffered the extreme penalty of the law. Since
their condemnation Cox has not ceased to declare his
innocence, and his wife has been equally as emphatic
in her dental of the charge. On the night preceding
the execution the male prisoner, who has conducted
himself as a penitent Christian, under the ministra-
tion of °Anon Platt? the Roman Catholic clergyman
who has attended him; retired to rest and slept until
five o'clock in the morning, when he arose and dressed
himself. He was, however, so ill that he was obliged
to lie down again, and he then slept until seven o'clock.
Shortly after that hour Canon Platt, who had previ-
ousty'read a 'mass in the Catholic church, visited the
prisoner and adminstered to him the sacrament. At
the request of the rev. father, Cox then took a little
breakfast;and at 9 o'clock he joined the procession and
proceeded to the scaffold. In the area in front of the
county gaol some three or four thousand perm's of the
lowest class of the population of the district had
assembled. The doomed man ascended the drop un-
ass'sted. His face was of corpse-like pallor, and he
repeated in 'a quivering voice the words 'Lord: Jesus
receive my soul.' As Askern, the hangman, drew the
white cap over his head he seemed to cling to these
words with extreme fervency, and at the last he gasped
them forth in a weeping tone that was extremely
affecting to hear. After the bolt was drawn the body
remained for a moment motionless, then followed two
convulsive starts, and the retribution of the law was
complete. As the drop fell several Roman Catholic
people in the crowd went down upon their knees and
repeated prayers for the departing soul. Confined in
the gaol, the wife of the ' condemned culprit, herself"
under sentence, became violently agitated on hearing
the prison-bell toll the death-knell of her husband;
and she exclaimed incessantly, Oh, Johnny. Johnny;
he's innocent. He wouldn't hurt a fly.' At 10 o'clock
the body, of the culprit was taken from the scaffold
and interred within the precincts of the gaol. The'
behaviour of the crowd was decorous and quiet.

articles.title: LATE PRINCE CONSORT.
articles.text:
THE LATE PRINCE CONSORT.

Aremarkable volume, entitled The Principal Speeches
and Addresses of His Royal Highness the Prince Con-
sort' (John Murray), appeared the day following the
anniversary of the Prince's death. The volume contains
many documents which have never hitherto been
published. Amongst these are Fev eral relating to sug-
gestions made by the Duke of Wellington that on his
death, the Prince Consort should assume tee command
in chief of the army. The occasion on which this
suggt stion was made was the death of Sir J. Macdonald,
the Adjutant-General, in March, 1850. It was then
proposed to amalgamate the two offices of Adjutant and
Quartermaster General under a single head, to be called
the Chief of the Staff. On this project the Duke of
Wellington had several conversations with the Prince
at Windsor. The following extracts from ihe Prince's
minutes of these conversations are now publish, d
'Windsor Castle, April 3, 18-%'
'I went yesterday to see the Duke of Welliç.
his room after his arrival at the Castle, our conversatiota
soon turning to the question of the vacant Adjutant-
Generalship. I asked the Duke what he was prepared
to recommend. He said he had had a letter on the
intbject recommending the union of the two offices of
Adjutant-General and Quartermaster-General, and he
placed his answer to it in my hands. He then pro-
ceeded to say that he thought it necessary that we should
cast our eyes a little before us. He was past 80 years,
and would next month enter upon iii 821 d. He was,
thank God; very well and ate, and ready to
do anything; but he could last for ev(r,
and in the natural course of t-vents we must
look to a change before long. As long as he
was there he did the duty of all the offices himself.
To form a new office by uniting the
duties of Adjutant-General and Quartermaster-General
in the person of a Chief of the Staff, as was the practice
in some foreign armies, would be to appoint two diffe-
rent persons to do the same duty, which would never
answer. The Chief of the Staff would again have to
sub-divide his office into an Adjutant-General and Quar-
termaster-General's Department, and nothing would be
gained.
'However, the Duke saw the greatest advantage in
having a Chief of the Staff, if, after his death, that
arrangement should be made which he had always
looked to, and which he considered the best—v:z , that
I should assume the command of the army.
He was sure I could not do it without such a Chief
of the Staff, who would be responsible before the public,
and carry on the official communications with the other
Government departments. For this contingency he was
prepared to organise the machinery now, and he would
answer for its success. .

I answered to the Duke that I should be very slow
to make up my mind to undertake so great a responsi-
bility—that I was not sure of my fitness for it on
account of my want of military experience, &c. (to
which the Duke replied, that with good honest inten-
tions one could do a great deal, and that he should not
be the least afraid on that score)—whether I could per-
form the duties consistently with my other avocation s,as I
should not like to undertake what I could, not carry
through, not knowing what time or attention they
might require. •
The Duke answered, that it would certainly require
both time and attention, for nothing could be done
without my knowledge, or without my order, but that
the details would be worked out ,by the . Chief of the
Staff. He had thoroughly considered that, and would
make it work He always stood up for
the principle of the army being commanded by the
Sovereign,, and he endeaN oared to make the practice
agree with that theory by scrupulously taking on every
point the Queen's pleasure before he acted. But, were
he gone, he saw no security unless I undertook the
command myself, and thus supplied what was deficient
in the constitutional working of the theory arising from
the circumstance of the present Sovereign being a lady.
Strictly constitutionally I should certainly be respon-
sible for my acts, but before the world in general the
Chief of the Staff would bear the responsibility, and for
that office the man of the greatest name and weight in
the army ought to be selected. He repeated that he
thought this the most desirable arrangement, and would
at once work it out to the best of his ability
I begged him to leave me time to consider the proposal
In the evening the Queen gave the Duke of Wel-
lington an and ence, I being present. After having set
out by saying he was most anxious to let the ,Queen
know and feel all he knew and felt about it—in fact,
to think aloud—the Duke repeated what he had said to
me in the morning, and we discussed the question
further. I said that there were several points which
still required to be considered. . . . . The offer
was so tempting for a young man that I felt bound to
look most closely- to all the objections to it in. order to
come to a right decision. . . . . The Queen, as a
lady, was not able at all times to perform the many
duties imposed upon her; moreover she had no private
secretary who worked for her, as former Sovereigns
had had. The only person who helped her and who
could assist her in the multiplicity of work which ought
to be done by the Sovereign was myself. I should be
very sorry to undertake any duty which would absorb
my time and attention so much for one deFartment as
to interfere with my general usefulness to the Queen.
. . . . The Queen added that I alr‘ady worked
harder than she liked to see and than she thought was
good for my health,* which I did not allow—answer-
ing that, on the contrary, business must naturally
increase with time, and ought to increase, if the Sove-
reign's duties to the country were to be thoroughly
performed; but that I was anxious no. more should fall
upon her than could be helped.
'The Duke seemed struck with this consideration, and
said he had not overlooked it, but might not have given
it all the weight it deserved, and that he would reflect
further upon it.
We agreed at last that this quest!on could not he
satisfactorily solved unless we knew the exact duties
which had to be performed; and the Queen charged the
Duke to draw up a memorandum in which these should
be detailed, and his general opinion explained, so that we
might found a decision on that paper. . This the Duke
promised to do.'

Windsor Castle, April 6, 1850.
After a good deal of reflection on the Duke of Wel-
lington's proposal, I went to pay him a visit yesterday
morning in his room, ard found him prepared with his
memorandum, which he banded me. , After having read
it, I said to him that I must consider my position as a
whole, which was that of a Consort and confidential
adviser and assistant of a female Sovereign. Her in-
terest and good should stand foremost, and all other con-
siderations must be viewed in reference to this, and in
subordination to it. The question then was simply
whether I should not weaken by means of attending
to all parts of the constitutional position alike—
political, social, and moral—if I devoted myself to a
special branch, however important that might be; and
that I was afraid this would be the consequence of my
becoming Commander-in-Chief. It was quite true that
the Sovereign being a lady naturally weakened her
relation to the army, and that the duty rested upon me
of supplying that deficiency, and would do so still more
when the protection which. the Duke afforded to the
Crown should be unfortunately withdrawn. But I
doubted whether this might not be accomplished without
my becoming especially responsible for the command of
the army. There was no branch of public business in
which I was not now supporting the Queen, &c
The Duke replied he quite saw that my position ought
to be looked at as a whole. He felt the extreme diffi-
culty and delicacy of it, and was kind enough to add
• that he approved of, and the public did full justice to,
the way in which I had hitherto maintained it. I
begged him to leave me a little time for consideration,
that I wanted to study his memorandum, and would
finally write to him upon the subject.'
Ultimately the Prince formally declined the position
in the following admirable letter
My dear Duke,—The Queen and myself have tho-
roughly considered your proposal to join the offices of
Adjutant-General and Quartermaster-General into one
of a Chief of the Staff, with a view to facilitate the
future assumption of the command of the army by my-
self The question whether it will be
advisable that I should take the command of the army
or not has been most anxiously weighed by me, and I
have come to the conclusion that my decision ought
entirely and solely to be guided by the consideration
whether it would interfere with or assist my position of
Consort of the Sovereign, and the performance of the
duties which this rsition imposes upon me.
'This position is a most peculiar and delicate one.
While a female Sovereign. has a great many disadvan-
tages in comparison with a Bing, yet, if she is married,
and her husband understands and does his 'duty, her
position, on the other hand, has many compensating
advantages, and, in the long run, Will be found even to
be stronger than that of a male Sovereign. But this
requires that the husband should entirely sink his own
individual existence in that of his wife—that he should
aim at no power by himself or for himself—should
shun all ostentation—assume no separate responsibility
before the public—but make his position entirely a part
of hers—fill up every gap which as a woman she would
naturally leave in the exercise of her regal functions--

• The anxiety of the Queen lest the Prince should iajure his
healtirby his excessive attention to public business naturally
'-ued to increase. In 1860, when the Society of arts re-
_ i' the proposal for holding a second International Exhibi-
tion,
i
ton, the queen wrote to Lord Granville, without the knowledge
of the Pi' ce, expressing her earnest hope that he (Lord Gran-
ville) would do all that n him lay to prevent the responsibility
and laboiir of conducting the undertaking being thrown in any
way oh his Royal Highness. The Queen felt deeply the
necessity f r averting any addition to the heavy work already
entailed on the Prince by the assistance and support (every day
more needtul to her) which he gave her in the transaction of
all public business; and her Majesty was convinced that he
could not again undertake the labour he had gone through
In conducting the first Exhibition to its successful termination
without injury to that health which was not only most precious
eo herself and his family, but to the country, and even to the
...se. , .

her at any moment in any of the multifarious and diffi-
cult questions or duties brought before her, sometimes
int rnationai, sometimes political, or social or personal.
As the natural head of her family, superintendent of her
household, manager of her private affairs; sole confiden-
tial adviser in politics, and only as,istant in her commu-
nications with the officers of the Government, he is
h sides the husband of the Queen, the tutor of the Royal

flow far would i, be consistent with this position to
andertlke the management and administration of a most
important branch of the public service, and the indi-
vidual responsibility attaching to it—becoming an
executive officer of the Crown, receiving the Queen's
commands through her Seel etaries of State, &c.? I
feel sure that, having undertaken the rtsponsibility, I
should not be satisfied to leave the business and real
work m the hands of another (the Chief of the 6t,lff,)
but should feel it my duty to look to them myself.
But white I should in-this manner perform duties which,
I am sure, every able General officer who has gained

With reference to this transaction the Times re-
marks The Queen could not have done greater
honour to the memory of her husband than by publish-
ing the history of this great act of self-denial. It is
more honourable to him than a hundred monuments. It
shows the Prince clear headed, self denying, and a

articles.title: PLEURO-PNEUMoNIA AMONGST
articles.text:
PLEURO-PNEUMoNIA AMONGST

CATTLE.

A ,meeting of graziers and -veterinary surgeons was
held lately at Leipsic to take into consideration the best
mode of preventing the spread of the lung inflammation
among horned cattle. Measures, such as the confine-
ment of the diseased animals, the prohibition of all sales,
&c., found zealous advocates, but the majority admitted
that all coercion, however ingeniously arranged, becomes
difficult in practice, and that any restrictions to trade in
catile would be ruinous to the feeder as well as to the
breeder. That principle having been admitted, the con-
ference turned upon the other measures of precaution,
and some curious facts with respect to inoculation were
listened to with great attention. This practice, which
was first tried some ten years back, was at first strongly
opposed, both in Germany and France, but it was
finally adopted when the malady was prevalent. Pro-
fessor Haubner, a Saxon veterinary surgeon, calculates
that the disease called pleuro-pneumonia carries off from
25 to 50 per cent. of the animals affected by it, whereas
in the districts where inoculation has been practised the
loss does not exceed 10 per cent., and the mortality is
sometimes reduced to 2 per cent. This calculation has
been confirmed by observations made in the neighbour-
hood of Magdeburg, where it has been practised on a
large scale for the last nine years' and where the local
practitioners, without any official character, have inocu-
lated as many as 16,000 head of cattle. It has been
further ascertained that this remedy is useless unless
adopted in time, and that it may be likewise used as a
preservative for animals in good health as well as a
remedy for diseased animals. The farmers who attended
this meeting more than once expressed their apprehen-
sion that the inoculation of healthy animals might intro-
duce the disease into their farmyards. Professor Haubner
stated that of 100,000 inoculations not one had produced
any injurious effect.

A YANKEE NOTION OF MACEETH.---‘ After having
witnessed the performance, from what I could make out
of the play, I don't think Macbeth was a good moral
character: and his lady appeared to me to possess a
tarnation dictatorial temper, and to have exceedingly
loose notions of hospitality—which, together with an
unpleasant habit of talking to herself, and walking
about en chemise, must make her a decidedly unpleasant
companion.'
_ _ . _ _ _

A-plan has just been tried on the Northern Railway
for receiving the letter-bags at the intermediate stations
without stopping the train. By means of a ring the bag
is attached to a post on the line; the engine is provided
with a rod so disposed as te catch the ring, and thus
carry off the letters. By a similar contrivance,, bags are
left by the train when necessary. •
Notice has been issued at Washington that ladies
desirous of going to their friends and families in the
South must obtain leave from the Federal Government.
and that no one must take more than one package of
female wearing apparel, not weigbing.above 1001 b., and
subject to inspection. If any contraband property is
found„ the party will be subject to imprisonment during
,the war.'

CRIMINAL PROCEDURE IN FRANCE.—The case of
Rosalie Doise is likely to produce some good. A com-
mission of jurists, with M. Devienne, first President of
the Paris Court of Appeal, at its head, and MM. Nouguier,
a lawyer of much eminence, Colmet d'Ange, and some
others of equal standing, as members, has been appointed
to examine into the existing system of criminal procedure
(‘ inw ruction criminelle;) and to present a report
thereon to the Council of State, with a view to effect
such reforms as may be thought indispeisable. I am,
moreover, assured that it is at the instance of the Em-
peror that this step has been taken. The greatest diffi-
culties will probably proceed, not from the bar, but from
the bench; but the opposition even of the Delangles
and Troplongs to the abatement of abuses like those
which wrung from an innocent woman, driven to freniy
by torture, the confession of a crime she did not commit,
will give way before Imperial will. A change, useful
so far as it goes, has already taken place, A person
charged with an offence in the jurisdiction of the Cor-
rectional Police may now, if he desire it, be tried at
once, instead of being sent to prison and detained there
for weeks at the pleasure of the judge before whom he
undergoes his private examination.—Letter from Paris.
ARTIFICIAL SIAMESE TWINS.'—A curious and inte-
resting experiment was lately made at Strasburg to
effect the union of two animals, so that they might, to a
certain degree, have a life in common. It was, indeed,
producing artificially what nature produced spontane-
ously in those extraordinary phenomena, the Siamese
twins. Two white rats, of the Albino species, were
selected for the experiment, probably as being more
manageable than their darker brethren. An incision
was made on the right side of the one, and on the left of
the other, engaging the skin and the cellular tissue under
it. The surfaces of the two wounds were kept closely
together by sutures and bandages until the 6th day,
When union by the first intention was found to have
taken place. They then walked side by side, being
united by a fleshy bank. An attempt to poison both by
the mouth of the one did not succeed, but an injecticei
thrown into the jugular vein of one animal was found
to have entered the superficial femoral veins of the
other, showing clearly that an intimate vascular union
had already taken place between them. This interesting
experiment may have a most important bearing on re-
storative surgery.
AN ORGANISED ROBBER BAND IN PARIS.—The police
have just succeeded in arresting a band ofthieves, twenty-
five in number, regularly organised for the commission
of all sorts of robberies, but chiefly from persons in the
streets, from carriages, and from the stalls of dealers.
Though numerous complaints of their proceedings ha.?
been lodged with the police, all attempts to discover the
criminals proved fruitless, until last week, when a most
daring robbery put the officers of justice on their track,
••nd "fhe Twenty-five,' as they called themselves, were
all arrested. Five of them, three evenings since, met o
man who lives in the Rue de Limoges, and perceiving
that he was in liquor they offered to conduct him home;
instead of doing so, however, they led him into the
middle of the.prain of St. Ouen, where they threw him
down and took away his watch, gold chain, and a purse
containing 27f. They afterwards had the impudence to
take him to a wine shop and treat him to wine paid for
with his own money, and then left him. The next day
he lodged a complaint with the police, and gave a descrip
tion of his assailants which led to their apprehension
and ultimately to that of all their accomplices.—Galignozi.
A SHIP CANAL THROUGH HOLLAND.—A telegram
from Holland announces that the Dutch Chambers
have ratified the concession for cutting a ship canal
through North Holland, by which a direct communication
will be made between Amsterdam and the North Sea.
This undertaking, when completed, will, according to
the description given, be one of the most important en-
gineering works ever executed in Europe. The canal
will be 13 miles long, navigable by ships drawing 24 feet
of water, and will shorten the distance from Amsterdam
to London and all ports south of the Texel by about 80
miles, and enable vessels to get to sea within a few hours,
• whereas they now generally spend three days, and often
a week, in that process. To form a safe entrance it will
be necessary to construct enormous sluices and an artifi-
cial harbour upon the unprotected coast of Holland, the
piers of which will have to extend more than a mile
into the sea. This will be the most difficult engineering
work to be overcome. To the undertaking is conceded
the reclamation of about 15,000 acres of rch alluvial
land, the value of which is estimated at £1,000,000 ster-
ling. The total capital required is stated to be £1,500,000
sterling, and this is to be raised by a Government
guarantee of interest at the rate of 44- per cent. The
concessionaires are Mr. J. C. Jager, of Amsterdam, and
the English engineers, Messrs. B. W. Croker and Charles
Burn, who, it is said, have been more than ten years

articles.title: TILE PERILS OF lIIA' CuLLILRY.
articles.text:
TILE PERILS OF lIIA' CuLLILRY.

During the 10,years ending December 31, 1860, it is
officiAly recorded that 9,090 lives were lost in our
collieries, and 605;154,940 tons of coal raised; s :hat
on the average one person was killed for every 66,573
tons, and there was an annual 'slaughter of 909 persons.
Of accidents which are not fatal no general summary
has yet, been presented; but it is wll known that there
is a irightful amount of maiining, fiom slight hurt to
actual crippling for life. All 'of 'woman born' are
exposed to risks of one kind or other, from the cradle to
the grave, but the pen i s of the collier are manifold,
and, in some rt spects, peculiar. He encounters perils
above and perils below; perils in descending and perils
in ascending; perils by fire and perils by water; and
perils of the most varied and remarkable character.
Thus w • are informed that one man was strangled by
his comforter winding round the axle of the wagg.,n on
which he was riding;' a second was strang ed by the
cage chain twisting round his neck on landing at the
bottom of the pit;' a third was smoking, when a lump
of coal fell and drove the stem of h:s pipe into the roof
of his mouth, whereof he died; and a fourth was
killed by the fall cf a piece of ice from the side of the
shaft while he was standing at the bottom. This list
might be greatly extended, and any one desiring copious
information on the subject may peruse the Reports of
Her Majesty's Inspectors of Coal Mines, which abound
in details of the most exciting, most instructive, and
frequently most shocking description. Crushing to
death by sudden falls of the roof is of common occur-
rence, and by jamming on tramways only occasional;
tumbling down shafts from the breaking of ropes or
chains, or otherwise, and overwinding, are not rare,
though less frequent than formerly; suffocation from
carbonic acid gas evolved from old workings is not very
unusual; sudden and overwhelming irruption of water
has occasioned great destruction of life; but of all the
causes of death in collieries explosion from firedamp
have been the most prolific. King Firedamp is the
veritable King of Dahomey of the coal pit; but, happily,
there is no point on which skilful and experienced
colliery engineers ,seem to be more agreed than that of
their power to render this monarch impo'ent. Of all
the dangers incidental to the life of a collier, it has been
amply demonstrated that the explosion of fire damp is
among the most .preventible. It is sickening to wade
through the ponderous folio volumes of the Reports
previously referred to, and to observe that, with very
few exceptions, ignition of the gas has been caused en-
tirely by the neglect of the most obvious precautions,
or from gross ignorance or mismanagement of those in
charge of the underground works. Efficient ventilation,
the exclusive use of the safety-lamp, and the enforce-
ment of the strictest discipline, are pretty sure and.
effectual preventives of explosions.—Letter in ths Times.

articles.title: SPRING EMIGRATION TO THE NORTH AMERICAN PROVINC_ES.
articles.text:
SPRING EMIGRATION TO THE NORTH
AMERICAN PROVINC_ES.

~Ar441P.:7,*

From all the accounts we receive the emigration from,
these isles during the coming year promises to be of a
very extensive character, and we are,. therefore, glad to
notice the efforts which are now bing made by the
British North American Association and the Colonial
Emigration Society to circulate reliable information in.
reference to the resources of the British North American,
provinces,. with the view of directing the emigration of
next year in that direction. The provinces of Canada,
Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick contain very nearly
650,000 square miles—the productions of the first
being timber, wheat, iron ore copper, lead, zinc, im-
portant fisheries, &c., of the second—timber, c
gold, iron and copper ore, &c;; and of the last—timber,
iron ore, coal, copper, gypsum, furs, fisheries, .ship-build-
jug, &c. In the first and second of these provinces free
grants of ono hundred acres are made to settlers, subject
to a log hut being built and a clearance of two or
three acres per annum. In Nova Scotia the land is
sold by Government at an upset priece of la 9d. per
acre. From the last returns the class of persons greatly
required are farm labourers, artisans, domestic servants,
farmers with small capital, and capitalists generally.
The wages paid average as follow :—To iarna labourers
about £3O pea annum, with board and lodging;
artisans, from ss: to 10s. per diem;. and domestic ser-
vants, £l2 to £l5 per annum, with board and lodging.
The price of provisions in the three provinces may be
taken at the following rates :—Besf, 21d. to sd. per lb.;
mutton, 2d. to 4d.; fowls is. 4d. to as. Bd. per couple;
butter, 7d. to is. ; flour, 245. per 200 lbs. ; and all the
other necessaries for the table proportionately cheap.
These, then, are a few of the leading particulars of
countries—but a. few days' sail from the Mother
Country—that are anxious to receive all new corners de-
sirous of settling down in their midst.—Canadian.-Kews
Dec.. is.

THE IRISH IN "'TRW YOEK.—A letter from NewaYork
says':—Yesterday Was a day of considerable excitement
in the city, but to day we are still more lively, in con-
sequence of the elections now going on for comptroller
and the alderman. The excitement yesterday was occa-
sioned by the President's Message and the funeral of
Tom Byrnes. The latter was shot about two o'clock
a.m., by a bill-poster named Sullivan, The cruising-
ground of Tom is in the First Ward, -where he had been
a terror to mild people for twenty years. Originally a
tailor, his physical development led him to *be a rough—
a fighting man. He became so much in demand by
politicians that he cleared about 50,000 dols. on politics.
lie held a *valuable office in the Street Department,
with 11,000 dole. ta year, and he was running his son-
in-law, Fox, for alderman' for the First Ward. It is
difficult for witnesses to tell a correct story in reference
to the death of such a man. Tom undoubtedly went
out of his way to abuse this poster who was in the
employ of his opponent, Alderman Smith. He attacked
him, and got shot. He was taken to the hospital,
where he died at five pin, the same day. Yesterday
was his funeral, He had a solemn requiem mass at St.
Peter's Catholic Church, Barclay-street. His pall-
bearers were John Van Buren, the Hon. E. B. Hart,
late Member of Congress, Elijah F. Purdy, Edward
Sachan, of Tammany Hall, Tom Mor:ssey, the prize-
fighter, Hon. John Kelley, Member of Congress, and
seven others. John Byrnes was one of the best of his
class. M'Clellan could not be more honoured, if he was
to die, than has been poor Tom Byrnes.
THE RACING CRAB OP CEYLON.:---These crabs Ton
with surprising swiftness, and it is by no means easy
to catch th.em before they escape into their burrows.
Sometimes they are made to afford a few hours' amuse-
ment to the military officers and other persons who ,
lave too much time on their hands,, the struggle
between man and crab being as exciting as the battle
between an eagle and a salmon. One device is
ingenious, and. often successful. Long strings are
a.ttached to flat pieces of slate or stone, which are
carefully laid near a burrow, and some tempting food
laid outside. The crabs crawl out to feed on the
bait, and while they are engaged, the slates are quietly
drawn over the entrance of the burrows. A sharp
rush is then made'‘ the crabs scuttle away to their
homes, and one or two are generally captured before
they have recovered their presence of mind sufficiently
to leave their barricaded doors, and ask for admission
into another habitation. Another amusement is to
chase the crabs on horseback, trying to ride them down
by main speed, and to kill them with a gun. —1? cid -
ledge' Natural _History.
It is reported in many quarters that the British Go-
vernment has offere4 on certain conditions to cede the
lonian Islands to Greece. The conditions seem to be
the retention of Monarchy, the adoption of a constitu-
tion which shall leave the faith of the monarch tree,
and peace and friendliness towards Turkey. The offer,
which is officially mentioned by the Greek Minister in
a dispatch published at Athens, has, we believe, been
made, but its acceptance is not absolutely certain. As
might have been expected, Austria' though she may not
resist, does not like any proposal which weakens the
Treaties of 1815, and, as might not have been expected,
the lonians are half inclined to be coy. Now that all
their wishes are to be granted, they begin to ask whether
they really wished them, and to be doubtful whether
nationality may not prove somewhat of a costly plea-
sure.—Spectator.
A NEW QUADRUMANE.—The Island of Madagasaar,
though so near the African coast, where there is a
wilderness of monkeys,' enjoys the peculiarity of not
counting a single species of that interesting genus among
its faunas. On the other hand, it has the exclusive
possession of the lemur, also a quadrumanous animal,
which forms the type of the family of the Lemuridm,
comprising the genus Indris. The French Academy of
Sciences has just received from M. -Vinson, attached to
the French mission lately sent to Madagascar to compli-1
ment Radama 11. on his coronation., a communication ,
concerning a new species of the genus Indris, called I
Simpoune, in the country. It differs from the Indris
niger by its colour, which is a yellowish white. Its ears
are quite bare, without a vestige of fur, and its tail is
longer than that of the other species. M. Vinson calls
this new kind Indris albus, and describes it as having a
I snout much resembling that of the lapdogs called after
King Charles, the skin of its face being bare and of a
brilliant jet-black tint. Its fur is long and woolly like
1 that of the lemurs; on the forehead it stands upright, and
is whiter than on the rest of the body. Its paws, or
rather hands, are bare and black; the fourth finger is
the longest; the thumb of the hind-paws (replacing the
gre it toe) is very thick and flattened. The whole animal
measures 86 centimetres, 15 of which belong to the tail.
The lower limbs are longe than the upper. The sim-
poune on which M. Vinson made his observations was
an old male; its ears were cut in various places, being
the marks of many a sharp hatt'e it had fought with its
rivals. It was seen on a tri eby the road-side eating
s me red berries, and received two wounds before it fell.
The cry of this animal res mbles that of a human Iseinkr
in distress; and who there are many together, they form

DAY, ])FCEMBER 27, 1862.

ASPECT OF A LANCASHIRE TOWN
UNDER THE FAMINE.

It is possible that an idea may exist in some minds
that there must be many outward indications in the
streets and byways of those cotton towns of the want and
suffering endured by the inhab tints. Any one who
visited these regions expecting to find me h scenes as
Flaxman has depicted in his Acts of Mercy would be dis-
appointed People do not lie starving in the streets, nor
clamour after the p esser-by for br ad as he walks along.
There is little begging, and what there is, is done, pro-
bably, by the habitually poor. The real Buff rers suffer
in secret. Their misery w its a decent veil; it is not
proclaimed in the mare et-places. The signs of what
has gone wrong in these t, wns are few, and may be
described in few words. First, there is less bustle in the
streets, less heavy traffic and carting of goods from place
to place. There is less ti affic of all kinds, and those
troops of factory hanos discharged, under ordinary cir-
cumstances at stated times in great numbers, are wanting.
As you pass the mine you hear no clack and vibration
of machinery, And after night has set in, the rows of
windows which should be all a-blaze with light are dark
and cheetless-looking. The great tall chimneys, too,
which rear themselves in all directions, discharge for the
most part no smoke, and though the ar is all the clearer
for this, you are yet surprised to find that the town where
these chimneys are thus enjoying a sinecure are all the
more dismal for the want of that. thick and sooty cloud.
The smoke is an indication of prosperity, and the absence
of it is felt like a want. One more indication there is
of the existence of some unaccustomed stete of things,
in these towns, and it is an indication which cannot
escape the most casual ob,erver. At certain times of the
day, as you walk the streets, you meet great numbers of
women and children carrying packages of bread and
meal, and tin cans or other vessels for holding soup.
These are the mill hands out of employment, who have
been to the depots of the relief committees to receive their
dole. Sometimes you meet a boy, or an old helpless man
thus loaded, but scarcely ever a young or middle-aged
workman. Beyond such indications, there is little else
to show what is going on eiiss in the manufacturing
towns. It may be that ti,e people you meet are more
poorly clad than usual, and it may be that their faces are,
in some c .sea, more pinched and careworn. But it must
be remembered that the manufacturing classes are never,.
at the best of times, characterised by robustness of ap-
pearance, and that pador and poorness of development
are to be observed among them as prominent charac-
teristics under all circumstances. It is within doors
that you must look for the real unmistakable evidences
of what has gone wrong. If there be rags, depend on it
those who wear them will hide out of view, and the
shoeless feet will not cross the threshold if there is any
way to help it. One man I went to see, a specimen, no
doubt, of a large class, said that he had not been out for
months, simply because he had not fit clothes to appear
in, and did not choose to show in the streets in tatters.
Sodden and wretched he looked; and, when I asked him
if he lost flesh, he said, 'Yes, he knew that he had lost
fleh, but that was not so much from want as from fret-
ting.' He said it was a man's mind that wasted him
away like that. And he was right, poor fellow.--. All
the Year Round. •

articles.title: AN AMERICAN IRON-CLAD.
articles.text:
AN AMERICAN IRON-CLAD.

We have-news of the- failure of the- iron-clad veesel
Eastport, whose completion and trial trip were reported
some time since. A little while ago she was com-
missioned to replace the Benton, an iron-clad also, used
by General Burnside in western waters as flagship.
General Porter has condemned the Eastport, which
vessel is at once to be put out of commision. The
failure of the Eastport is a trifling matter compared with
the principle, the impracticability of which it apparently
involves. It would seem that an exclusively wooden,
vessel cannot be mailed heavily and retain her buoyancy
and usefulness. The keel of the Eastpert was too weak,
and the weight of metal put on her btu& her back. If
other wooden vessels are as susceptible of destruction by
plating, a most important point is settle/. The con-
verting of old frigates and liners into iron-clads must
cease.. England has already gone into the business ex-
tensively, and one of our great screw frigates of 1855
is at present receiving an immense armour. The Benton,
we believe, before alluded to, also proved unsucccessful
on account of her old wooden hull, but hers was deemed
an exceptional case. The United States frigate Niagara
is in course of cutting down, and if the Roanoke succeeds
she will possibly be mailed. Nothing now save a com-
plete demonstration of the exceptional nature of the ex-
periments made with the Eastport and Benton would
probably warrant the plating of the Niagara should the
Roanoke fail. The Eastport was once a rebel stf amer.
The hull was taken by the brave Lieutenant Phelps at
the village of Eastport, near the southern ,boundary of
Tennessee immediately after the capture of Fort Henry
in last I",bruary. The rebels were busily engaged
making a man-of-war of her when she was seized. She
lad a solid wrought-iron ram, weighing 5,7,001b.—New
York World.

articles.title: ACCOUNT OF AFRICAN RUNNERS.
articles.text:
ACCOUNT OF AFRICAN RUNNERS.

We find the following interesting aeeount of Arab
roamers or Couriers in an able article by General
Dumas, published in this fortnight's Berne Contem-
poraine. The following sketch of one of them will give
an idea of these singular men :—Ben-Saydane, about
35 years of age in 1858, was tall, spare but robust, with
well-shaped arms and legs. His only raiment•was a
cotton ehirt surmounted by light burnous;. a few reeds
stuck into his belt in front formed a kind, of basket in
which he carried his provisions. He wore a kind of
sandals, which he used-to manufacture himself out of
camel and goatskin and a small sheathed knife, with
his faithful Kezoolal or stick, completed his equipment.
The Arabs maintained that he had received from God
the gift of swiftness, the faculty of never losing his way
even in the wildest regions, and that of being able to
live upon the smallest quantity possible of food. Ita
1845 he was sent by his chief with a highly-important
secret message to Abd-el-Kader, and, startinc, from a
place called El-Had, sim leagues from Alfa, he arrived
at Taguedemt, where Abd-el-Kader was, on the fol-
lowing morning, having performed 216 kilometres (125
miles) on foot in 26 hours, his food during that time
consisting of about ten ounces of flour, and a draught
of water whenever he happened to meet with a spring.
The Emir and his chiefs would not believe him when
they told them so - but his dispatch, which was cor-
rectly dated, dispelled all doubt on the matter. He is
-now ernylloyed by the French, and is amply paid for his
pedestrian services, which have often proved valuable.
In order not to loose the habit of walking, he often goes
from Jelfa to Laghouat, a distance of 115 kilometres
(72 miles) in 14 hours. When he was inscribed on the
registers of Jelfa as one of the couriers of the French
office there, the chief of the office said to him:.—' Buy a
good horse;, you know a mekhazani (courier) must be
well mounted? Upon which Ben-Saydans burst out
toughing, and at length replied Humble not thy
servant by bidding him buy a horse, which eats more
than a whole family does, which neighs and leaves the
prints of his roofs behind, prints which most frequently
discover us to our enemies l What am Ito do with a
horsb Be satisfied that thou hest a man who can do
more than thy best horses can do, and who will never
ask thee either for oats or straw or horse-shoes.' Since
then he has been as good as his word, and generally
beats the mounted couriers in speed, especially in the
case of long distances.

AN ENGLISHMAN IN RUSBIA.—An article in a French
paper, published at St. Petersburg, says Died at St.
Petersburg, on the 26th 4,,0f November, 1862, Mr.
Thomas Budd Shaw,. M.A., of Cambridge, Professor of
English Literature in the Imperial Lyceum, and Lec-
turer upon the same subject in our University. Mr.
Shaw was only 49 years of age ; he died of an aneurism.
This distinguished man was one of the most worthy re-
presentatives of the British nation that we have ever had
among us, and leaves behind him the unanimous regrets
of the large circle of persons who had the advantage of
knowing him. His happy and smable temper, and the
firmness of his charaeter, acquired for him the attach-
ment of those who were admitted to his intimacy, whilst
his vast erudition, the originality and vivacity of his
great intelligence, his talent as a writer, and his high
moral qualities, to which was added a rare modesty, se-
cured for him universal respect.'
THE PACIFIC Rannoan.---The Atlantic and Pacific
Railroad is fairly launched. The route will be by way
of it-:acramento, Washoe, and the Salt Lake. The stock
subscril,ed on the first day was 400,000 dollars. The
railroad will pass over the Sierra Nevada, where there
is an unbroken ridge from base to summit, so that the
grade will not exceed 105 feet per mile. The expense
of construction is estimated at 88,000 dollars per mile.
In order to prevent the snows of the Sierra Nevada
from interrupting traffic engines will be kept on the
summit, with snow-ploughs to run over the line when
snow begins to fall. The Indian title to all lands
donated to the railway company will be extinguished.
To prevent speculation in land near the railway route,
all lines within 15 miles will be withdrawn from pre-
emption. A grant of -United States Government Bondi
of six million dollars is made to the railway company.
These bonds run for thirty years, and they. draw inte-
rest at the rate of six per ceut.,.and are irredeemable
for that period.
The merchants of Lyons, tlking into consideration the
,great increase in the quantity of foreign silk imported
into France, have decided, it is said, on building store.
houses for its reception. Japan produces 3,000 bale;
of silk, being more than the produce of France ani
Italy. The East produces 300,000 hales. The greater
part of these silks arrive in London by the Cape o:
Goad Hope, but it is expected that when the canal
wross the Isthmus of Suez is completed (if it ever be
completed) silk from the East will arrive first it
France.

articles.title: LORD ELGIN AND THE INDIAN FAMINE RELIIF FUND.
articles.text:
LORD ELGIN AND THE INDIAN
FAMINE RELIIF FUND.

The subjoined communication has been addressed by
Lord Elgin, the Viceroy of India, to the Lord Mayor,
touching the application of the unappropriated surplus
of the money subscribed in this country for the relief of
the sufferers by the Indian famine:—
'To the Right Hen. the Lord Mayor of London.
My Lord—ln reply to a communication addressed
to the Lord Mayor of London in the year 1861 by the
Government ot Bombay, on the subk ct of the appropria-
tion of the surplus then remaining on hand of the fund
so generously contributed from Great Britain for the
relief of the sufferers by the Ineian famine of 1860, his
lordship observed "that it might be held in reserve for
the relief of distress of the same nature in any
part of India; for (his lordship wrote) although not
likely to recur to the extent to which it has lately
existed in the north western provinces and the Punjaub,
destitution must be expected to prevail from time to
time in particular localities,owing to the failure of crops,
inundations, and other causes." Notwithstanding the
injunctions contained in these words, so deep and gene-
ral is the sympathy which the distress now existing in
some of the manufacturing districts of England has
awakened in this country, that the Government of India
has been strongly urged to remit this surplus at once to
your lordship, in order that it may be added to the funds
which are now being raised for the relief of the Lanca-
shire operatives.
We do not consider that, as trustees for this surplus,
we should be justified in diverting it, on our own and
sole responsibility, from the destination originally im-
parted to it by the subscribers, and subseqently con-
firmed by the decision of the Lord Mayor, which I
have cited above; but we think that, under the circum-
stances, we may invite your lordship to review that
decision, and inform you that if, acting on behalf of
the subscribers, you should be of opinion that it may,
without impropriety, be applied in the manner which
I have indicated, th.e Government of India will
heartily concur with your lordship in giving effect to'
that opinion.
The precise amount of the surplus available is not
yet ascertain, d, as certain claims arising out of the
famine of 1860 are still unadjusted, but your lordship's
drafts on the Government of India for the sum of
£20,000 (twenty thousand pounds) will be at once
honoured, should your lordship see fit to add this con-
tribution to the funds placed at your disposul for the
relief of our suffeling fellow-subjects in Lancashire.
I have the honour to be, &c.,
(Signed) ELGIN and KINCARDINE.
'Fort William, Nov. 17, 1862.'

articles.title: GARIBALDI AND THE STUDENTS 01
articles.text:
GARIBALDI AND THE STUDENTS 01

PISA.

The following is a copy of a letter sent by General
Garibaldi to the students of Pisa, in reply to a request
that he would become honorary president of their
Democratic Club.

PISA, Dec. 11.
I accept with pleasure the honorary presidency of
your club. I accept it because I know that you will
always be reconciled and united with all who sincerely
wish our liberty and unity. Yes; let us obtain at any
cost the liberty and unity of the country; after having
gained the triumph of those two• great principles which
forms your programme, it will be easy, by the light of
liberty, which is civilisation—by the light of unity,
which is strength—to occupy ourselves. And we shall
succeed again with equal triumph, by introduring
modifications into, and by more fully developing, the
institutions which should govern us. In this work—
you will see, and I will ensure it—we shall have 2.
valiant coadjutor in the Italian army.
G. GARIBALDI.

articles.title: DEST_RUCTION OF IRON SIIIPS.
articles.text:
DEST_RUCTION OF IRON SIIIPS.

The French floating battery La Glaire has lately been,
examined, and found to be seriously injured by the
action of copper on her iron plates, the whole of which,
below the water-line, will have to be removed, being
converted into a kind of plumbago by galvanic action.
We had occasion some time since to call, attention to the
extraordinary state of her Majesty's ships Triton and
Sharpshooter. On their being docked for examination,
the iron plates were in some places reduced to the thick-
ness of writing paper, and in the Triton the scrapers
actually went through the plates when removing
the tons of oysters, barnacles, &c., attached to
the bottom. It appears that the ship had been
coated with a preparation of copper, and the des-
truction of the plates and rivets arose from gal-
vanic action on the exposed surfaces of the iron,
where the undercoating has become rubbed off under the
bow and forefoot and along the light-load water-line.
The salvation of this ship om foundering was no doubt
occasioned by the adhesion of the h. She has
, just been thoroughly repaired at Devonport Dockyard,
and is LOW coated with Messrs. Peacock and Buchan's
preparation, which is superseding the copper preparation
hitherto used in her Majesty's dockyards. We under-
stand that Captain Peacock, formerly, a master in her
Majesty's navy, who published a pamphlet on tins sub-
ject some years s"nce, actually warned the late Ministre
de Marine in Paris against what has now taken place,
two years ago; he also wdited on the Ministerof Marine
in Madrid on the same subject, and has been for several
years in communication with our own Admiralty autho-
rities on the importance of preventing galvanic action
upon the iron ships of the British navy, and we are
glad to see that their lordships and our dockyard officials
are at length alive to this important subj ec E.—Shipping
Gazette.

Din MonElul CURFEW. - We want a little more
common sense in the magistracy. When the streets
are so unsafe and ruffianly assaults upon women so rife,,
what is to be thought of Mr. Commissioner Kerr's dic-
tum at the Criminal Court, that no girls having respect
for themselves-would be out after eight o'clock ?
how many thousands of virtuous, girls arc obliged to be-
out after that hour by the conditions of the service by
which they earn their bread? Row many servant girls-
are out of errands; how many shop-girls also, and
returning from their day's work; how many dress-
makers who have been kept at their monotonous labour
for many hours to finish some hasty order? And Mr.
Commissioner Kerr encourages the treatment of these
poor helpless creatures as loose women, by the pre-
posterous.dictum we have quoted. It passed, however,
upon a stupid jury who acquitted a couple of fellows
who had assailed two girls in a very suspicious way,
and who, whether with felonious intent or not, had
treated them with indecent violence. We have no-
thing to be robbed of,' cried one of the girls with
touching simplicity; but in the defence an attempt was
made to rob them of their only little possession—their
characters. And it might have succeeded upon the
strength of the judicial dictum that virtue does not go
out after eight, if decisive testimony to good repute
had not fortunately been forthcoming.—Examiner.
THE COLD AT ST. PETERSBURG.—A letter from St.
Petersburg, in the Nord of Thursday, says:—' In the
memory of man there has not been such a winter as this
at St. Petersburg—twenty degrees of cold ; the river
and the sea locked in ice for a long time past, and not a
flake of snow. Thanks to the glassy frost, horses and
pedestrians cannot keep a footing upon either the road
or the pavements. The air is extremely dry; we breathe
it with difficulty. Nervous people are particularly
affected by it, accordingly, no one stirs out except on
business, and of carriages and promenaders there are
literally none, even at the Nevskia perspective, between
two and four in the afternoon, where there is ordinarily
a great crowd.'
An extensive system of obtaining money from servant
girls is now practised. A circular is thrown down every
area, offering to state the name and circumstances
of your future husband, when you may see him, how
you may know him, his age, and whether dark or fair;
and haw to win the affections of as many as you please;
few can resist the charm.' Of course, after the languish-
ing young housemaid has forwarded the stamps, she
hears no more of the husband.

The modification of the ticket-of-leave system, car-
ried out with success in Ireland by Sir Walter Crofton
i ,
seems to be most n favour with those who are lit to
control the Government. Its chief features are solitary
confinement in the earlier period of punishment, and
police supervision and assistance in finding employment
after it terminates. It is said, however, that soliary
confinement has terrors for impulsive and superstitio.us
Irish criminals, which do not exist amongstEnglidi
prisoners of the same class. It is hard to believe that
national character or habits can produce effects so
striking, yet those who make the statement have had the
best means of testing the truth of the observation, and
have not been led to it by any preconceived theory.
A GRATEFUL OFFERING.—The Liverpool pilots have
subscribed amongst themselves £1.4, and have presented
the same to the crew of the Lythap lifeboat, belonging
to the National Lifeboat Institution, as a grateful ac-
knowledgment of the gallant services rendered by the
one of their. comrades, in
lifeboat's crew, in rescuing
conjunction with thirteen others, from the American
ship Anne E. Hooper, of Baltimore, which, during
a heavy gale of wind, was totally wrecked on the Horse
Bank, at the mouth of the Ribble. some weeks ago.
The Portuguese Government have transmittcd £lO
to the crew of the Dungeness lifeboat, belong ng to the
National Lifeboat Institution, for their valuable ser-
vices in rescuing the crew of fourteen men from the
Portuguese barque Cruz V., of Oporto, which, da-ing
a dark and stormy night, was wrecked off Dungeness,
two or three months ago. The lifeboat's crew had pre-
viously received £9 from the National Lifeboat Institu-
tion for their services. The cost of this valuable lifeboat
had been presented to the society by the Rev. IL J.
Hutchessoa.

articles.title: SOCIETY AT WASHINGTON. •
articles.text:
SOCIETY AT WASHINGTON. •

The Washington correspondent of the Ledger says
that very few Foreign Ministers were present at the
opening of Congress. The French and English Minis-
ters were both absent. We see nothing woodel ful in
this. Congress has become such a 'contemptible body
that even a minister from Liberia or Hayti might afford.
to despise it. Foreign Ministers have become so dist
gusted with the ignorance, vulgarity, and buffoonery in
official circles at Washington that they have many of
them removed to New York, so that they may avoid the
necessity of making mere visits of courtesy to the White
House and to Cabinet officials. They only encounter
our President and Cabinet when they are compelled
to—when actual business eequires them to do so. By
residing at New York they escape the necessity of at-
tending the State dinners at the White House, and this,.
during this Administration, must be a great relief to any
well bred man, and our own people ought to be thankful
that so few foreign representatives are present on such
occasions to observe the disgraceful caricaturing of good,
breeding, and the ludicrous attempts at style and gen-
tility est the part of those who, for the present, misrepre-
sent the American people. The change in Washington
society is remarked by all visitors to that city. But
few well bred people, and but few honest people, are
now to be found there. In place of such we now see
lank, lantern jawed New Englanders, many of them of
a poor, parson like aspect, in faded black, soiled linen,
and once white chokers, with blue cotton umbrellas and
cheap oilcloth satchels, half filled with crackers and.
cheese. These gentlemen are chiefly applicants for
chaplainships in the army. They we:ir a sanctimonious
air, rub their hands unctuously toge t her (when they are not
engaged w ith the cotton umbrellas and the oilcloth satchels)
roll up their eyes piously, and comb their hair to the
back of their ears. A set of meaner bigots and more
profound ignoramuses could not be found on the face of
the earth. Another large class, of people now in Wash- ,
ington are the contractors and contract seekers—
shoddyites and swindlers generally, who are too well
known to need description at our hands. Then we
have abolition emissaries and apostles of every variety,.
who are in Washington to urge extreme emancipation
measures and to pick up whatever plunder they can.
These men are generally the friends and associate&
of the abolition members of Congress,l and are
of a similar grade in the social, moral, and in-
tellectual scale. Add to these the correspondents
of the abolitien Press, small pebbles; and such
wretches as Forney, who do the obsequious for their
bread and butter, and you have a tolerable idea of the
chief elements of Washington society at present, so
far as the male sex is concerned. The females present
are, of course, the wives and daughters of these, and
of course are their fit companions. The sharp-nosed,
sharp-voiced daughters of New England are the ruling,
spirits at present. They all spell cow k-e-o-w, and.
pronounce it accordingly, and exprLss wonder in such
terms as, Now, I want to know!' Du tell!' &c., and
invariably ask their neighbours what tht-y had to pay'
for this or that article of clothing. If, in the society of
a Foreign Minister and his lady, these 'ladies' would,.
of course, ask them the cost of each and every article
of their dress; how much dried apples and m gale
sugar are worth; where they come from, and. how
much wages their King,, Queens, and Emperors re-
ceived. Is it any wonder that Foreign Ministers slid.
not attend the opening of Congress—that they refuse to-
reside in Washington at this time.—Thiladaphia Even-.
iny Journal.

articles.title: SALE Of DIS_EASED CATTLE.
articles.text:
SALE Of DIS_EASED CATTLE.

[From the Medical Times and Gazette].
We learn from the Times that the Royal Dubliit
Society met on Saturday evening to hear a lecture from
Professor Oamgee,. on 'Disease and Mortality among
Cattle." When he had concluded, Mr. Ganley, sales-
master, made an extraordinary statement. He said that,
unless some means were devised to give some compensa-
tion to the farmer for diseased cattle, it was impossible
to prevent him from selling them, or the butcher from
killing and selling them. Unless some society were
termed to have diseased meat paid for, it would be killed
and eaten. There was no use in mincing the matter, he
said; every one of the salesmen sold diseased cattle. The
farmer could not otherwise pay his rent. The disease
is so prevalent that he could not live were he to sub-
mit his cattle to destruction. Professor Gamgee said he
would have gone 1,500 miles to hear this confe.ssion,
and he agreed with Mr. Ganley that some plan should
be adopted for paying the farmer or diseased cattle.'
This does•but add superfluous confirmation to a fact that
is already notorious. There is no doubt whatever that
the prudent farmer, so soon as a bullock is seized with
the lung disease, does have him killtd forthwith; that
so killed he is eaten; and that, according to the English
mode of cookery, much of the blood, of the diseased mi.,
mal•must pass, in an unaltered state, into the stomachs
of those who cut the juicy sirloin, or underdone round
of beef, with its delicious gravy. Underdone meat la
really, as Liebig taught us, raw meat, and the red
gravy, so much prized as a restorative, is in reality
tinged with the colouring matter of blood that has
never, in the inside of the joint, reached a temtPE's
of 180 deg. There is one consolation which
philosopher may extract from all this. If the consump,
tion of diseased meat be so universal, it does no eem to
hurt those Who can get enough of it. The human
stomach is a wonderful organ.

YACHTS IN THE MEDITERRANEAN:The schooneryacht
Pilgrim, belonging to the Duke of St. Albans, arrived
on the 7th instant at Valetta, from Algiers in five days.
The Duke and a party of friends were On board. Several
other yachts arrived at Malta last week. The Brunette
cutter made a rapid run out of 16 days from Cowes.
A fine Russian yacht of 180 tons, called the Georgian,
belonging to a Scotch gentleman from Tunis, anchored
in "Valetta harbour on the Bth inst. ; and the English
schooner yacht Glam, 140 tons, left Malta for Corfu the
same day. There is an unprecedented number of English
yachts in the Mediterranean this season.. There are, it
said, no less than 26 at present on the coast of Albania.
WHALE-STEAS.S.—In passing along the streets we
saw strips of whale flesh, black and reddish coloured,
hanging
outside the gable of almost every house to dry,
just as we have seen herrings in fishing villages on our
own coasts. 'When a shoal of whales is driven ashore
by the boatmen, there are great rejoicings among the
islanders, whose faces, we are told, actually shine for
weeks after this, their season of feasting. What can-
not be eaten at the time is dried for future use. Boiled /
or roasted it is nutritious, and not' very unpalatable.
The dried flesh which I tasted resembled-tough beef,
with a flavour of venison. Being 'blood meat,' I
would not have known it to be from the sea; and have
been told that when fresh and properlY cooked, tender
steaks from .a young whale can scarcely be distinguished
from beef steak.—Pen and Pencil Sketches of Faroe and
Iceland.
--

In his speech at Birmingham, Mr. Bright apologised
for the quality of Indian cotton. He admited, however;
that it was very bad indeed for the workmen, and ilk?...
trated their excessive distate by a story, which will
offend only those who think that men should never prey
for the bread they need. The other day, while a Me-
thodist minister was supplicating the Supreme Being at
a prayer meeting, and asking, among other things, for a
supply of cotton for the famishing operatives,, one man,
with a keen sense of what he had suffered, interposed
the ejaculation, Yea Lord, but no Surat.' This man

LATER FR 011 AMERICA.

NEW YORX, Dec. 13 kMorning).--The main body of
General Burnside's army crossed. the Rappahannock
yesterday, and occupied the south side of the .iver and
Fredericksburg. The, Confederates have two strong
lihes of batteries, the first one mile in the rear of
Fredericksburg, and the second one mile in the rear of
the first. The Confe erates opened fire yesterday from
their first line of batteries upon the FederaLs who were
in Fredericksburg, and upon those who were crossing
the i;ver, but the Federal batteries along the banks of
the river silenced them in half an hour. The Confede-
rates have concentratel th force-, and it is supposed
that unless the Confederates retreat, a decisive battle
will be fought to-day. General Sigel has marched to
join General Burnside, and it is upposed that he has
now reached his destination. The Federal losses have
bee"' slight.

articles.title: PRINCE OF WALES'S 3LikkrAGE.
articles.text:
THE PRINCE OF WALES'S
3LikkrAGE.

(From th-.. Court Circular.)

We cannot bitt think that, on her own account, and
on that of her own family, and on that of the whole
nation, it is devoutly to be wished that our beloved
Sovereign should be earnestly entreat d by those about
her to do her beA to throw off the terrible weight that
bows he.r down, and, to remember that she has to live
for others. We by no means hint or imply that any
vital business has been neglected, but the mere absence
of all the usual receptions, and ceremonies, and festivi-
ties of the Court, and the personal seclusion of the
Sovereign herself, are apt to he regarded with some sort
of jealousy and dissatisfaction by the people, for the
whole country takes something of its tone from the
Royal PaLce and the influence of its unusual dulne.s-
spreads far and wide; and many branches of trade are
supposed to suffer.
There is a time for all things, and if the time to be
wedded for the eldest son of

The silent father e our kings to he"
is now properly near at hand, it might be fittingly at-
tended with all the usual public rejoicings connected
-with. Royal marriages. Why shouli one unnecessary
shadow, one inauspicious omen, be thrown upon an
occasion ,of. such deep interest not only to the parties
most itruf,,,ecliately concerned but to the whole nation?
And wirrshould a national. event be made almost a
privatf,-orte ? Why should it be celebnted in, the
country in the pre.enee of a fe:w hundreds of people,
instead of in the great metropolis of the kingdom in the
presence of three millions of loyal subjects who yearn to
greet the Roytd pair with every demonstration of good-
will, rejoicing and congratulation? Every one feels that
En gland has lately haden ougla of calamityan d gloom. The
loss of the Prime we so highly appreciated, the great
cotten,famine, and the general stagnation of commerce
and trad have all contributed to make merrie Eng-
land!, for the present a land of gloom, and we should,
therefore, rejoice to learn that the Globe newspaper is
correct in itsassertion-that the approaching Royal wed-
ding of the heir to -the throne is not to be obscurely,
solemnised at Windsor, but that the wishes of the me-
tropolis are to be consulted and its trade benefited by a
grand, and : glorious, and happy and triumphal display
in every way worthy of the occ+sion. We should be
glad also to hear thateven Majesty herself had resolved
to cast off her sombre weeds for that one day, satisfied
that her late, Consort, if he be still observant of the con-
*erns of this world, will approve of that cheerful sym-
pathy with,the happiness aud hopeo of hist owit son, and.
the feelings of the people of his adopted country.

articles.title: DEPARTURE OF THE COURT FROM'
articles.text:
DEPARTURE OF THE COURT FROM'

WINDSOR.

'Saturdfty morning, at ten o'clock, her Majesty
the Queen, accompanied by their Royal Highnesses the
the Prince of Wales, the Prince and Princess of Hesse,
and the junior branches of the Royal family, with their
numerous suite, occupying _ seven carriages, left the
Castle, and proceeded to the Great Western railway
terminus where they were received by Major-General
F. H. St;ymour, and Col. the Hon. Sir C. Phipps Mr.
Matthews Mr. Kelly (general superintendent of the
line,) and Mr. Lane (chief engineer). The two latter
gentlemen took charge of the Royal train to Basing.
stoke, when the traffic manager of the- South-Western
line attended the 'train to Gosport, the distance being
completed in two hours, _ _ _

There were some doubts in the morning as to whether
her Majesty's departure should be postponed until Mon-
day, in consequence of the boisterous state of the
weather during the night, until a telegraph dispatch
from the Admiralty arrived at the Castle to state that
the sea was favourable for crossing.
The return of the Court to Windsor' according to the
present arrangements, is fixed for the llth of Feburary
next

Great preparations will be made at the Castle, during
her Majesty's abspnce, foi the forthcoming Royal
wedding, particularity. in Edward the Fourth's Tower,
which will be sumptuously fitted up for the reception of
The Princess Alexaldra.

The Colonial Government has been compelled to
borrow £30,000 from the Table Bay Harbour Works.
The Customs' return for the quarterexceed by £lO,OOO

Cattle are dying in the northern districts throug-h the

Five thousand pounds has been subscribed in the
