articles.title: DISASTROUS GALE AT TM ISTHMUS OF PANAMA:
articles.text:
DISASTROUS GALE AT TM
ISTHMUS OF PANAMA:

The latest news from the Pacific, brought by the
American mail steamer Africa; is as follows :

PANAMA, Nov. 27.
Probably the severest gale ever experienced at Aspin-
wall was felt on Friday and Saturday, the 21st and 22nd
Inst. The gale commenced about midnight, and by day--
break the British brig Bolivar was reported as a total
wreck) having gone on the reef, and was soon followed
by the Royal Mail Company's steamer Avon) also
reported a wreck, the crew having escaped to the shore
by ropes after having used all possible exertions to save
the ship. The Ocean Queen carried away her paddle.bor
against' . the wharf but succeeded in -getting to sea. The
United States' ship Bainbridge at last accounts was con-
sidered in danger. Her Britannic Majesty's frigate
Jason was lying off the port, but owing to the heavy sea
could render no assistance. Since Saturday, the 22nd
inst., no communication was had with Colon until
Monday night, when a messenger crossed the Isthmus
partly by the engine and by hand cars and canoes; he
came "el- the track 13 miles in a canoe, finding at some
place 10 feet of water on the track. As the storm is
now abating.the-track will probably be clear to-morrow.
It is contemplated sending the Pacific Steam Naviga-
tion Company's steamer Callao for the south coast to
sea to- day, without .the mails and passengers from
Europe, now at Aspin,„all, unless they- can come over
this morning. The Orizaba is in from California. There
are now in port four French, three
_United States',
and one British ship of war. According- to the very
latest from Colon, there is no hope of saving the Royal
Mail steamer Avon. It was expected she would be a
total wreck She had gone over on her side and had
several large holes through her hull. She had on board
1,000,000 dole. of San Francisco and Mexican treasure,
for Europe, which will probably be saved. The steamer
Bogota, with mails from the Pacific-coast, for transmis-
sion to Europe via Colon, arrived- on the 21st. Her
dates are Valparaiso, November 2; Coquimbo, 3rd
Caldera, 4th; Cobija, 6th; Arica, 7th; Islay, Bth-'
risco, 10th; Callao, 13th; Paita, 16th; Guayaquil,
17th. In addition to mails and passengers to Bogota
brings 385,776 dols. specie for transmission to South-
ampton, also 399 bales bark, 278 serons.bark, and 20
packages general merchandise.

THE COTTON DISTRESS.—Nothinfr he believed,
would tend more to unite together all Classes in this
country than the sympathy which had been shown
towards the operatives in all parts, and in this county as
well as others, lie hail recenVy read a speech made by
Lord Brougham in 18-17, when there was great distress
in the cotton districts, not only in the North, but
throughout all England, and his lordship stated that it
then took. L 20,000 a week to supply them with the bare
necessar es of. life. At the present time, however, it
required no less than £40,000 to provide them with the
simplest necessaries of life. The people of this country
had come forward in the noblest manner, and he trusted.
that, as ,the suffering was not unprecedented,' we should-
weather the storm, and the cotton trade might soon be ,
in a flourishing condition.--The 2Ton. TV. .EI. Portman, I
ILE., at Blandford.

articles.title: .INERICA'S D 4 fOTRETRIB ITHE DREAM Oji TRAAVS.PORTATION.
articles.text:
.INERICA'S D 4 fOTRETRIB ITHE DREAM Oji TRAAVS.PORTATION.

The fbllowing is an extract of a sermon preached on
Thanksgiving-day, by the Rev. F. G. Clark, in the
Pr, sbyterian Church, Twenty-third-street, New York:
—4 The substance of the strife, as every body knows, is
slavery. Settle this question and our battles end. Over
this vast problem we are fighting the most desperate
war the world ever saw. The questions to be decided
are too profound for mortal solution. No man has
yet risen up to tell us what to do with this insti-
tution, or it once rid of it, what we shall do with
the race thus emancipated. The fruit of slavery
has fattened the nation. It has become the
most influential thing in the land, because the
most profitable. We found it first a foundling on our
door stone. It grew up to rale the house. We
baptised it and called it Christian. We canonised it
and called it Saint. We deified it and served it as God.
God waited, but did hot forget. If God is just, so
huge a wrong can never die a natural death. The day of
reckoning has come. What we have been hearing for
a year is only the rumbling of the world's great clock
before it strikes the hour of God's full time. God has
taken this great quest:on out of the hands of States and
statesmen, and politicians. He (14-creed that it should
not be adjusted; and this because he is just. We are
powerless now. We can fight and die, but we can
decide nothing. Why did we not conquer at Bull Run?
Our General never failed befere. Our supplies, our
troops, our courage, were enough for victory. Why
then a defeat?

We would have conquered a hundred times, but God
is not ready. His retributions are incomplete. He is
holding everything in suspense until the world shall
palm to give attention. He hrs a sublime work to do.
The retributions now falling due are rising like a
tide; and running into 41 the coves and fissures of
society. Our land is finding out more and more what
God means.

God is just. Nations must remember their sins.
God is doing a thing in the earth which all nations will
see and remember. Let us pray God to do this work
thoroughly, if we can bear it. May he settle our trou-
bles on the principles of truth and justice.
Better have the geld in the furnace twenty years
than have it come out ought else than gold. To
God we commit, with implicit faith, our bleeding
country. 'Our soul waiteth for the Lord.: he is our
help and our shield. For our heart shall rejoice in him
because we have trusted in. his holy name.'

(From the Fieonotni3t.)
The prevalent outcry for the revival of transporta-
tion as a mode of punishing and disposing of our
dangerous criminals will not, we are convinced, survive
many weeks' consid.- ration and discussion of the subject.
It could scarcely have ar sen, had the guides and in-
structors of the public mind, either official or amateur,
given the slightest attention to the past history of the
question, or duly weighed the plain and notorious facts
bearing on the case. Transportation, as that word is
ordinarily understood, cann,t be restored; and if it
could, it would not answer the purpose of a punish-
ment. We want to punish our ruffians, to inflict
upon them some punishment adequate to their
offences, and of a character to 'deter them from
a continuance or a repettion of them. We wish
to menace them with a penalty which is at once
severe and dreaded—which they will not lightly run
the risk of bringing on their heads. This being our
object, it is proposed to attain it by reviving a penalty
which was Ling since abandoned (independent of other
secondary and conclusive masons), partly because it was
so light, partly because it was so uncertain in its cha-
racter, and partly because a change of eircumstane s
had almost transmuted it into a boon—which numbers
of convicts now earnestly desire as their sentence, and
are jealous if more favoured offenders than themselves
obtain—which (with a comparatively unimportant mo-
dification of details and the brand of shame apart)
thousands of honest and industrious labourers envy and
exert themselves to secure. Transportation to a penal
colony has been tried for generations under every con-
ceivable variety of plan, and under all has been aban-
doned and condemned.

If the proposed plan of transportation were merely a
larger Pentonville or Portland, it would, if similarly
conducted in other respects, be a less severe punishment
just in proportion as it was larger—and with additional
chances of escape. Even from Portland and from
Western Australia convicts now manage to escape by
water- If it is to be a mere prison, it would be cheaper
securer, more open to sueervision, and certain to be
managed better at home. The fare, indeed, might be so
peer, the labour so incessant and severe, and the penalties
for breach of discipline so stringent and so harsh, that
prisoners would learn to dread being consigned to such
a place more than death; but all these objects could be
secured just as easily at home and now. A short act of
parliament, intrusted for execution to a resolute Secre-
tary of State and a rational direeter of convict prisons,
could to-morrow render Dartmoor, Portland, or
Pentonville as terrible as any penal settlement at the
antipodes—so terrible that no convict who had once
visited them would ever risk the penalty of visiting.
them again. Finally, the proposed penal, settlemen;
'might be so located that the convicts would he :rozen
in winter and broiled in summer • for Great Britt; has
possessions both in the tropics and in the Arctic circle.
They might be placed where life itself would ibe neces-
sarily short, and necessarily wretched while it lasted—
at the mouth of the Niger, in the swamps of Guiana,
or on the icebound coast of Greenland or Labrador.
We might thus quietly slay our convicted ruffians as
France is said to slay hers at
,Cayenne. Mut What
minister would venture to recommend the establishment
of such a colony? What parliament would sanction it?
What decent governor, or gaolers, or soldiers would go
out to manage it ?—for they must die as 'well as the
convicts, and nearly as fast, and be nearly as miserable
while they lived. Lastly, how much would such
a settlement cost in comparison with the establish-
ments at Dartmoor, Portland, or Chatham.? And why
not face the facts, and hang our desperate criminals at
once It would be more honest, more merciful, as de-
cent, and far cheaper. But it is clearly and noto -
riously not such a penal settlement as this that the
public is thinking of when echoing the demand for a
revival of transportation. What .is meant is exile for
ever (or for such a long series of years as would vir-
tually be for ever) to some colony, some prospetous and
tolerably populous place where land is abundant, where
labour is greatly in detnand, where antecedents are un-
known, where no questions are asked, and where, there-
fore, the convict might be absorbed into the mass of the
community, might easily earn an honest living if he
would, might be dispersed into the backwoods if he
would not, and would be shot down like a beast of prey
if he became noxious. Such were our old penal colo-
nies, and a renewal of a recourse to such is the thing
now desired. It is a sad and wicked dream, and utterly
incapable of realisation.
(From the qpeetator.)
There never was .a more hopeless waste of power than
the attempt to revive transportation—a system only
abandoned after desperate resistance and out of a proved
necessity. The arguments on which it Is condemned
may be stated in ten lines, but all the researches of the
most acute commission cannot add to their force. The
convicts must obviously be sent either to a land with
inhabitants or to a land without them. In the latter
case they will, while in durance, by mere force of associa-
tion, turn the settlement into a scene so dreadful that
the instant it is exposed the system will be abolished. In
the second ease the assent of the free colonists must first
he obtained, and there are no colonies left whose
settlers are willing to fertilise their own .soil by im-
porting English manure. They say the stench breeds
diseases for which the increase of production does not
compensate. Western Australia will take a few, but
Western Australia already objects to the class we wish
to be rid of, the irreclaimable, or apparently irreclaim-
able ruffian. There is no other...colony available, and a-
new one would be merely a repetition of the old Nor-
folk Island failure. There is, indeed, one land where
r convicts might be employed without close association,
and settled after release, without much fear of return.
The Hudson's Bay territory might, under certain
arrangements, take off any number econviets; hilt the
result would be in three years either a rebellion in
Canada, or a war with, the United States.- Decent
settlers cannot and will not bear an influx of escaped
convicts, whom they did not sentence, and for whom they
have no responsibility. It might be possible, perhaps, to
settle a few, according to a popular sugeestion, in some
inhospitable region.' say within the Antarctic circle,
whence escape would be impossible, and nature herself
would inflict sufficient punishment. But how long
would public opinion, once relieved of its demoralising
terrors, tolerate that panacea.?, Not a month; and, as
in the case of flogging, the reaction would produce a
worse access of humanitarian feebleness. Statesmen
know too well the flux and reflux of the public mind to
run the risk, as the Terrorists used to say, of' demoral-
ising the guillotine.' The instant that punishment be-
gins to shock instead of toning the moral nature of those
who inflict it, it becomes worse than useless. Larceny
was never so frequent as when it was punished with
death, for juries could not be relied on; and criminals
who shrink from a smael but inevitable penalty will
rim any risk for gain. For one man who would put his
finger in to the fire fifty would lead a forlorn hope.

articles.title: EXTENSIVE FIRE AT A SHIPPINGYARD 1117 LIVERPOOL.
articles.text:
EXTENSIVE FIRE AT A SHIPPING-
YARD 1117 LIVERPOOL.

Soon. after six o'clock on the 22nd, a fire was dis-
'covered in the extensive shipbuilding yard of Messrs.
Cato, Miller, and Co., at Brunswick Dock, Liverpool.
An alarm was immediately given, and hose and reels
from the Brunswick-dock lire station and the West of
England fire engine were speedily in attendance, as were
also hose and •!ton from the Steel-street station. The
fire had brokeo out in the store shed connected with the
mast and spar makers' shop, and it contained a large
quantity of materials of an exceedingly combustible
nature. Thee consisted chiefly of a number of barrels
of pitch, of resin, and an iron tank containing oil of
naphtha, besides a considerable quantity of dry timber.
Above the sheds were piles of timber set up to dry, and a
large amount of timber of various kinds was- piled in
proximity to the seat of fire. As maybe readily conjec-
tured, the conflagation raged with great fierceness,
and in an incredibly short time the interior of the shed
was completely filled with flames of intense heat,
which, bursting through the roof, seized on the piles of
dry timber on the top, and caused an extensive and
alarming blaze, which illuminated the sky and was
seen from a great distance. A detachment of men were
dispatched from her Majesty's -ship Hastings, and they.,
arrived at the scene of the fire soon after it had broken
out, and they immediately joined the fire brigade in
their efforts to extinguish the flames and to save pro-
perty. Fortunately there was a good supply of water,
and by the combined efforts -of the firemen and the
'tars,' the fire was confined almost entirely to the shed
in which it broke out, and there it was subdued in
about an hour and a-half after it had been discovered,
not however before a large amount of property had
been destroyed. The full amount of damage -done
cannot be as yet ascertained, but it is considered that
about -.C1,200 in value of property has been destroyed.
The loss is covered by insurance with the Liverpool
and London Insurance Company.

I (From Manhattan,' the vew York Correspondent of
the Morning Iferald.)
l• Meantime a local ,calamity has happened that affects us
I snore than all the bad war news. it is the advance of
paper. Every newspaper is on the brink of ruin. Yes-
terday all of our daily journals (save one) advanced the
price from 2to 3 cents. Yl is said that all must fail,
even at these prices, unless paper falls. Even Beruxett,
of the .Herald, who has accumulated a fortune, has no idea
that he can save it, except in one way. It is announced
that James Gordon Bennett goes out of the Herald on
the Ist of January next, and is succeeded by his son,
who takes the whole business. The eon is James Gar-
don_Bennett, jun. By taking this course, if matters do
not take a favourable turn, the old Bennett may save
a portion of his property, and have something to live
upon in It's declining years. Every paper that his son
sells will be so much loss; meanwhile it becomes evident
that his early rival (from 1835) the Sun, will take away
all his advertising that the Lierald has had for some
years. It announces today—' The other New, York
City morning papers have raised their prices to 3c., bat
the New York Sun will continue to be sold aq it has been
for nearly thirty years past, at This is not all.
Unless paper can be kept at its present rate all the jour-
nals in the city must fall; they cannot even issue single
sheets. They have all united to make paper. Here is
what they announce
To CAPITALISTS AND PAPER-MAKERS.—The under-
signed, a committee appointed by and. acting for the
Asso,Aated Press in the city of New York, will receive
proposals for the supply of the whole or any part of
.300,0001 b. of paper per week, for five years' from the
Ist day of January next (or as soon theYeafter as the
necessary arrangements can be perfected). —M. S.
Beach, Sun Office, corner of Nassau and Fulton streets;
Samuel Sinclair, Tribune Office, corner of Nassau and,
Spruce-streets.' - -
__

-All of the weekly papers have raised their price from
four to six cents. The Albion (British) has been raised
to ten cents. The bookmakers and publishers are hold-
ing meetings. They have resolved not to publish a
book for six months 'unless the price of paper falls
below the present rate.'

articles.title: AUSTRIAN COURT AND ITS
articles.text:
THE AUSTRIAN COURT AND ITS

GU_ESTS.

The Vienna papers give- such erroneous accounts of
I the movements of the Prince and Princess of Prussia
that it it may be well to state what they have done since
their arrival here. After their reception by the Em-
peror at the railway terminus their Royal Highnesses
drove to the residence of the Pru,sian Minister, which
is at the southern extremity of the Karnthuer Strasse.
Soon after eight o'clock in the evening of Sunday the
Empresi paid a visit to the Princess, who is still in
mourning. The illustrious ladies met on the stair-
case, where those compliments which are customary,
between strangers were paid, but on reaching the land-
ing-place the Empress affectionately embraced the Eng-
lish wile of her Prussian- cousin. In the course of the
evening the Arch-Duchess Sophia and one or two mem-
bers of the Imperial family called en the Princess of
Prussia, who yesterday morning returned the visits she
had rec,ived. In the 'course of the day-the Prince of
Prussia went to see the Arsenal and the Military Riding
School, and in the evening he accompanied the Emperor
and Empress to the Opera. The Princess dined with the
Imperial family, but she speedily returned to her own
rooms, which she did not quit during the rest of. the
day. The Emperor and the Prince are now reviewing
troops on the glacis and in the course of the after-
noon his Majesty will act as cicerone to his Royal
visitor, and show him some of the sights of Vienna. At
half-past six there will be a grand dinner at Court, and
in the evening the Imperial Family and the Crown
Prince of Prussia will go to the Burg Theatre to see a
new and popular dramatic work. After the 'gala'
dinner the Princess will return to her apartments. To-
morrow morning their Royal Highnesses will go to the
Imperial Mews to see the state carriages and their high-
bred teams, and in the evening they purpose leaving for
Berlin. It is said that the Princess of Prussia was loth
otoblitravel on S,unday, the 14th instant, but she was
as the Prince, her husband, must be in
Berlin on Thursday next. A person who chanced to be
at the Prussian Legation when the Empress called in the
evening of Sunday, says that her Majesty looks perfectly
well, and is 'handsomer than ever.'—Vienna Letter of
the 16th.

OUTBBEAK 4110N6c FEMALE

CONVICTS' AT PE.R.TIT.

• On Sunday forenoon during the time of rublic wor-
ship, an alarm was raised throughout the city of Perth
to the effect that the convicts in the general prison at
Friarton had overpowered the warders, and that many
of, them had made their escape. The truth of the alarm
was apparen ly confirmed by the circumstances of a
detachment of the 25th Regiment marching quickly
with fixed bayonets through the South Inch, in the
direction of the general prison, and a body of city police
being conveyed thither in cabs. The rxeitement in
town was intense, but it was much allayed when the
actual state of matters, though sufficiently serious, was
ascul ained. The circumstaeces under which the out-
ak commenced are as follows :—The female convicts
about 300 in number, assembled in the chap 1 of the pri-
son on Sunday forenoon, as usual, to engage in public
worship, but the chaplain had not proceeded far with the
service when the convicts, ins, most excited state com-
menced shiuting, making disc irdant noises, and defying
the female warders. One of the latter was knocked
down, much abused, and eventually carried out in a
state of ii•sensibility. The scene of disor ler which the
chapel presented was one which baffles description. On
the male officials being apprised of the outbre k among
the female convicts, the former promptly hastened to the
chapel, from which all, egress was strictly prohibit-id.
As the female warders had lost all control over the
female convicts, who, with increased rage and energy,
uttered most dreadful yells, it was resolved by the head
male officials present to fire several shots from revolvers
over the heads of the women. This, being continued
, for some time, had the. desired effect of quieting them in
I a great degree, until at last they were completely sub-
dued. At the same time, great fears were entertained
of an outbreak among the male convicts, many of
whom, it had been learned OR Saturday, were in
possession of keys wherewith to open their eells ;
and accordingly it was resolved to call in the assist-
ance of the Perth city police and the military in Perth
barracks. On being apprised of the outbreak, Mr. Welsh,
superintendent of the eity police, repaired with a large
body of constables to the gmeral prison, armed with
'swords, batons, and cutlasses. The 'city police were
'conveyed to the general prison in cabs, and under the'
superintendent, rendered most efficientservice. A detach-
ment of the 25th Regiment e as also promptly ('U the spot.
With the assistance -of the military and police the female
convicts were conveyed one by one from the chapel to
their cells, and by two o'clocic in the •afternoon things
within the walls of the general prison had assumed their
ordinary quietness. There was no movement among or
attempt at an outbreak by the male convicts, but it was ,
considered necessary to keep the military and pollee on ,
duty within the prison. the whole of last night There is
every reason to believe that the insubordination of the
women in the chapel on Sunday was partof a preconcerted
scheme to -enable the male convicts to overthrow their
keepers, and set all the convicts, both 'male and female,
liberty.

articles.title: O.ENERAL STATE OF TRADE
articles.text:
O.ENERAL STATE OF TRADE

We have to report this.week a more satisfactory-state
of trade from the manufacturing districts than has pre-
vailed for some time past. This improvement may be
attributed to the ready sale for fabrics suited to the
winter season, and the steadily improving condition of
the Liverpool cotton market, which has shown a decided
change for the better. The greatest improvement is
exhibited in the leading markets of Manchester, Leeds,
Halifax, Huddersfield, Leicester, .and Nottingham. In
the latter marh et the improvement only applies to the
hosiery mid some departments of the lace trades which
have suffered greater depression than has been known
for some years past, and is still insufficient to make up
for the -(lHplorable dulness that still pervades the cotton
fancy trade. With respect to trade in the leading ma-
nufacturing towns generally, a strong feeling prevails
in all quarters that a more general improvement will be
experienced before long, which will be felt not only by
the. manufacturers but by wholesale and retailers in
general throughout the kingdom. The carpet and
worsted braches of trade in Halifax since our report up
to Thursday last in the columns of the Drapers Weekly
News have exhibited greater activity; and the cloth
hills.of Leeds have been ;better attended by large buyers
than for the past three, weeks. The Manchester yarn
trade is more animated. The Leicester hosiery trade is
brisker than ever, and a renewal of trade to a certain
extent has been experienced, 'we are glad to say, both
by the wholesalers and retailers in the metropolis. We
earnestly trust to witness .an increased: revival to assist
in carrying us over the dull .season near at hand.—
Drapers' Weekly News.

The Tumour recently circulated of the resignation of
the- Secretary of the-Great Western Railway is con-
tradicted.
The Temps .says it has reason to believe that the ces-
sion of the lonian Islands is complete and absolute with-
out any reservation respecting ,Corfu.
A POLICEMAN SENTENCED TO PENAL SERVITUDE.—
An ex-police officer, named Joseph Scott, has been sen-
tenced to three years' penal servitude; at the South
Lancashire Assizes, for forgery. In connection w ith
the police force, of which the prisoner was a member,
a sick and burial society had been established, and hav-
ing been appointed its secretary, he broke his trust and
forged various certificates of death in order to obtain
sums of money belonging to the proprietary.
A young damsel, who is engaged, and will shortly be
united to a gallant son of Neptune, lately visited the
Mariners' Church, at the East end of London. During
the serthon the parson discoursed eloquently and with
much earnestness of the dangers and temptations of
sailors. He concluded by asking, IS there one who
thinks anything of him who wears a tarpaulin hat and
blue jacket, or a pair of trousers made of duck? In
short, is there any one who cares aught for the poor
sailors?' A little girl, sister of the damsel, jumped up.
and looking archly at her sister, said, in a tone loud
enough for every one to hear, Yes, Sir; our Beeky
does.'
A FEAT or Anars.—A feat of arms (says the Con-
stitutionnel) has just been performed in Senegal which
is worthy of mention. A detachment of 14 French
Marines, under the command of a sergeant named Burg,
who were entrenched in the post of liaol ikh, kept in
check for fourteen hours, and finally repulsed a body of
5,000 fanatics under the orders of two desperate chiefs,
named Maba and Macodou. When the enemy retired
before such an heroic resistance' there were found lying
round the post the bodies of 250 men and 70 horses.
The remainder of the army had fiedin-disorder across
the Saloum.

articles.title: AITERICAN PATRIOTIC ROPES.
articles.text:
AITERICAN PATRIOTIC ROPES.

The Rev. Dr. Stephen.- Tyng, of New York, who is
known by report to a large circle of Englishmen,
preached the sermon at St. George's Church, on Thanks-
giving Day. In the progress of his discourse he said :
No class, no fcirm of human government, in its institu-
tions and its promises, ever attained to an exaltation
like this. lam grateful, under God, to those venerable
and elevated men, the fathers of the generation past,
who humbly and solemnly said, We owe it all to the
grace and beneficence of God.' The people are the
rulers by their elected representatives. They devise,
enact, proclaim the laws, by their elective commis-
sioned mag strates ; they command their laws to be
justly executed and enforced by their own appointed.
judges; they interpret me decide the particular ap-
plication of their laws, as occasions demand; and
having thus, in the majesty of thfir power and the
rght of their control, under God, from whose benefi-
cence they confess the right to proceed to establish their
authority, they claim, and rightly claim' that it shall be
thoroughly and properly adminTstered for their good;
ani having thus settled its authority in evcry depart-
ment of execution of their sovereign will, they, as volun-
tary subjects of their own law, submit themselves to
every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake, whether it
be to the king, as supreme, or to governors as unto them
that are sent by them for the punishment of evildoers
and for the praise of them that do well; for so is the
will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence
the ienorance of foolish men. The justice of our ruler
is a righteousness in the fear of God. It is not our theory
merely to restrain, but to uproot the crimes of the wicked.
Our Inherited, adopted view of public justice is the protec-
tion, of the innocent, the secured welfare of the deserving
—the education of the ignorant—and the destroyin g those
who d, stroy the earth. This has been the great posi-
tive scheme which the beneficence of God permitted eur
fathers to inaugarate for us, and have transmitted to us
as ourdearest inherit amt. It he established a system
of free public education, constantly improving—pro-
claimed laws for the faithful honouring of the Lord's
Day, which have made, as the eminent Duponceau de-
clared, the American Sabbath to be the chief distinction
and honour of the nat.on. It has constantly restrained.
and limited, and in some highly favoured sections of our
country absolutely prohibited, the sale of intoxicating
liquors, the direct instrument in forty years past of
consigning to a drunkard's grave more than 1,000,000
of the men of our land. It has regularly com-
pressed the power, den ed the claims and testified
against the wickedness. of African slavery, until it has
realised the dawn, and given the promise of a universal
'emancipation. It has solemnly i estified for the validity
and authority of public law, of majestic national sove-
reimty, over all inferior:dissent, and agamst every
aspect of individual and sectional rebellion, until it has
even cisked the issues of a war of unprecedented extent,
and of terrific inflictions of individual suffering and cost,
rather than yield to any rebellion that national sovereignty
and integrity which is the only foundation of indi% ideal
security. It has raised up a spirit of energy transmitted
from father to son which will stop at no sacrifice, and
flinch from no danger, in 'defending and maintaining a
national unity so justly dear. Can you suppose that a
nation so educated will yield? It is impossible. Its
going forth in its high.progress is as sure as the dawn of
morning. Clouds may come over it—l have unbounded
hopes for the glorious advancement of my nation, and I
have no abiding or overwhelming fears. NO internal re-
bellion can break it' down. No outward assaults in
whatever combination can overthrow it.

articles.title: GENERAL TION AND THE – NEGRO.
articles.text:
GENERAL TION AND THE
-
NEGRO.

General Cameron, American minister to St. Peters-
burg, now in Washington on business is known to
be a very agreeable and entertaining talker. One in-
,cident, which he relates with great humour,' deserves
reprodust on in the columns of the _Thi,Ty Chronicle.
Arriving at a small German town on the evening of
Whitsuntide—which is a famous and favourite holiday
with the Lutherans— he was struck with the decent and
comfortable awearance of the people who crowded the
-streets; but what-most interested h:m was a tall, stout,
and impressive negro. Supposing him to be an
American negro, Mr. Cameron went up to him and
said How are
.you, my friend?' using the Pennsyl-
vania German, in which the general is a sort of
adept—when, to his infinite horror, the coloured
individual turned upon him and said, in good guttural
Dutch, am no American; I am an African, and if
you are an Anaelican, Ido not want to talk to you. I
won't talk to any man who comes from a country
professing to be free, in which human beings are
held as slaves.' And this was said with a magisterial
and indignant air that would have been irresistibly
severe, if it had not been irresistibly comic. General
Cameron made his escape with the best grace possible
from his stalwart and sable antagonist, and supposed he
had got rid of him, but passing into an adjoining
saloon with his secretary, iyard Taylor, to take a glass
of lager beer, h ‘c]vas agaii confronted by the German
Africaaaus, who re-opened his vials of wrath, and con-
cluded by turning to the General and asking him in
broad German, Sagh, bin ich recht, or bin ich unrecht
which means, Am I right or am I wrong? Answer
me.' General Cameron made an inquiry as to the negr, o,
and ascertained that one of the nobility in the neigh-
bourhood, who had spent some years in Africa in a
scientific and hunting tour, brought lack with him to
Germany a very 11:indvme native, who in course of time
developed into the individual that sought the opportunity
to afl:l,inister a rebuke to an American who lived in a
country professing to be free, yet recognising the insti-
tution of human slavery.
21B7ROPOLITAN RAILWAY.

The oflo ial inspection of this railway took place on:
Monday last. Colonel Yolland, the Government inspec-
tor, had made a most careful examination of the stations,
the points, and the mode of woiking the signals, and we
hoped to have been able to announce a date on which
the lino would be opened for traffic. We regret, how-
ever, to say that the opening of the railway appears to
be as uncertain as at any period since the Ist of Octo-
ber--the day on which the directors assured their too
c, -
confidin shareholders that would be open to the pub-
lic. Col. Yolland, acting undef a sense of the great respon-
sibility imposed upon., him, has deolined to grant the
usual certificate; and untj',. this is obtained, passengers
cannot be conveyed upon he railway. The reason for
withholding the certiacate s, we are infornied, the im-
perfection of the mode of working the signals. This is
a point upon-which- considerable -negotiation has taken
place for several weeks, and has been repeatedly put
forward as the ground of the numerous postponements
that have taken plate. The signals are arranged to be
worked from each end of the tunnel. Considering, how-
ever, the number of trains which will be run, and the
short intervals between the times of starting them, and
that there will never he fewer than three trains rn the
tunnel at one time during the whole day, it is obvious
that great care is required in all matters relating
to signals. The mode of working these signals as
arranBed by Mr. Fowler, the engineer, is certainly a
very ingenious one; but, if we are correctly in-
form: d, they require a very large amount ckf physicl
force on the part of the men intrusted with their work-
ing; and being exceedingly complicated, the communi-
cations are liable to get out of order. Colonel Yolland,
with a view to the safety of the public, has withheld his
approval_ of this, scheme, and will continue to do so
until another and more effiCient mode of working the
signals has been provided. How long it may take to
design and arrange .a new system we are unable to say.
It is now, however, perfectly clear that the lino can-
not be opened for traffic by the Ist of January, as was
anticipated, and it is not improbable that several weeks
may yet elapse before the necessary arrangements are
completed. The further delay is no doubt very annoy-
ing to the shareholders; but the safety of the travelling
public imperatively requires that every precaution
should be taken for the prevention of accidents. Pre-
parations had been made for an inaugural banquet to be
given to the shareholders to celebrate the open-
ing of the railway on New Year's-day. The
decision of the Government inspector will, of course,
lead to a postponement, sine die, of this interest.ng cele-
bration. The Great Western Railway Company have
months since made all the necessary arrangements for
working the railway ; fourteen engines, specially adapted
for working lathe tunnel without smoke or annoyance to the
passengers, have been constructed, and the eight-wh,eled
passenger carriages for the local trains had some weeks
since been completed, and only wait the comp'etion of
an efficient system of signals to commence working im-
mediately.

The house in the Rahlenberg, Vienna where Mozart
resided when he composed his Enchanted Flute, is now
being demolishcd, and a splendid restuarant is about to
be erected on its site.

The Dublin _Freeman states that Mr. Edward Levinge,
of the Irish bar, who has been appointed one of the new
Indian judges, with a salary of £5,000 per annum, and
a retiring salary 'of £1,200, is well known by his profes-
sion as the author of the Irish Justide of the Peace,' a
work of considerable merit. The learned gentleman
was called to the bar in 1848, and is much respected-
He is a younger brother of Sir Richard Levinge, Bart.,
M.P. for Westmeath, of Knockdrin Castle.
The body of students at the Berlin University, who
this se,sion number 1,925, intend next February to cele-
brate the appeal to the people in the war of freedom and
foundation of the Landwehr by a grand torchlight pro-
cession to Kreuzberg and back. It may be remembered
that when the above-mentioned appeal was made none
but cripples were. left to hear the lectures at the uriver-
sity. The students of that period took up arm 3 to a
man in defence of their country.

AGRICULTURAL P.ROSPECTS.
Tlb

Ire has been a continuance of mild open weather
throtighout this week. Wi4-3, the exception of the wind
being around to the north-north-east during a few
houra on Wednesday, it has prevailed from the south-
west for about five days. During the remaining two
there blew a heavy gale from the north-west, ap-
proaching to a hurneane during Thursday and Friday
nights.
The humid state of the weather had been much,
against the condition of wheat thrashed for several
days, but the more recent piercing winds may have
been very serviceable' and if they continue a short
time longr, there will be an improvement in the sample.
This Most probably will lead to a better demand, as more
disposition is evinced to hold stock now -113. t prices are
so moderat-. There has been a slight increase in ths
deliveries of the week, these amounting to 85,329 qrs.
at 465. 10d., whilst the quantity returned during the
corresponding week of last ye,r was 98,763 qrs. at
60s. Bd., showim; a difference in price of 13s. 10d per
qr., and of 13,434 qrs. on quantity. The immense im-
ports appear to be the main cause: those in the month
of November amounted to 1,039,340 qrs. ; for December
they may not, be quite r o large, and after that period no
doubt a conriderable falling off will take place, until
spring shipments begin. Up to then our farmers may
have a better opening for their produce.
Barley still aids the agriculturists more than any
other crop on the farm, at least as far as grain is con-
cerned. Large as the deliveries were last week, they
have been larg r, amounting to 127,314 quarters at
345. 9d., against 113,628 quart.rs at 365., 3d. the corre-
sponding week of last year. Norfolk returned 31,551
qrs., Suffolk 14,556' qrs., Lincolnshire 11,130 qrs.,
and Yorkshire 7,863 qrs. Toe yield has no doubt been
a heavy one, but these large detiveries we fancy cannot
be kept up much longer, and when we get well into
next month, we look for a steady falling off, up to the
close of the malting season. Some, however, think
that the superabundance of the growth will enable the
farmers to keep up their supplies. Be this as it may,
maltsters cannot do wrong in securing as much of fine
qualities as they can obV n, for we think these have
been brought out more fre( y than others. In compari-
son to the portion of such ,vhich has been grown this
season, one-third would be the extreme, and perhaps
only one-fourth of the entire crop would be all that was
produced; the remainder from good useful malting
quality, with very little only adapted for grinding.
Could the malt duty be got off, our farmers would .do
well with this grain, not having the competition of the
whole world to contend with, as little is grown in the
American states, and not much of a superior quality from
any part of the north of Europe. The most at prest4
comes; from France.—Dee. 20.

articles.title: YELVERTOY CASE.
articles.text:
THE YELVERTOY CASE.

COURT OF SEBSION.-FIRST DIVISION.
_ _ _

On Friday theintense interest manifested during the
whole of this extraordinary trial seemed to have ;ncreased
to the highest pitch, in consequence of its having become
generally known that their lord,hips would deliver their
decision in this• case on that day. Crowds of persons
outside the Parliament House who had not been success-
ful in obtaining admission were trying every means in
their power to gain entrance, but the dimensions of the
court, even had a,tithe of those anxious to be present
been admitted, would have been found totally inadequate
for their accommodation. So great was the pressure that
even those engaged in the case had a difficulty in reach-
ing their proper places.
The Judges were the Lord President, Lord Curriehill,
and Lord Deas.
It will be recollected that the case was, in the mouth.
of July last, before Lord Ardmillan, who, at the conclu-
sion of the arguments, pronounced his decision adverse
to the Hon. Mrs. Yelveiton (nee Longworth). The
learned judge was of opinion that no marriage had been
established by the pursuer (Mrs. Yelvertcm) according
to any of the irregular modes recognised by the law. of
Scotland.

The decision wag. appealed against, and was carried
by reclaiming petition before the First Division of the
Court of Session, and was argued at length during the
early part °nest month.
The counsel for the purstier (Mrs. Yelverton) were
the Lord Advocate and the Solicitor-General (since
raised to the bench) ; Major Yelverton being repre-
sented by Mr. Gordon, Mr. Young (now Solicitor-
General), and Mr. Millar.
The statement of the pursuer on that occasion was
that:the engagement to marry was first entered into at
Galata, in September, 1855; was renewed in the Crimea
in March, 1856; again renewed in the spring of 1857,
that the parties were married at Rosstrevor in August,
1857, and again carne to Scetlandiwhere they lived with
each her for some time as husband and "wife. It was
not till after the Irish ceremony that intercourse took
place, and the pursuer consented that the marriage
should be kept a secret from the defender's family,
owing to his pecuniary relations with his unel-, who
had lent him money, and who wished him not to marry.
The marriage, however, was acknowledged by the
defender to the pursuer's friends, who consented• to keep
it secret, and the parties travelled together in the High-
lands and elsewhere as husband and wife.
The defender, on the other hand, said there never was
any engagement, promise, or contemplation of marriage
on his part, that he entered into the Irish marriage as a
device to satisfy the lady' conscience, and that he had
had intercourse with her during the first Edinburgh visit
and during the three weeks that elapsed aftertheir meet-
ing at Waterford and marriage at Rosstrevor, whenthey
lived in different hotels together.
In the form in which the case was at present raised
the questions the Court wq asked to decide were two—
first, whether there was an interchange of mutual consent
to marry proved by written declarations or verbal
acknowledgments of the defender; and, second, whether
there was a promise of marriage followed by intercourse
in faith of that promise. The pursuer maintained the
affirmative ; the a6felider the negative of these proposi-
tions.

The marriage ceremony at Rosstrevor, in Ireland, was
not insisted upon by the pursuer as a specific ground in
the present case there being in evidence the opinions of
Irish constitutional lawyers to the effect that that cere-
mony did not constitute marriage, but the point was
expressly kept open in order to be raised anew should
the question come before the House of Lords, who,
being versed in Irish as ell as Scotch law, would of
course set aside legal opinions as evidence, and form
their own judgment on the cause. Refeitnce, however,
was made- by the pursuer to the Irish ceremony, as
throwing light both on the alleged interchange of con-
sent and the alleged promise to marry.
The excitement in court at the moment the judges
took their seats on the bench was intense, in con-
sequence of it having been reported that two of them
were in favour of reversing the decision of the Lord
Ordinary.
Lords Peas and Curriehill first addressed the Court,
and were of opinion that the marriage was valid, and
that the decision of Lord Ardmillan ought to be re-
versed.

The Lord President, after an elaborate speech, ex-
pressed his opinion that the decision of Lord Ardmillan
ought not to be reversed.
Majority in favour of the validity of the Scotch mar-
riage—One.
Immediately the decision in favour of Mr's. Yelverton
was pronounced, the spectators in court gave vent to
their feelings by loud and continuous cheering, which
all the authority of the court was for some time unable
to suppress. On the result of the trial becoming known
outside the court, the same demor tions of approval
took place.

RAILWAY Co=Brox "mart lamis.—On the 19th, an
accident occurred on the North Eastern Railway,
between the Bramhopetunnel and the Horsforth sta-
tion, from a ballast train running into the tail end of
a goods train which was at-that time standing near to
the Moseley siding. The engine of the ballast train
came into collision with the other train with such
velocity that the guard's van and one of the trucks
were smashscl, the engine itself being thrown off the
up, and projecting across tho down line. The guard cf.
the goods train, observing his danger, jumped out of
the van,and thus escaped- injury, and the driver and
fireman of the ballast train were equally fortunate.
The line was completely-blooked-uprand--a number-of-
men having been obtained, under the direction of Mr.
DOnaldson and Mr. Johnson; the traffic and.looomotive
superintendents, the broken fragments of the waggons-
were cleared as rapidly asi possible, but the line. was
not in proper working order until about midnight.
The traffic during the evening, between Arthington
and Hoz sforth, was worked by pilot engines, and the
passengers each way had to change trains at the place
where the eollision occurred.

, PARIS Permanent Umversal Exhi-
. TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success its stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast nninber of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establishment there of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhi• ited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is opea, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, with liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties, or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff
The whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
oaurse of construction) will be opened early in the sum
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has alleady been taken up.
A dmission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a Gener.l Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be esta-
blished in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the same nature from different countries,
being placed in juxta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
will be charged, the space being taken for six years.
The first rate (£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
Tne second rate (El per square metre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisement.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.
Drawings of the Building can be seen at the principal
Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition; and at the Offices of Messrs. J.
STUDDY LEIGH &CG., 27. Leadenhall-street, London.

THE Rev. G. C. (" Boatswain ")
.1 SMITH. now in his 81st year, has become greatly
enfeebled, and is in straightened circumstances. He
needs an attendant, but cannot pay one. Mr. Smith has
been labouring as a Christian Minister about fifty-eight
years. It will be remembered that he commenced
Destitute Sailors' Asylums and the first Sailors' Home,
bona whence sprang all the other Srilors' Homes. He
gave grei blows to the crimping system, revived open-
air preaching, and commenced and carried on for many
years all the efforts for the religious instruction of
sailors. Besides which he originated the first Temper-
ance Society in Pritain. and established the London
Mission (1814) and Sailors' Orphan and Magdalen
Homes, and commenced the efforts for the religious
instruction of soldiers. For all this Mr. Smith has
passed unrewarded by his countrymen. Now that he is
aged and poor, a friend pleads that public gratitude and
sympathy might be manifested.
